profil.repartition: Darjeeling district (West Bengal, India): tributaries of the Teesta, Brahmaputra basin
profil.presentation:
Described in 1921 by the Indian ichthyologist Sunder Lal Hora, *Aborichthys elongatus* owes its genus name to the Abor Hills of Arunachal Pradesh and its species name to its very elongated, compressed body, crossed by thin dark bars. It belongs to the family Nemacheilidae.

The type series came from “the Riang river, at 2,000 feet”, a river that cannot be found on today's maps. Most fish sold under this name are collected lower down, in Jalpaiguri district, and may belong to other species.
profil.habitat:
It lives in the streams and small rivers that come down from the Siwalik Hills in Darjeeling district (Relli, Chel, Ghish), tributaries of the Teesta and therefore of the Brahmaputra.

It occupies shallow, fast, sloping stretches over rock and pebble beds, where it slips into the gaps. There are no aquatic plants, but a rich biofilm covers the stones. The water is cool (15 to 21 °C) and highly oxygenated.
profil.comportement:
Not really aggressive, it is still poorly suited to a community aquarium because it needs cool, flowing water. It lives alongside danios, rasboras, *Garra*, hillstream gobies and fast-water catfish; slow or long-finned fish should be avoided.

It feeds on insect larvae, worms and small crustaceans: live or frozen prey on top of dry food. Its breeding in the aquarium is not documented.

profil.repartition: Amazon and Orinoco basins, Paraguay-Paraná system
profil.presentation: The genus *Abramites* owes its name to its superficial resemblance to the European bream, and *hypselonotus* means “high-backed”. It is a deep-bodied anostomid with a ventral keel peculiar to the genus, which has only one other species, *A. eques*, in Colombia.
profil.habitat: A generalist, it lives in the main channels with murky, flowing water as well as in small tributaries and oxbows, and moves into flooded areas during the annual floods.
profil.comportement: Keep it in a group in a large aquarium, with sturdy cichlids, characins and catfish: it may nip long fins. Omnivorous, it searches the bottom for larvae, debris and algae; in the aquarium it accepts prepared foods, to be topped up with frozen prey and plant matter.

profil.repartition: Amazon, Xingu and Tocantins basins (Brazil)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1951 by William Gosline, the sheep pacu is named after the English ichthyologist John Roxborough Norman (1898–1944). It is a Serrasalmidae, the family of pacus and piranhas, not a Characidae: it is also sold as “tiger pacu” for its dark vertical bars.

The genus has three species; *A. normani* differs from *A. setnai*, of the Rio Jari, by a deeper body and stiff gill rakers. It reaches nearly 20 cm.
profil.habitat:
It occurs in the Amazon, Xingu and Tocantins basins in Brazil. In the Rio Sono, a tributary of the Tocantins, it lives in crystal-clear water that crosses a savanna with no riverside forest, alongside other characiforms, current-loving cichlids and loricariids.

The water is tropical (22 to 28 °C), soft to moderately hard and slightly acidic.
profil.comportement:
Often described as a fruit or plant eater, it also feeds partly on the scales of other fish: in the aquarium it tends to tear scales off larger species while ignoring small ones. It is therefore not recommended for a standard community aquarium.

It can live in a group if there is enough space (a tank of at least 1.5 m). It readily accepts dry and frozen sinking foods. Its captive breeding is not documented; large males have a lobe on the anal fin.

profil.repartition: Amazon basin (Peru, Colombia, Bolivia, Brazil)
profil.presentation: This armoured catfish of the family Doradidae bears small pale spots or bars that vary greatly from one individual to another. Its species name refers to the forehead “combed” with small spines. Common in the trade, hardy and long-lived, it suits beginners as well as experienced fishkeepers.
profil.habitat: It prefers slow or still water rich in submerged or floating cover, where it hides by day, such as the whitewater tributaries of the Rio Pacaya in Peru, flooded for most of the year.
profil.comportement: Peaceful, but an adult can swallow very small fish: it fits into a medium to large Amazonian tank with peaceful characins, cichlids and catfish. Gregarious, it behaves more naturally in a group of four or more. Omnivorous, it feeds mostly at night on sinking foods and frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Tanganyika (mainly its southwestern part)
profil.presentation: Its genus name refers to its very high back profile, and *calvus* (“bald”) to a scaleless patch between the eyes. Its extremely flattened body lets it slip into rock crevices to hunt eggs, fry and small fish there, and its thick scales protect it.
profil.habitat: It lives only in the rocky areas of the shores and islands of Lake Tanganyika, where it patrols a few dozen centimetres from the rocks.
profil.comportement: Territorial but peaceful towards fish too large for its mouth, it is rather shy: keep it with calm Tanganyikans (*Julidochromis*, *Neolamprologus*, *Cyprichromis*, Synodontis) and never with mbuna. In pairs or colonies. It prefers live or frozen prey and often refuses dry food.

profil.repartition: Central America: Pacific and Atlantic slopes of Guatemala, El Salvador and Honduras; introduced elsewhere
profil.presentation: The “convict cichlid”, also called zebra cichlid, is one of the most widespread fish in the hobby, long sold under the names *Cryptoheros* or *Cichlasoma nigrofasciatus*. Its genus name comes from Lake Amatitlán in Guatemala, and *nigrofasciata* describes its black bands.
profil.habitat: It lives in very varied habitats, from streams and flowing rivers to ponds and lakes, always close to cover: rock crevices, roots or debris.
profil.comportement: Hardy and easy to breed, it is nevertheless not a community fish: aggressive and territorial, it turns violent when breeding and attacks much larger fish. Keep it as a pair on its own, or in a very large tank with robust Central American cichlids. It accepts all foods.

profil.repartition: Mae Klong basin (western Thailand) and Ataran basin (Myanmar)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1959 by Wolfgang Klausewitz from aquarium fish imported into Germany from “northern Thailand”, the dwarf chain loach does not exceed 6 cm. Its name is said to honour Aree Sidthimunk, a researcher at the Thai fisheries department; *Ambastaia* takes up the ancient name of the Mekong in Ptolemy.

It is listed as endangered by the IUCN. Long impossible to find, it is now produced by commercial farms using hormones. It belongs to the family Botiidae.
profil.habitat:
Old records from Laos, Cambodia or the Yom actually concerned *A. nigrolineata*, a related species. *A. sidthimunki* appears to be restricted to the Mae Klong basin in western Thailand and the Ataran basin in Myanmar.

In the Ataran it lives in forested headwater streams that are fairly slow, clear and well oxygenated, over sand and rock with plenty of wood and dead leaves.
profil.comportement:
Active by day, it often swims in groups a little above the bottom. Gregarious, it forms hierarchies and must live in a group of at least 6, ideally 10; alone it becomes shy or aggressive. Some aquarists report attacks on slow or long-finned fish.

Mostly carnivorous, it feeds on aquatic invertebrates. Its breeding by hobbyists remains practically unknown. Females are rounder; males have a slightly longer snout and fleshy lips.

profil.repartition: Mexico: Río Ameca basin and Sayula valley (Jalisco)
profil.presentation: The only species of its genus, this livebearing Goodeidae owes its name to the upper Río Ameca basin, and *splendens* to its brilliant colours. Listed as critically endangered, it survives in only a few localities, but strong captive populations exist among aquarists.
profil.habitat: It lives in clear springs where aquatic plants thrive.
profil.comportement: Poorly suited to a community tank: males can be aggressive and the species is very competitive at feeding time. A species tank, or sturdy tankmates of the same size, suits it better. A voracious omnivore, it eats a lot of algae in the wild: its diet must include plant matter. Efficient filtration is essential.

profil.repartition: South and Southeast Asia, from India and Pakistan to southern China and Indonesia; introduced in the Philippines, Papua New Guinea and Pacific islands
profil.presentation: The climbing perch is famous for its ability to survive out of water and to move over land from one pool to another. It must breathe air and makes audible sounds. Farmed for food in several countries, it is uncommon in the hobby despite its interest.
profil.habitat: It lives in almost every freshwater habitat in its range: marshes, lakes, canals, ponds, rice fields, puddles, oxbows and rivers, often heavily vegetated, in murky still water. It tolerates extreme conditions and buries itself in mud during the dry season.
profil.comportement: Its adult size and predatory instinct make it unsuitable for a community tank: much smaller fish are eaten, but sturdy cyprinids, catfish, cichlids and spiny eels of a suitable size do well in a large tank. Its aggression towards its own kind varies between reports. Mostly predatory: worms, shellfish, frozen prey and pellets.

profil.repartition: Middle and lower Rio Negro, Amazonas (Brazil); other Amazonian basins are mentioned
profil.presentation:
Described in 1854 by the Austrian ichthyologist Rudolf Kner from fish caught near Manaus, *Ancistrus dolichopterus* (“long-finned”) differs from all other *Ancistrus* by its 9 soft rays in the dorsal fin. In the hobby it corresponds to the “starlight” pleco (L183), black dotted with white with white-edged fins.

The genus has more than 60 species, recognisable by the spines on their cheeks and, in males, by the fleshy tentacles on the snout. The name was long wrongly applied to the common aquarium bristlenose, hence much confusion over its range.
profil.habitat:
According to Seriously Fish, the species is endemic to the middle and lower Rio Negro in Amazonas state; other sources list it in other Amazonian basins and in Guyana, probably because of misidentifications.

It lives in flowing blackwater streams and tributaries, acidic and very soft, among submerged wood and rocks.
profil.comportement:
Fairly peaceful towards other species, it is territorial towards its own kind and similarly shaped fish. It spends the day hidden in cavities and wood.

Omnivorous, it enjoys small invertebrates and sinking foods as well as plant matter. It is a cave spawner: the male guards and fans the eggs, then the fry. Adult males bear tentacles on the head and odontodes (small skin teeth) on the pectoral fins and gill cover.

profil.repartition: Trinidad and Tobago and northern Venezuela; introduced elsewhere
profil.presentation: The blue acara, long placed in the genus *Aequidens*, is a classic beginner's cichlid. Its genus name recalls the Andes and the Tupi word *acará* for cichlids; *pulcher* means “pretty”. Many fish in the trade, from long-established farms, are less colourful than wild ones, or even hybrids.
profil.habitat: Very adaptable, it lives in murky, still water as well as in clear, flowing streams and rivers.
profil.comportement: Fairly peaceful for its size, it lives with fish too big to be swallowed: medium characins, Corydoras, loricariids and, in a large tank, other calm cichlids. The pair guards eggs and larvae. Mostly carnivorous, it enjoys frozen prey and accepts dry food; it needs well-kept water.

profil.repartition: Coastal rivers of Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia
profil.presentation: The only species of its genus, this small West African cichlid takes its name from a peculiarity of its lateral line system. Young fish look dull in the shop, but a settled adult is very colourful: it is one of the best choices for discovering dwarf cichlids.
profil.habitat: It lives in shaded forest streams, whose water is often the colour of tea, and in shallow, muddy savanna waters that approach 30 °C in the dry season; when disturbed, it can bury itself in the mud.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful for a cichlid, it only becomes territorial when spawning. Shy, it goes well with small characins, other African dwarf cichlids, Corydoras and small anabantoids, but not with boisterous species. Both parents care for the eggs, laid on an exposed surface. It accepts all foods.

profil.repartition: Amazon and Orinoco basins (Peru, Brazil, Venezuela, the Guianas)
profil.presentation: The name *Anostomus* (“mouth upwards”) describes its upturned mouth. This fish, striped with black and gold bands, belongs to the Anostomidae; the genus has only two species well known in the hobby, *A. anostomus* and *A. ternetzi*.
profil.habitat: It lives along the rocky banks of fast rivers, where it grazes the algae and small invertebrates covering the rocks.
profil.comportement: Found in large shoals in the wild, it is quarrelsome with its own kind when they are few: keep a single fish in a community tank of medium to large fish, or a group of six or more in a large aquarium. An omnivorous grazer, it needs frozen prey and plenty of plant matter, along with a good current.

profil.repartition: Paraná basin (Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina)
profil.presentation: The bloodfin tetra, described from Asunción in Paraguay, is a hardy, long-lived characin: individuals over ten years old are known in aquariums. Adult males bear small hooks on the anal fin.
profil.habitat: It frequents streams, rivers and tributaries, especially areas shaded by floating or overhanging vegetation.
profil.comportement: Fairly peaceful, it may nip the fins of slow or long-finned fish. A shoaling fish, it should be kept in a group of at least six, with other characins, Corydoras and small loricariids. It swims in the middle and upper layers and accepts all foods. A good beginner's tetra, it tolerates fairly cool water.

profil.repartition: Coasts of Gabon and the Congo (Cape Lopez area), up to Cameroon and Cabinda (Angola)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1921 by the German aquarist Arthur Rachow, the Cape Lopez killi takes its common name from its type locality, Cape Lopez, near the mouth of the Ogooué in Gabon; *australe* (“southern”) recalls that it was then the southernmost *Aphyosemion* known.

One of the first killis to become popular, it remains ideal for beginners: beautiful and easy to breed, it often lives more than three years. Orange, gold, chocolate or albino aquarium strains exist, alongside wild populations labelled by place and year of collection.
profil.habitat:
It lives in the coastal lowlands of Gabon and the Congo, and is also reported from Cameroon and Cabinda (Angola).

It inhabits permanent waters, marshes and small forest streams, in soft, slightly acidic water; it is not an annual killi.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful and shy, it can live in a community aquarium if its companions are carefully chosen: small characins, rasboras, dwarf cichlids, corydoras, small loricariids. The males, with lyre-shaped fins edged in white and orange, display without doing much harm.

It prefers small live or frozen prey, but aquarium-bred fish also accept flakes. It “hangs” its eggs among fine-leaved plants or a spawning mop, even in a small tank.

profil.repartition: Middle Mungo basin, western Cameroon
profil.presentation:
Described in 1971 by the Danish killifish specialist Jørgen Scheel, *Aphyosemion celiae* is named after Celia Epie of Mambanda (western Cameroon), the eldest daughter of a rubber plantation manager who helped collect the fish.

The blue-green male is decorated with red spots and lines and a tail edged in yellow and red. It is a non-annual killi, easy to keep.
profil.habitat:
It is endemic to the middle Mungo basin in western Cameroon.

It lives in springs, streams, marshes and pools in rainforest and secondary savanna, in very soft, slightly acidic to neutral water between 22 and 26 °C.
profil.comportement:
Males are fairly lively with each other; preferably keep one male with two females, in a small planted tank with calm companions.

A micro-predator, it prefers small live or frozen prey. It lays its eggs among fine-leaved plants or a spawning mop; incubation takes place in water, as in other non-annual killis.

profil.repartition: Southern Equatorial Guinea and northwestern Gabon (Mitémele, Komo and lower Ogooué basins)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1911 by George Albert Boulenger, *Aphyosemion striatum* (“striped”) is a small African killi whose blue-green male bears lengthwise red streaks on the flanks and caudal peduncle. *Aphyosemion* means “small fish with a banner”, for the lyre-shaped tail of the males of many species in the genus.

It is a non-annual killi, easy, attractive and fairly long-lived, often recommended for beginners. Note: the name “paradise fish” usually refers to another species, *Macropodus opercularis*.
profil.habitat:
It lives in the Mitémele basin in southern Equatorial Guinea, and in the Mbei, Komo, Abanga and lower Ogooué basins in northwestern Gabon.

It frequents permanent streams, pools and marshes of lowland coastal rainforest, in soft, slightly acidic to neutral water that is rather cool for the tropics (21 to 25 °C).
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful and fairly shy, it can live in a community aquarium with calm, not too large companions: small tetras, cyprinids, dwarf cichlids, corydoras. The males display and spar with each other without much harm.

It feeds on small aquatic and terrestrial invertebrates; live or frozen prey are preferred. It spawns in fine-leaved plants or a spawning mop, often in a trio (one male, two females).

profil.repartition: Amazon basin, from Peru to Brazil (Amazon–Solimões river as far as the Capim basin)
profil.presentation: One of the best-known Apistogramma, described in 1875 and named after the naturalist Louis Agassiz. The genus, one of the richest among South American cichlids, has about 70 described species; many colourful varieties of *A. agassizii* have been bred for the hobby.
profil.habitat: It lives in slow tributaries, oxbows and creeks where leaf litter piles up, in black, white or clear water depending on place and season.
profil.comportement: Aquarium-bred fish suit a community tank; wild ones are kept alone or with small midwater fish such as *Nannostomus*, without other Apistogramma. Keep one male with several females; the female lays her eggs on the ceiling of a cave and cares for eggs and larvae alone. Mostly carnivorous, it needs live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Paraguay and lower Paraná basins (southern Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina)
profil.presentation: Described in 1906 by Regan, this small Apistogramma from southern South America is one of the easiest in the genus. Several coloured forms have been bred for the hobby.
profil.habitat: It inhabits the creeks and small tributaries of the Paraguay and lower Paraná basins, down to the Uruguay system.
profil.comportement: Territorial like all dwarf cichlids, it is kept as a pair, with small, peaceful midwater fish and no other Apistogramma. The female lays her eggs on the ceiling of a cave and guards them. Mostly carnivorous, it needs live or frozen prey; it likes water a little cooler than most Apistogramma.

profil.repartition: Upper Amazon basin: Ucayali and Amazon in Peru, Solimões in Brazil, as far as Colombia
profil.presentation:
Described in 1951 by Jan Hoedeman, the cockatoo cichlid owes its name to the first rays of its dorsal fin, very elongated in the male like a cockatoo's crest. Males reach 7.5 cm, females about 5 cm.

The type locality was first wrongly given as Suriname, before being corrected by Sven Kullander. Populations differ in colour according to their origin, and many aquarium forms exist (“double red”, “orange flag”).
profil.habitat:
It is widespread in much of the upper Amazon basin, from the Ucayali and Amazon in Peru to the Solimões in Brazil.

It lives in slow tributaries, oxbows and creeks where dead leaves pile up, in black, white or clear water depending on place and season.
profil.comportement:
Aquarium-bred fish suit a well-planned community aquarium; wild ones do better alone or with small, peaceful shoaling fish such as pencilfish. It is best not mixed with other *Apistogramma*.

Mainly carnivorous, it hunts small invertebrates on the bottom. The female lays her eggs on the ceiling of a cave, then cares for the eggs and fry alone; in a small tank she can become very aggressive towards the male, who must then be removed. A male can live with several females, each with her own territory.

profil.repartition: Orinoco basin: Río Vichada and middle Río Meta (Colombia), middle Orinoco (Venezuela)
profil.presentation: Described in 1979 by Kullander, this Apistogramma carries the code A110 in the numbering system of the magazine DATZ; neighbouring populations, perhaps of the same species, are coded A111 to A115.
profil.habitat: It lives in small tributaries and calm waters of the Orinoco basin.
profil.comportement: Unlike many Apistogramma, it does not form a harem: both parents stay together and raise the young. Keep it as a pair, with small midwater fish such as *Nannostomus* and no other Apistogramma. Mostly carnivorous, it needs live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Colombia: upper Río Meta basin (ríos Guaytiquía and Metica), Orinoco system
profil.presentation: Described by Kullander in 1979, this Apistogramma carries the code A120 in the DATZ system; a neighbouring population is coded A122 and the ornamental “red” form A121.
profil.habitat: It is only known from the basins of the ríos Guaytiquía and Metica, in the upper Río Meta, a tributary of the Orinoco in Colombia.
profil.comportement: It is kept with one male for several females; the female lays her eggs on the ceiling of a cave and cares for eggs and larvae alone. Aquarium-bred fish do well in a peaceful community tank, wild ones rather alone or with small midwater fish, without other Apistogramma. Mostly carnivorous, it needs live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Guaporé basin (southern Amazonia), Paraguay and middle Paraná basins (Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina)
profil.presentation: Its species name refers to its three dark bands. Described from Paraguay in 1903, it carries the codes A204 to A206 in the DATZ system depending on the population; the Rio Guaporé population comes in red and blue forms that live together in the wild.
profil.habitat: It lives in slow creeks, tributaries and small rivers, especially where leaf litter piles up.
profil.comportement: Unlike many Apistogramma, both parents care for the eggs, laid on the ceiling of a cave, and for the larvae: keep it as a pair. It suits peaceful tanks, with small midwater fish and no other Apistogramma. Mostly carnivorous, it needs live or frozen prey and water free of organic waste.

profil.repartition: Peninsular India and northern Sri Lanka
profil.presentation:
Described in 1846 by Achille Valenciennes from fish caught at Bombay (Mumbai), the striped panchax is a large surface-dwelling killi that reaches 10 cm. The greenish males are dotted with golden scales and bear thin dark bars on the rear of the body.

The golden “golden wonder” form, very widespread in the hobby, was bred in captivity and does not exist in the wild. In its home country the species is used to control mosquito larvae.
profil.habitat:
It is widely distributed across peninsular India and northern Sri Lanka; it has been introduced in Singapore and Hong Kong.

It occupies very varied habitats: mountain streams and lakes, lowland wells, rice fields, marshes and even the brackish water of estuaries. Unlike many killis, it lives in permanent waters and is not annual; it stays mostly under floating or overhanging vegetation.
profil.comportement:
A surface predator, it hunts insects and small fish: keep it with peaceful species too large to be swallowed (calm cichlids, large tetras, corydoras, loricariids). It can be aggressive towards its own kind, but a group works in a large enough tank.

An excellent jumper, it needs a well-covered aquarium. It breeds easily: the sticky eggs are laid among fine-leaved plants or a spawning mop.

profil.repartition: South and Southeast Asia: from Pakistan to India, Bangladesh, Myanmar and the Indo-Malay archipelago
profil.presentation: Described in 1822 by Hamilton, this small killi is one of the most widespread Aplocheilidae in Asia. It lives just below the surface, where it hunts insects.
profil.habitat: It occupies a wide variety of lowland habitats: ponds, ditches, canals, reservoirs and peat swamps, down to estuaries and mangrove creeks, preferably in clear water rich in rooted or floating plants. It even tolerates very salty water.
profil.comportement: A surface predator, it can swallow very small fish but stays peaceful with species of similar size. It feeds mainly on insects: live or frozen prey, topped up with floating foods.

profil.repartition: South America, from Venezuela to Paraguay: Orinoco, Amazon and Paraná basins
profil.presentation: This black knifefish with white markings swims in every direction by rippling its long ventral fin. It gives off weak electric discharges and senses its surroundings through electroreceptors spread over its whole body. Often sold at 10 cm, it can grow large.
profil.habitat: It lives in fast-flowing streams and rivers, most often over sand, and moves into flooded forest during the rainy season. It is nocturnal.
profil.comportement: Peaceful to the point of shyness, it nonetheless eats small fish as it grows: its companions must exceed about fifteen centimetres (Geophagus, Satanoperca, angelfish, discus). A predator of insects and worms, it needs live or frozen prey. The adult requires a very large aquarium, strong filtration and spotless water.

profil.repartition: Nigeria: Ogun and lower Niger basins
profil.presentation: The only species of its genus, this African tetra stands out for its large scales, hence its names “big-scale tetra” or “Niger tetra”. Very popular in the hobby, it is nevertheless listed as endangered: known from fewer than ten localities, it suffers from deforestation and pollution.
profil.habitat: It lives in the streams and rivers of southwestern Nigeria.
profil.comportement: Peaceful but very active, it disturbs shy species. Keep it in a group of at least ten, with other African tetras, small Synodontis and robust dwarf cichlids such as *Pelvicachromis pulcher*. It accepts all foods, especially small live or frozen prey. Hardy once settled, it lives several years.

profil.repartition: Western Amazon and Orinoco basins; introduced elsewhere (Singapore, United States)
profil.presentation: The oscar, described by Agassiz in 1831, owes its species name to the orange-ringed black eyespot on its tail fin. Very popular, it exists in many aquarium forms (red oscar, tiger, long-finned). It lives ten to twenty years and is also a valued food fish in South America.
profil.habitat: It mainly frequents shallow, slow or still waters in forested areas, preferably silt-laden whitewater, near submerged roots or bank vegetation.
profil.comportement: Not especially aggressive for its size, it is a predator that swallows any fish that fits in its mouth. Only a very large aquarium lets you keep it with characins, anostomids, other cichlids and large catfish. Omnivorous, it prefers meaty foods and accepts pellets and plant matter.

profil.repartition: Caves of the Sierra de El Abra and neighbouring ranges, San Luis Potosí and Tamaulipas (Mexico)
profil.presentation:
The blind cave tetra is the cave form of *Astyanax mexicanus*, a surface tetra that colonised caves in northeastern Mexico. Discovered in 1936 during an expedition to the state of San Luis Potosí, it was described the same year by Carl Hubbs and William Innes and named after C. Basil Jordan, a Dallas fish dealer who received most of the specimens. FishBase keeps it as a separate species, but many researchers consider it a population of *A. mexicanus*.

It is a major model in evolutionary biology: in the embryo the eyes start to form and then degenerate, and several cave populations have lost eyes and pigment independently. It is listed as endangered by the IUCN.
profil.habitat:
The blind form lives only in caves and underground passages of northeastern Mexico, in total darkness, where the water is stable and poor in food. Its surface form, on the other hand, is very widespread, from southern Texas and New Mexico to Guatemala, in rivers, ponds and lakes.

The cave water is rather hard and neutral to slightly alkaline, around 20 to 25 °C.
profil.comportement:
Hardy and peaceful, it finds its food through its lateral line and highly developed taste buds. While searching for food it may bump into or nibble its neighbours, without real aggression; very shy or slow companions are best avoided.

It does not form a true shoal but does better in a group of at least 4. It breeds easily in the aquarium, with a grid on the bottom to protect the eggs from the adults. Females are larger and rounder; the male's anal fin has a slightly curved edge.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Malawi: west coast (Usisya, Nkhomo reef, Benga, Maleri islands, Chipoka)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1985 by Manfred Meyer and Rüdiger Riehl, *Aulonocara baenschi* is one of the “peacocks” of Lake Malawi: the adult male sports a bright yellow coat with blue sheens on the head. It is also sold as “yellow peacock” or “Nkhomo-benga”.

Like all *Aulonocara*, it has large sensory pores on the head that let it detect the vibrations of invertebrates hidden in the sand. It is listed as critically endangered by the IUCN, as its range is limited to a few sites on the west coast of the lake.
profil.habitat:
It is endemic to Lake Malawi, where it is known from Usisya, Nkhomo reef, Benga, the Maleri islands and Chipoka, on the western shore.

It lives in intermediate zones, where rocky shores give way to sandy bottoms scattered with rocks, usually between 4 and 6 m deep, sometimes down to 16 m. The water is warm, hard and alkaline.
profil.comportement:
Fairly peaceful, it becomes aggressive towards fish of similar colour, especially other yellow males. Keep a single male with 4 to 6 females, and no other *Aulonocara*, with which it readily hybridises; most mbuna are too boisterous.

It feeds by sifting sand or hunting small invertebrates that it detects by touch. A mouthbrooder, the female keeps the eggs and fry in her mouth.

profil.repartition: Lake Malawi: western and eastern shores (Malawi, Tanzania)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1995 by the Dutch cichlid specialist Ad Konings, *Aulonocara gertrudae* is a “peacock” of Lake Malawi. The adult male wears a blue coat with an orange-yellow throat and belly, and fins dotted with pale spots; it reaches about 11 cm without the tail.

Like other *Aulonocara*, it finds its prey in the sand thanks to the large sensory pores on its head.
profil.habitat:
It occurs on the western and eastern shores of Lake Malawi.

It lives above sandy bottoms between 3 and 30 m deep, most often below 15 m. The water is warm, hard and alkaline.
profil.comportement:
Fairly peaceful for a Lake Malawi cichlid, it suits a tank of calm haplochromines without boisterous mbuna. Males are aggressive towards fish of similar colours: one male for several females is recommended.

It hunts small invertebrates in the sand. A mouthbrooder, the female keeps eggs and fry in her mouth. It readily hybridises with other *Aulonocara*.

profil.repartition: Endemic to southern Lake Malawi (Cape Maclear, Domwe islands, Monkey Bay…)
profil.presentation: One of the first Aulonocara to reach the hobby, sometimes called the “Freiberg's peacock” and long sold under the name *Trematocranus*. Several aquarium forms exist (“eureka”, albino…).
profil.habitat: It lives in the lake's intermediate zones, where rocky shores give way to sand scattered with rocks; the males defend small caves, whereas most Aulonocara feed above the sand.
profil.comportement: Less peaceful than its cousins, the male goes after fish of similar colours. Keep it with calm Haplochromis and quiet mbuna such as *Labidochromis caeruleus*, but not with other Aulonocara (hybrids). It searches the sand for invertebrates, which it detects through the sensory pores on its head.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Malawi, near Kande Island (Malawi)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1987 by Manfred Meyer, Rüdiger Riehl and Holger Zetzsche, *Aulonocara steveni* is a Lake Malawi “peacock” of about 9 cm without the tail; the male is blue, often tinged with orange on the flanks.

Its status is debated: some authors place it under *A. stuartgranti*, a very variable species. Many forms sold under this name are aquarium varieties or hybrids.
profil.habitat:
It is known from around Kande Island, on the Malawian coast of the lake.

It lives among sediment-covered rocks at the edge of sandy areas, in warm, hard, alkaline water.
profil.comportement:
Fairly peaceful, it behaves like other *Aulonocara*: one male for several females, no other *Aulonocara* in the tank to avoid hybrids, and calm companions rather than mbuna.

It feeds on soft-bodied invertebrates it finds in the sediment. A mouthbrooder, the female keeps eggs and fry in her mouth.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Malawi: western and eastern coasts (Malawi, Tanzania, Mozambique)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1985 by Manfred Meyer and Rüdiger Riehl, this *Aulonocara* is named after Stuart M. Grant (1937–2007), the legendary exporter of Lake Malawi fish. *Aulonocara* means “flute head” in Greek, for the highly developed system of sensory canals in its skull.

It is a very variable species: many local populations have been given trade names (“flametail” from Ngara, “Chitimba”, wrongly sold as “*A. masoni*”…), and some forms have been described as separate species, such as *A. baenschi*.
profil.habitat:
It is widely distributed along the western and eastern coasts of Lake Malawi; its type locality is Mpanga Rocks, at Chilumba.

It lives in intermediate zones, where rocky coasts give way to sand scattered with rocks. Some individuals stay hidden in caves, others form large shoals above the sand. The water is warm, hard and alkaline.
profil.comportement:
Fairly peaceful, it becomes aggressive towards fish of similar colours. Keep a single male with 4 to 6 females, without other *Aulonocara* (easy hybridisation) or boisterous mbuna.

It feeds on sand-dwelling invertebrates that it detects through the sensory pores on its head or extracts by sifting the sand. A mouthbrooder, the female keeps eggs and fry in her mouth.

profil.repartition: Lower Paraná and Río Uruguay basins (Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1912 by Charles Tate Regan, the blackfin pearlfish is a South American annual killi: the blue-black male is studded with light blue dots like a starry sky. FishBase now places it in the genus *Argolebias*, as *Argolebias nigripinnis*.

Its life cycle follows the seasons: it lives in temporary pools that dry out in summer; the adults die, while the eggs, buried in the mud, wait several months for the rains to return before hatching.
profil.habitat:
It comes from the plains of the lower Paraná and Río Uruguay basins, in Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay, under a subtropical to temperate climate.

It lives in pools and depressions that flood temporarily, filling in the southern autumn and winter. The water is cool (often 18 to 22 °C, sometimes much lower in winter), shallow and rich in vegetation.
profil.comportement:
The males display and compete for females, without serious harm in a well-planted tank; keep one male for two or three females, in a small species tank of cool water.

It feeds on worms, crustaceans and insects. It spawns in the substrate: in the aquarium, use a tray of fine peat, kept damp for 2 to 4 months before being flooded again to hatch the eggs. Its life is short, about a year.

profil.repartition: Colombia: upper Río Meta basin (Orinoco system)
profil.presentation: The ruby tetra owes its genus to Dr Herbert R. Axelrod and its species name to William Riese, who collected it together. Bright red in the wild, it often fades in the aquarium. It is sold more rarely than its cousin *A. stigmatias*.
profil.habitat: It is thought to be linked to the black waters of small forest tributaries of the upper Río Meta, but field data are lacking.
profil.comportement: Peaceful but tiny and demanding, it is kept alone or with very small characins and peaceful catfish. Gregarious without forming a tight shoal, its males contest small territories: a group of at least 8 to 10 makes it less fearful. A micro-predator, it needs small live or frozen prey and very stable water.

profil.repartition: Ganges and Mahanadi basins, Assam (India, Bangladesh, Nepal), reported from Bhutan and Pakistan
profil.presentation:
The badis (*Badis badis*) was described in 1822 by Francis Hamilton solely from notes and drawings; a neotype was designated in 2002 by Sven Kullander and Ralf Britz, in a revision that took the family Badidae from five to fifteen species.

It is nicknamed “chameleon fish” for its ability to change colour and pattern very quickly according to its mood. It grows to 7 cm; the 8 cm sometimes quoted is exaggerated.
profil.habitat:
It lives in the Ganges basin, from the Yamuna to the delta in Bangladesh, in tributaries in Nepal, in the Mahanadi basin and in Assam, near the Brahmaputra.

It prefers slow, rather murky water among submerged vegetation, often near beds of water lilies: rivers, ponds, ditches and marshes. The neotype locality is a wide, shallow, muddy-bottomed stream that crosses rice fields.
profil.comportement:
Slow and discreet, it lives rather alone and is outcompeted by livelier species. Rival males are aggressive towards each other: keep a pair or a male with several females, with caves spread around. Do not keep it with other *Badis* (risk of hybridisation), and it eats small shrimp.

A micro-predator, it often refuses dry food and needs live or frozen prey. It spawns in a cave, which the male defends while guarding the eggs and then the fry.

profil.repartition: Borneo, Sumatra and perhaps the Malay Peninsula
profil.presentation: Sold as “silver shark” or “bala shark”, this cyprinid owes its genus name to the pouch formed by its lower lip. Contrary to what is often read, it does not live in Indochina: it is limited to Borneo and Sumatra, and its populations have declined to the point that it is listed as vulnerable.
profil.habitat: An open-water fish, it lives mainly in rivers, but also in natural lakes such as those of Danau Sentarum in Borneo.
profil.comportement: Peaceful but very active, it eats very small fish and disturbs slow species. Sold young, it exceeds 30 cm: it needs a very large aquarium, in a group, with sturdy tankmates of the same size. Omnivorous, it accepts all foods.

profil.repartition: Southwestern China (including Hainan), Taiwan, Vietnam and northern Laos
profil.presentation: The gold barb is the golden aquarium form, which appeared in the 1960s, of the Chinese “green barb”. It is so widespread that many aquarists do not know that the natural form is green. Its name means “half-striped with small bands”.
profil.habitat: It prefers slow tributaries and still waters (marshes, irrigation canals) with dense vegetation, where it forms shoals near the bottom.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful and undemanding, it suits beginners. Keep it in a group of at least 8 to 10, with other peaceful cyprinids and loaches. Omnivorous, it searches the bottom for diatoms, algae and small invertebrates, and accepts all foods. It tolerates fairly cool water.

profil.repartition: Southeast Asia: Mekong and Chao Phraya basins, Malay Peninsula, Sumatra and Borneo
profil.presentation: Sold as “tinfoil barb”, like its cousin *B. altus*, this large silvery barb with red fins is almost always offered at 5 cm, with no mention of its adult size, which exceeds 30 cm.
profil.habitat: It lives in medium-sized rivers that overflow in the rainy season and then moves onto the flooded plains and forests to feed and spawn; it is also found in canals and artificial lakes.
profil.comportement: Not aggressive, it nonetheless eats small fish and disturbs calm species with its activity. A shoaling fish, it needs a huge aquarium and sturdy tankmates of the same size. Mostly herbivorous, it also eats invertebrates and accepts all foods, plants included.

profil.repartition: Rio Xingu basin (Pará, Brazil): Volta Grande and upper Rio Curuá
profil.presentation:
Long known under the code L047 or the name “mango pleco”, this loricariid was described in 2011 by Lúcia Rapp Py-Daniel, Jansen Zuanon and Renildo Ribeiro de Oliveira. Its name *chrysolomus* refers to the golden edge of its fins, on a dark body scattered with yellow dots.

*Baryancistrus* are recognised by the widened membrane that extends their dorsal fin towards the adipose fin. It reaches nearly 30 cm.
profil.habitat:
It is endemic to the Xingu basin: the Volta Grande, just upstream of the Belo Monte falls, and the upper Rio Curuá, a tributary of the Iriri.

Adults live under large slabs of rock lying on the riverbed, where fine sediment builds up; the young shelter under stones at the edges of rapids, in a weak to moderate current. The water is clear, warm (27 to 32 °C) and oxygenated.
profil.comportement:
Fairly peaceful when young, males become increasingly intolerant of their own kind and of any bottom-dweller seen as a rival. It is best kept with medium to large characins that occupy open water.

Analysis of stomach contents shows a diet mostly of algae (diatoms, *Spirogyra*) and a few invertebrates: in the aquarium, algae wafers, spirulina and biofilm on stones. Its breeding is not documented; the sexes are very hard to tell apart.

profil.repartition: Southern China and northern Vietnam
profil.presentation:
Described in 1927 by John Treadwell Nichols and Clifford Pope, *Beaufortia leveretti* is a hillstream loach with a very flattened body, almost circular seen from above, marbled in brown and beige. The genus *Beaufortia* honours the Dutch ichthyologist Lieven Ferdinand de Beaufort.

Like *Gastromyzon*, it belongs to the family Gastromyzontidae: its paired fins form a sucker that holds it to stones in the current. The IUCN lists it as data deficient.
profil.habitat:
It lives in mountain streams of southern China and northern Vietnam.

It frequents torrents with gravel and stone beds and clear, cool (18 to 24 °C), highly oxygenated water, where it grazes the biofilm on the rocks.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful, it spends its time stuck to stones and glass. It may defend a small territory against its own kind, without serious harm.

It needs an aquarium with a strong current, well oxygenated and not too warm, with smooth algae-covered stones; top up with algae wafers and small prey. It copes badly with the warm, still water of standard tropical tanks.

profil.repartition: Eastern Madagascar: lower reaches of rivers between the Ivoloina (near Toamasina) and Vatomandry
profil.presentation: Imported as early as the 1950s, this Malagasy rainbowfish is still often sold as *Bedotia geayi*, a related species from the Mananjary basin. It is listed as endangered.
profil.habitat: It lives in clear, shaded lowland streams with very soft water and a moderate current, and sometimes in acidic blackwater marshes. Where the habitat is open or murky, it has been replaced by introduced species (mosquitofish, platies).
profil.comportement: Peaceful and undemanding, it is a shoaling fish that lives with rainbowfish, barbs, characins, peaceful cichlids and catfish, but not with other Bedotia (hybrids). It mainly eats insects: live or frozen prey and good-quality dry food.

profil.repartition: Indonesia: Sebuku basin, East Kalimantan (Borneo)
profil.presentation: Its name (“white-edged”) refers to the white border of its fins. With *B. channoides*, it forms a small species group that differs from other Betta in colouring and in having 9 to 12 spines in the anal fin. Listed as endangered, it is known from a single basin in Borneo.
profil.habitat: It lives in forest streams with a moderate current, in barely 5 to 10 cm of water, among the roots of bank plants and leaf litter.
profil.comportement: Tiny and discreet, it is kept alone or with small, peaceful species; larger or lively fish intimidate it. It lives in pairs or small groups. It feeds on insects and small invertebrates: it accepts dry food once it recognises it, but needs live or frozen prey. It also breathes air at the surface.

profil.repartition: Peninsular Malaysia (Perak, Selangor, Pahang, Terengganu, Johor) and northeastern Sumatra
profil.presentation:
Described in 1884 by the French zoologist Henri Émile Sauvage, the warlike fighter (*bellica*, “warlike” in Latin) is one of the largest *Betta*, up to 10 cm. Long lost from view, it was found again in 1996; a neotype was then designated in a swamp forest in northern Selangor.

It gives its name to the “*bellica* group”, fighters with long, slender bodies, dark brown with an iridescent green spot on each scale.
profil.habitat:
It lives mainly in peat swamp forests and the blackwater streams flowing out of them, sometimes in freshwater swamp forest. Under the dense canopy very little light reaches the brown, acidic water (pH sometimes 3 to 4), which is almost free of minerals.

The bottom is covered with leaves, branches and roots. At some seasons, with no open water left, the fish survive for several weeks in the damp leaf litter. It lives alongside other fighters, such as *B. livida*, *B. tussyae* or *B. waseri*.
profil.comportement:
Discreet, it is intimidated by larger or lively fish: it does better alone or with very peaceful species. Opinions differ on keeping it in groups; most breeders recommend one pair per tank, as dominant fish can harass the others.

In the wild it feeds almost exclusively on insects, especially damselfly larvae, which it hunts at the surface; an excellent jumper, it even leaps to catch prey above the water. The male builds a bubble nest.

profil.repartition: Maliau basin, Sabah (Malaysian Borneo)
profil.presentation:
Described in 2005 by Tan Heok Hui and Peter Ng, the gladiator betta owes its name to its combative temperament. It belongs to the *Betta unimaculata* complex, fighters with long bodies and large rounded heads with a big mouth.

It differs from its relatives by a yellowish-brown body and the lack of a spine in the dorsal fin. The species is known only from a small basin in the interior of Sabah.
profil.habitat:
It lives in the Maliau basin, a remote and protected plateau in central Sabah. The type series was collected in heath forest, in very acidic water (pH 4.2 to 4.8), alongside a small barb and a catfish of the genus *Hemibagrus*.

In the wild, adults keep about a metre apart from each other, each accompanied by a few juveniles.
profil.comportement:
Aggressive and territorial towards its own kind: in captivity, individuals kept together fight relentlessly and can kill each other in a confined space. Keep it as a pair, in a spacious tank with plenty of hiding places.

Towards other species it is rather discreet and easily outcompeted by livelier fish. A mouthbrooder, the male keeps the eggs in his mouth. It hunts insects and small invertebrates.

profil.repartition: Southern Thailand, Malay Peninsula and northern Sumatra; introduced in Singapore
profil.presentation: Its Latin name means “peaceful”, yet it is bred for fighting in southern Thailand, like *B. splendens*. It has also been crossed with other Betta for the hobby, giving coloured forms that do not exist in the wild. Like other Betta, it builds a bubble nest.
profil.habitat: It lives in calm or still water, often shaded and poor in oxygen: rice fields, marshes, ditches, streams and ponds, sometimes in coastal brackish water. Releases of aquarium forms threaten the genetic purity of some populations.
profil.comportement: It does not suit a standard community tank: keep it alone or with small, very peaceful species. With enough hiding places several males can live together, but a pair remains safer. It hunts invertebrates: dry food, and above all live or frozen prey. It breathes air at the surface.

profil.repartition: Northern Borneo: Labi district (Brunei) and Baram district near Marudi (Sarawak, Malaysia)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1910 by Charles Tate Regan, the Brunei beauty is one of the most spectacular *Betta*: the red male bears a red spot on the gill cover and a white-ringed black eyespot on the dorsal fin. *Macrostoma* means “big mouth”.

It is listed as vulnerable by the IUCN because of its tiny range. Its populations differ slightly in colour by locality and are kept separately by breeders.
profil.habitat:
Endemic to Borneo, it is known only from a few localities along the Mendaram river and the Labi forest in Brunei, and from Baram district near Marudi in Sarawak.

It lives in calm, shaded pools at the top of waterfalls in rainforest or along clear, fast streams. Each pool holds a single adult, a pair or a few juveniles. The slightly brown water is almost free of minerals, with a pH of 4.4 to 5.7.
profil.comportement:
Discreet with other fish, it is easily intimidated by larger or livelier species. Among themselves, however, males fight constantly, and females squabble until they establish a hierarchy: keep it as a pair, possibly formed from a small group.

It is a mouthbrooder: the male keeps the eggs and then the fry in his mouth. It hunts insects and small invertebrates, perhaps the red shrimp that share its habitat. A tight-fitting lid is essential to keep the humid air the fry need.

profil.repartition: Gulf of Thailand coast around Bangkok (Samut Sakhon and neighbouring provinces)
profil.presentation:
Described in 2012 by Chanon Kowasupat and colleagues, this fighter is named after the coastal subdistrict of Mahachai, in Samut Sakhon province just south of Bangkok. It was long taken for a hybrid, before morphological and genetic analyses confirmed it as a species in its own right.

It is recognised by its brown to black body covered with iridescent blue-green scales and two vertical green bars on the gill cover. It has not yet been assessed by the IUCN.
profil.habitat:
It is the only *Betta* that lives exclusively in brackish water: it inhabits tidal coastal marshes associated with the nipa palm (*Nypa fruticans*), the only palm adapted to estuaries. Males build their bubble nests between the fronds or in the water held at the base of the bracts.

Measurements in Samut Sakhon province show a pH of 6.9 to 7.8 and a salinity of 1 to 10 g/l. It lives there alongside the croaking gourami, blue gourami, climbing perch and panchax.
profil.comportement:
Not suited to a community aquarium: it does better alone or with a few very peaceful species of slightly brackish water. With enough hiding places and visual barriers several males can live together, but pairs are separated for breeding.

It hunts insects and small invertebrates. The male builds a bubble nest; a tight-fitting lid keeps above the water the warm, humid air needed for the fry's labyrinth organ to develop. Populations from different localities should not be crossed.

profil.repartition: Khorat Plateau (eastern Thailand) and Mekong tributaries in central Laos
profil.presentation: The “emerald betta” owes its name to its emerald-green sheen. Like *B. splendens*, it is bred for fighting in eastern Thailand, and aquarium forms crossed with other Betta circulate in the hobby. It builds a bubble nest.
profil.habitat: It lives in the rice fields, marshes, ditches and ponds of the Khorat Plateau, in calm, shaded water that is sometimes poor in oxygen.
profil.comportement: Poorly suited to a community tank, it is kept alone or with small, very peaceful species. A pair is preferable, even though several males can live together with plenty of hiding places. It needs live or frozen prey as well as dry food, and breathes air at the surface.

profil.repartition: Central Thailand, from Chiang Rai to the Isthmus of Kra (Chao Phraya basin)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1910 by Charles Tate Regan of the British Museum, the fighting fish owes its name to a Thai tradition: males are bred to face each other in fights that are bet on. *Betta* comes from *ikan betah*, the Malay name of these fish, and *splendens* means “brilliant”.

The short-finned wild form is rare in the hobby; there are countless aquarium lines with extreme colours and fins, sometimes hybridised with related species. It is listed as vulnerable by the IUCN: habitat destruction and the release of aquarium forms threaten wild populations.
profil.habitat:
According to Seriously Fish, it naturally lives in central Thailand, from Chiang Rai to the provinces of Surat Thani and Phang Nga; records from the Mekong basin probably concern other species or introduced populations. It has become established in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Brazil, Colombia and the Dominican Republic.

It frequents still or slow water: rice fields, marshes, ditches and ponds, often shaded by vegetation and poor in oxygen. It breathes air at the surface through an accessory organ, the labyrinth.
profil.comportement:
Males are extremely aggressive towards each other and attack any long-finned fish they take for a rival: one male per tank, avoiding veil-finned companions. Females are kept apart outside breeding.

It feeds on zooplankton and insect larvae, mosquitoes in particular. The male builds a bubble nest at the surface, places the eggs in it after spawning and watches over them; the female must have plenty of hiding places. A tight-fitting lid keeps warm, humid air above the water, which it needs to breathe.

profil.repartition: Amazon basin, from Peru to the Tocantins (Brazil) and as far as Bolivia; Essequibo basin (Guyana)
profil.presentation: Its genus name (“house of life”) alluded to fry carried in the gills, which does not apply to the species known today. This “earth eater” is sold in several geographic forms (“Santarém”, “Belém”, Peru).
profil.habitat: Probably a generalist, it avoids torrential water. Its habitats change a great deal with the annual Amazon flood, in depth as well as turbidity.
profil.comportement: Outside breeding it is surprisingly peaceful and only hunts fish a few millimetres long: it lives with most peaceful species of soft, acidic water. Gregarious, it lives in a small group. It sifts sand: it needs a fine substrate and fine foods, with some plant matter.

profil.repartition: Amazon basin (Colombia, Brazil)
profil.presentation: Described by Géry in 1966, this small characin with blue sheens is sold as the “Peruvian blue tetra”. It is the only member of its genus.
profil.habitat: It lives in the upper Amazon basin; its natural habitats are poorly documented.
profil.comportement: An active shoaling fish, it is kept in a group with species of similar size, and not with slow, long-finned fish. It accepts dry food and small live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Southern Borneo, Kalimantan (Indonesia)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1978 by Dieter Vogt, who named it after his wife Brigitte, the “chili rasbora” barely exceeds 2 cm. The genus *Boraras*, created in 1993, is an anagram of *Rasbora*: it alludes to the reversed ratio between abdominal and caudal vertebrae in these fish.

It is often confused with *B. urophthalmoides*, sometimes sold under its name. *B. brigittae* differs by a slightly larger adult size, a short and often broken lateral stripe and a more uniform red colouring. The IUCN lists it as data deficient.
profil.habitat:
It lives in southern Borneo, in the blackwater streams and pools of ancient peat swamp forests. The brown, very acidic water (pH down to 4) has virtually no hardness; the bottom is strewn with leaves, twigs and branches, and the light is filtered by the canopy.

Throughout Southeast Asia these biotopes are threatened by rubber and oil palm plantations and by urbanisation.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful but tiny and shy, it is happy alone or with other dwarf species (microrasboras, small corydoras, *Otocinclus*), discreet anabantoids or shrimp in a planted tank. It lives in a shoal: a group of at least 8 to 10 makes it less fearful and pushes the dominant males to show their best colours.

A micro-predator, it hunts small insects, worms and zooplankton. It spawns continuously, a few eggs a day, with no parental care; fry may appear on their own in a well-planted tank.

profil.repartition: Peninsular Malaysia, southern Thailand, Singapore, eastern Sumatra and Bintan Island
profil.presentation:
Described in 1904 by Georg Duncker from fish caught at Bukit Terah, near Muar in Johor state, the dwarf rasbora is one of the smallest cyprinids in the world: about 2.5 cm. Its Latin name *maculatus* means “spotted”, for the dark dots on its red body.

Long placed in *Rasbora*, it has belonged to the genus *Boraras* since 1993. Its colouring varies between populations, some being clearly redder than others.
profil.habitat:
It is widespread throughout Peninsular Malaysia, as far as southern Thailand, Singapore, eastern Sumatra and Bintan Island.

It lives in the blackwater streams and rivers of peat swamp forests: calm, very soft, acidic water (pH down to 4), stained brown, over a bed of leaves and branches, under the canopy. These habitats are shrinking before plantations and urbanisation.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful but tiny and shy, it is best kept in a species tank or with other dwarf species and shrimp. It lives in a shoal: a group of at least 8 to 10 gives it confidence.

A micro-predator, it feeds on worms, small crustaceans and zooplankton. It spawns continuously, a few eggs a day, without caring for them; mature females have rounder bellies, dominant males the most intense colours.

profil.repartition: Southern and western Borneo (Kalimantan, Indonesia)
profil.presentation: *Boraras* is an anagram of *Rasbora*, and *merah* means “red” in Indonesian. This micro-fish looks like *B. brigittae* and *B. maculatus*, but its red is concentrated around the dark spots. It is sometimes sold as the “phoenix rasbora”.
profil.habitat: It lives in the blackwater streams of peat swamp forests: brown, very soft, acidic water (pH down to 4), dimly lit, over a bottom of dead leaves and branches. These habitats are threatened by oil palm and rubber plantations.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful but tiny and shy, it is kept alone or with other micro-fish (*Microdevario*, *Trigonostigma*, dwarf Corydoras, *Otocinclus*) or small, discreet anabantoids. A micro-predator, it needs small live or frozen prey as well as fine dry food.

profil.repartition: Thailand (centre and south); also reported from Cambodia, Laos and Malaysia
profil.presentation: One of the smallest aquarium fish (1.5 cm). It is recognised by the round dark spot on its caudal peduncle and its complete lateral line; some populations show an orange stripe that leads to confusion with *B. brigittae*.
profil.habitat: It lives in shallow, clear water with dense submerged vegetation: marshes, floodplains and rice paddies, moving into flooded areas in the rainy season.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful but too small and shy for a classic community tank: keep it with other micro fish or small, discreet anabantoids. A micropredator, it feeds on zooplankton: small live or frozen prey and very fine dry food.

profil.repartition: Ganges basin (northern India) and possibly Nepal
profil.presentation: Named after the Almora district in the Indian Himalayas, this botia belongs to a group of very similar species. Often wrongly called the “Pakistani loach”, the true *B. almorhae* may never have been sold: fish traded under this name are mostly *B. lohachata* or other related forms.
profil.habitat: A foothill river fish, it stays in pools and calm stretches with a rocky or gravel bottom; it migrates upstream before spawning.
profil.comportement: Not really aggressive but very active, it can intimidate small fish and nip long fins (Betta, guppies, many cichlids). Keep it in a group, with midwater cyprinids. Mostly carnivorous (molluscs, insects, worms), it also eats soft plants.

profil.repartition: Upper Salween basin, on the Myanmar–Thailand border
profil.presentation: Named after Katsuma Kubota, this marbled botia was on sale even before it was described in 2004, under names such as “Botia angelicus” or “marbled loach”. It belongs to the *B. histrionica* complex.
profil.habitat: It lives in forest-shaded headwater streams with a fairly slow current and clear, well-oxygenated water, over sand and rocks scattered with wood and leaf litter.
profil.comportement: Active and sociable, it is kept in a group; it can intimidate small fish and nip long fins. It lives well with midwater cyprinids. Mostly carnivorous (molluscs, insects, worms), it takes dry and frozen food and also eats soft plants.

profil.repartition: India: endemic to Kerala
profil.presentation: Probably the smallest of the pufferfish (under 2.5 cm), also called the “Malabar puffer”. Popular for its face and its surprising way of swimming, it is often sold without the information needed to care for it, and it is listed as vulnerable.
profil.habitat: Strictly a freshwater fish, it lives in the slow, heavily vegetated waters of inland Kerala.
profil.comportement: Poorly suited to a community tank: it nips the fins of slow fish and is outcompeted at feeding time by lively species. It is best kept in a species tank, possibly with *Otocinclus*. It needs small shelled snails to wear down its ever-growing teeth, and live or frozen prey. Very sensitive to water quality.

profil.repartition: Amazon basin (Brazil, Peru, Colombia, Bolivia), Orinoco and coastal rivers of the Guianas
profil.presentation: This marbled hatchetfish, with its keel-shaped belly, owes its genus name to Margaret Carnegie. Very popular, it is not bred commercially: every fish sold is wild-caught, most of them in the Rio Negro basin.
profil.habitat: It lives in the black water of flooded forests (igapó) and forest creeks, under dense overhanging vegetation, in acidic, very soft water stained brown by leaf litter. The level of the Rio Negro can rise by 15 metres there in the rainy season.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful and shy, it lives near the surface and leaves fry alone: it is a good companion for dwarf cichlids. A schooling fish, it is kept in a group. It hunts insects and zooplankton at the surface: small live or frozen prey and floating dry food. It jumps: the aquarium must be covered.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Inle and its basin, Shan State (Myanmar), and around Loikaw (Kayah State)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1918 by the British zoologist Nelson Annandale, the emerald dwarf rasbora has a Greek name meaning “small and red”. It was placed in the genus *Celestichthys*, created for the “galaxy”, but FishBase now puts it in *Danio*, as *Danio erythromicron*.

It is a case of miniaturisation: it breeds at under 2 cm. Listed as endangered by the IUCN, it has reportedly sometimes been hybridised with the galaxy (*Danio margaritatus*), the hybrids being sold as females of the latter.
profil.habitat:
Lake Inle lies in a karst valley at almost 900 m above sea level on the Shan Plateau. Shallow (2 to 3 m), with clear water over a fertile silty bottom, it is home to nine endemic fish species.

It is famous for its stilt villages, its Intha fishermen who row with one leg, and its floating gardens made of tangled plants. These plant rafts line the lake and give many fish shelter among their roots. The water is rather hard and alkaline.
profil.comportement:
Gregarious without forming a true shoal, it lives in a loose group in which the males, striped with iridescent blue bars, spar all day long. It is easily intimidated by larger or boisterous fish: a species tank, or one shared with other Lake Inle species, suits it better.

It feeds on small invertebrates, algae and zooplankton and rarely comes up to the surface. An egg scatterer with no parental care, it often spawns in a well-planted tank. Do not keep it with the galaxy, with which it can hybridise.

profil.repartition: Central and southern China (up to the Yangtze), Hainan, Hong Kong and the Red River basin (Vietnam)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1758 by Carl Linnaeus, *Channa asiatica* is one of the longest-known snakeheads. It is recognised by its black vertical bars on a brown background and the many white dots that speckle its body and fins; it has no pelvic fins.

Its closest relative is the darker *Channa nox*. It has been introduced to Taiwan and to Ishigaki Island, in the Ryukyu archipelago.
profil.habitat:
It is native to central and southern China, the Yangtze marking the northern limit of its range, as well as Hainan Island, Hong Kong and the Red River basin in northern Vietnam.

A generalist, it lives in ponds, lakes and slow rivers in rainforest regions, hidden among crevices and roots. It tolerates oxygen-poor water and can even crawl short distances over land to reach another body of water.
profil.comportement:
A predator, it is kept in a species tank. Young fish can live together, but once a pair has formed the other fish are in danger.

It feeds mainly on small fish, crustaceans and insects, and readily accepts non-live food. From about 18 cm, a well-fed pair breeds at least once a year: the parents embrace, thousands of eggs float at the surface and both parents guard the eggs and young. Males have more silvery spots and longer fins.

profil.repartition: Brahmaputra basin: northern Assam and Arunachal Pradesh (northeast India)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1991 by Jörg Vierke, the rainbow snakehead is named after Heiko Bleher, who collected the type series. It is one of the smallest and most colourful *Channa*: about 20 cm, with orange spots on the tail fin. Like a few other species in the genus, it has no pelvic fins.

Listed as near threatened, it is scarce, needs a particular microhabitat and suffers heavy fishing for food and the aquarium trade. Like all *Channa*, it breathes air at the surface.
profil.habitat:
It is endemic to the Brahmaputra basin: northern Assam and the area around Doimukh, in the Dikrong basin, in Arunachal Pradesh. The climate is tropical monsoon forest, with heavy rain and hot summers.

The fish dig burrows near tree stumps in forests flooded during the monsoon; they shelter there during the dry winter, then come out to hunt and breed when the forest floods. They tolerate oxygen-poor water and fairly cool temperatures in winter.
profil.comportement:
A predator, it does best in a species tank, but can live with peaceful fish too large to be swallowed. Young fish tolerate one another, then become aggressive towards each other at maturity; a pair, once formed, stays together but is hostile to other members of its species.

It hunts small fish and insects, and readily accepts non-live food (shrimp, worms). The pair embraces like anabantoids; several thousand eggs float at the surface, without a nest, and both parents guard the eggs and then the fry.

profil.repartition: Headwaters of the Kyeintali Chaung basin, Arakan Mountains, Rakhine State (western Myanmar)
profil.presentation:
Described in 2007 by the German ichthyologist Ralf Britz, together with *Channa ornatipinnis*, *Channa pulchra* (“beautiful”) is a snakehead with blue-grey flanks dotted with dark spots and fins edged in a pale colour. Although sometimes called a “dwarf”, the species reaches 30 cm.

The IUCN lists it as data deficient: it is known only from one small basin in the Arakan Mountains.
profil.habitat:
It lives in the Kyeintali Chaung basin, in the Arakan Mountains (Rakhine Yoma), in western Myanmar.

Its streams are fast, clear, well oxygenated and relatively cool, under a subtropical climate: the water rarely exceeds 23 °C. Like all *Channa*, it breathes air at the surface.
profil.comportement:
A predator, it is kept alone or in a pair in a species tank; members of its species become rivals at maturity, and any fish that fits in its mouth is prey. A covered tank is essential, as *Channa* jump.

It feeds on fish, insects and crustaceans, and in the aquarium accepts shrimp, mussels and worms. British and German hobbyists have bred it; sources disagree on how it incubates its eggs (in a cave or in the mouth).

profil.repartition: Amazon basin (Ecuador, Peru, Brazil), western Orinoco (Colombia), coastal rivers of the Guianas
profil.presentation: Its genus name combines “lip” and “tooth”, and *punctatus* describes its rows of dots. This characiform, also called the “checkerboard headstander”, often swims with its head tilted down. Its colouring varies between localities.
profil.habitat: It lives mainly in slow rivers, tributaries, oxbows and floodplain lakes.
profil.comportement: Shy and peaceful, it dislikes boisterous species: it lives well with tetras, small Loricariidae, Corydoras and calm cichlids. In a group, squabbles remain harmless if there are enough hiding places. An omnivore, in the wild it mostly eats insects, fruit and even scales. Sensitive to organic waste, it does not tolerate a newly set-up tank.

profil.repartition: Lake Malawi: Pombo Rocks, Tanzanian coast
profil.presentation: This blue-striped dwarf mbuna, described only in 1994 by Ad Konings, was long placed in the genus *Pseudotropheus*. Listed as vulnerable, it lives at a single rocky site. It often presses its body against the rocks, even swimming on its side.
profil.habitat: It lives only around the Pombo Rocks, often in shallow water near the tops of the rocks, and rarely ventures into open water.
profil.comportement: One of the most aggressive and territorial mbuna, which readily attacks much larger fish. It is kept in a large group, in a deliberately crowded tank, with other robust mbuna of different patterns, never with Aulonocara or Utaka. Its diet should be mainly plant-based (spirulina, spinach, nori), with no red meat. For experienced hobbyists only.

profil.repartition: Lake Malawi: Taiwanee Reef, near Chizumulu Island
profil.presentation: Described by Ad Konings in 1990 and long placed in the genus *Pseudotropheus*, this small mbuna shows marked dimorphism: males are blue with black stripes, females bright yellow. It is listed as critically endangered.
profil.habitat: It lives in large groups on sediment-free rocky reefs, in the upper part of the reef where the current is strong.
profil.comportement: Like other mbuna, it is territorial and kept in a group, one male to several females, with other mbuna. It grazes and picks at the coating of algae and small organisms that covers the rocks: its diet should be mainly plant-based.

profil.repartition: Sumatra and Borneo (Indonesia)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1852 by Pieter Bleeker, the clown loach is the only species in the genus *Chromobotia* (“coloured botia”), created for it in 2004. Bright orange with three broad black bands, it can exceed 30 cm and live for more than 20 years. It belongs to the family Botiidae, split from the Cobitidae.

It makes audible clicking sounds, especially when it eats or squabbles, and sometimes lies on its side to rest, a normal behaviour that often worries beginners. Some of the fish in the trade are produced in Indonesia by hormone-induced breeding.
profil.habitat:
It lives in Sumatra (Batang Hari, Musi and Indragiri basins) and in Kalimantan on Borneo (Kapuas, Kayan). The populations of the two islands differ slightly in genetics and fin colour.

Adults live at the bottom of large channels, hidden under rocks and wood or in hollows in the mud. In the rainy season they move up into tributaries and flooded plains to spawn; the young stay there for several months, in soft, tea-coloured water among leaves and roots.
profil.comportement:
A gregarious fish, it forms complex social hierarchies and must live in a group of at least 5. Active and sometimes noisy, it intimidates small fish and may nip veil fins; it lives well with midwater cyprinids and other loaches.

Mostly carnivorous, it eats molluscs (it is a good snail eater), insects and worms, with a little plant matter. Its adult size calls for a very large tank (at least 1.80 m).

profil.repartition: Guiana Shield: from the Maroni (Suriname, French Guiana) to the Essequibo (Guyana)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1801 by Marcus Elieser Bloch and Johann Gottlob Schneider, the mariposa (“butterfly” in Spanish) or peacock bass is a large predatory cichlid that exceeds 70 cm and nearly 7 kg. It has three dark bars and a gold-ringed black eyespot at the base of the tail, hence its name *ocellaris*.

A 2006 revision of the genus restricted *C. ocellaris* to the Guiana Shield; fish from the Amazon basin belong to other species. Highly prized by sport anglers, it has been introduced to Florida, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, Panama, Singapore and Malaysia.
profil.habitat:
Its natural range runs from the Maroni basin, between Suriname and French Guiana, to the Essequibo basin in Guyana.

Adults live in rapids and in calm water of medium depth over a rocky bottom, where they form shoals. The water is warm (24 to 27 °C), soft and close to neutral.
profil.comportement:
It is an exclusive fish predator: it eats any tankmate that fits in its mouth. Territorial and fairly aggressive, it can only live with very large fish (arowanas, stingrays, large catfish) in an aquarium of several thousand litres.

It breeds all year round, with a peak at the start of the rainy season: the pair spawns on a flat stone in shallow water, then guards eggs and fry; the eggs hatch in about three days. The adult male develops a nuchal hump.

profil.repartition: French Guiana, Suriname, Guyana, Orinoco delta; formerly Trinidad
profil.presentation: The keyhole cichlid, described from the Maroni River in French Guiana, is recognised by the “keyhole” spot on its flanks: its genus name in fact comes from the Greek *kleithron* (“lock”) and the Guarani *acará* (cichlid). It is the only species in its genus; most fish sold come from commercial farms.
profil.habitat: It lives in slow or stagnant blackwater creeks and tributaries at low altitude: brown, very soft and acidic water (pH 4 to 5), with a bottom of leaves, branches and roots.
profil.comportement: Peaceful outside breeding and hardly predatory, it is one of the most peaceful cichlids. Shy, it feels safer with a group of small midwater characins. When frightened, it presses itself against a branch and changes colour. The pair cares for the eggs. An omnivore, it accepts most foods.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Malawi (Malawi, Mozambique, Tanzania)
profil.presentation: Together with the genus *Mchenga*, the Copadichromis make up the “Utaka” group, open-water cichlids specialised in zooplankton and very numerous in Lake Malawi. Males of *C. borleyi* are among the most colourful.
profil.habitat: It lives near rocky areas and large isolated boulders, between 5 and 20 m deep, and forms large shoals in open water, often with other species.
profil.comportement: Fairly peaceful, it does not tolerate boisterous companions and never mbuna. It lives with most Aulonocara and calm Haplochromis, but not with fish of the same colour or other Copadichromis (hybridisation). A zooplankton eater, it accepts small live, frozen and dry foods, with a little plant matter.

profil.repartition: Lower Amazon and coastal rivers of Brazil (Pará, Amapá), the Guianas and eastern Venezuela
profil.presentation: The splash tetra owes its name to its unique way of breeding: the pair leaps out of the water to stick its eggs under an overhanging leaf, then the male splashes them with flicks of his tail until they hatch. Its genus honours the naturalist Edward Drinker Cope, its species J. Paul Arnold.
profil.habitat: It lives in groups near the surface of streams and small tributaries, often under overhanging vegetation, in tea-coloured water; it moves into flooded forest at high water.
profil.comportement: Peaceful but poorly suited to a classic community tank, it lives with characins, hatchetfish, pencilfish and small peaceful catfish. Keep it in a mixed group of at least 8 to 10. A surface micropredator, it needs small live or frozen prey. It jumps: the aquarium must be covered.

profil.repartition: Brazil: upper Rio Negro, near São Gabriel da Cachoeira
profil.presentation: Named after the famous collector Adolfo Schwartz, this Corydoras has a dark oblique band on its back, like several related species from the Rio Negro, and an orange patch on the nape. Since 2024, researchers have placed it in the genus *Hoplisoma*.
profil.habitat: It lives in blackwater tributaries and flooded forests of the upper Rio Negro: tea-coloured water with almost no hardness, pH 4 to 6, alongside small characins, pencilfish and Apistogramma.
profil.comportement: Peaceful and gregarious, it is kept in a group. An omnivore, it sifts the substrate: sinking dry food and live or frozen prey, without relying on the other fish's leftovers. It needs soft, acidic and very clean water.

profil.repartition: Trinidad and much of South America, from Colombia to the Río de la Plata (probably a composite species)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1858 by the American Theodore Gill from fish caught on the island of Trinidad, the bronze corydoras owes its Latin name *aeneus* to its metallic golden-green sheen. *Corydoras* comes from the Greek for “helmet” and “skin”, for the bony plates that armour its flanks.

It is one of the most widespread aquarium fish, with albino and long-finned forms. But its identity is in question: its huge range looks more like that of a complex of similar species than of a single species. FishBase now places it in the genus *Osteogaster*.
profil.habitat:
It is reported from Colombia and Trinidad to the Río de la Plata basin, east of the Andes: Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, the Guianas, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay, Venezuela. On Trinidad, it survives in a few rivers in the centre and south of the island.

It lives mainly in calm, shallow water over a soft bottom, but also in flowing water. Adults form groups of 20 to 30 fish; spawning is triggered by the changes in the water at the start of the rainy season.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful and gregarious, it is kept in a group of at least 6. Rather nocturnal, it sifts the bottom for worms, crustaceans, insects and plant debris.

It breathes air through its gut: it rises to the surface 1 to 45 times an hour to gulp a bubble. In the aquarium, a large change of cooler water mimics the arrival of the rains and often triggers spawning; the eggs are stuck to the glass or to plants.

profil.repartition: Upper Amazon basin (Brazil, Peru, Ecuador, Colombia)
profil.presentation: This corydoras owes its name (“arched”) to the curved black band that runs from its snout to its tail. Described in 1938 from an aquarium fish, it carries the number C020 and looks like other species such as *C. narcissus*. It is now placed in the genus *Brochis*.
profil.habitat: It lives in the upper Amazon basin, upstream of the confluence with the Rio Negro, where it occurs alongside *C. narcissus*.
profil.comportement: Peaceful and gregarious, it is kept in a group and suits calm community tanks. An omnivore, it accepts sinking dry food and live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Brazil: upper Rio Negro
