profil.presentation: Described in 1995 by David Sands, this Corydoras has a dark oblique band on its back and an orange patch on the nape; it is easily confused with *C. adolfoi*. It is now placed in the genus *Hoplisoma*.
profil.habitat: Where it was discovered, the water was flowing and the bottom sandy; it probably lives in the very soft, acidic blackwater tributaries and flooded forests of the upper Rio Negro.
profil.comportement: Peaceful and gregarious, it is kept in a group. An omnivore, it accepts sinking dry food and live or frozen prey, and needs soft, acidic and very clean water.

profil.repartition: Upper Orinoco, left-bank tributaries in the Llanos (Venezuela, Colombia)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1960 by Stanley Weitzman, *Corydoras habrosus* (from the Greek *habros*, “graceful, delicate”) is a dwarf corydoras of about 2.5 cm, with a beige body marked by two or three dark blotches along the flank, which sets it apart from *C. cochui*.

It is sold as the “salt and pepper cory” or “Venezuelan pygmy cory”. FishBase now places it in the genus *Hoplisoma*. The IUCN lists it as near threatened.
profil.habitat:
It lives in the upper Orinoco basin, mainly the Río Apure basin in Venezuela, and in Colombia in the Arauca and Casanare rivers. Its type locality is the Río Salinas, near El Baúl.

It is a fish of the Llanos, vast grassy plains flooded in the rainy season. It prefers lagoons, small tributaries, flooded forest and grassland and margins with little current, and gathers near submerged vegetation, branches or roots.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful and gregarious, it is kept in a group of at least 6, ideally 10. Its small size calls for calm companions of similar size.

It sifts the substrate for small prey: fine sinking food, bloodworms, tubifex. For breeding, a change of soft, cooler water mimics the rainy season; the females, broader, stick their eggs to the glass or to plants.

profil.repartition: Amazon, Madeira and Paraguay basins (Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, Argentina)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1888 by Carl and Rosa Eigenmann, an American couple of ichthyologists, the dwarf corydoras owes its name *hastatus* (“armed with a spear”) to the dark diamond- or arrow-shaped spot on its caudal peduncle.

It measures under 3 cm. Less common in the hobby than *C. pygmaeus* and *C. habrosus*, it is often confused with the former. Since the 2024 revision, FishBase places it in the genus *Gastrodermus*.
profil.habitat:
It has a wide range for a corydoras: the type locality is on the Amazon between Santarém and Manaus, and it is also known from the Madeira basin in Bolivia and the whole Río Paraguay system, down to north-eastern Argentina.

It lives in side channels, oxbows, marshes, floodplain lakes and small tributaries, in shallow, clear to turbid water over mud or clay, sometimes among weed beds or floating plants (water hyacinths and water lettuce).
profil.comportement:
Unlike most corydoras, it often swims in open water, in small shoals among the plants. In Paraguay it mixes with shoals of small silvery characins with a tail spot, which it seems to imitate: a resemblance that may protect it from predators.

Peaceful and gregarious, it is kept in a group of at least 6, ideally 10, with small species. It feeds partly in open water, on small prey. Females are larger and broader than males.

profil.repartition: Lower Amazon and coastal rivers of north-eastern Brazil (Parnaíba basin)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1906 by Franz Steindachner, the leopard corydoras is named after a certain “Julius” whose identity remains a mystery. FishBase now places it in the genus *Hoplisoma*.

Many fish sold under this name are actually *C. trilineatus*, a very similar species from the upper Amazon that is caught for the trade more often. They are traditionally told apart by the head, covered with small clear dots in *C. julii* and with wormlike markings in *C. trilineatus*; but some *trilineatus* are dotted too.
profil.habitat:
It lives in the lower Amazon and the coastal rivers of north-eastern Brazil. Its type locality is a stream flowing into the Rio Parnaíba, near Alto Parnaíba.

Like other corydoras, it frequents the bottom of small sandy streams, in soft to moderately hard water between 20 and 26 °C.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful and gregarious, it is kept in a group of at least 6 and sifts the substrate for worms, crustaceans, insects and plant debris.

It breeds like most corydoras: a large change of cool water triggers spawning, the eggs being stuck to the glass or to plants. Females are larger and broader than males.

profil.repartition: Upper Amazon basin (Peru, Colombia, Ecuador)
profil.presentation: One of the most abundant Corydoras in the wild, caught in large numbers and often sold in batches of “mixed Corydoras” with related species that are hard to tell apart. It is now placed in the genus *Hoplisoma*.
profil.habitat: It lives mainly in blackwater rivers and tributaries, acidic and stained brown by tannins, where it swims in very large groups over soft, muddy bottoms.
profil.comportement: Peaceful and gregarious, it is kept in a group. An omnivore, it accepts sinking dry food and live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Coastal rivers of the Guianas (Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana)
profil.presentation: This black-masked Corydoras belongs to a genus of more than 180 described species, and many others, still undescribed, carry a “C number”. It is now placed in the genus *Hoplisoma*.
profil.habitat: It lives in coastal rivers and their tributaries.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, it suits many community tanks, with small characins, cyprinids, anabantoids, dwarf cichlids and other peaceful catfish. Keep it in a group of at least six. It needs a clean substrate, as it loses its barbels on a dirty bottom. An omnivore, it accepts sinking food and frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Colombia: upper Río Meta basin (a tributary of the Orinoco)
profil.presentation: The “Meta corydoras” or “bandit corydoras” has a dark oblique band on the rear of its body that stops at the base of the tail. It is now placed in the genus *Hoplisoma* and listed as vulnerable.
profil.habitat: It lives in several tributaries of the upper Río Meta (Humea, Guatiquía, Manacacias, Metica) and seems absent from the lower Meta.
profil.comportement: Peaceful and gregarious, it is kept in a group. An omnivore, it accepts sinking dry food and live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Southern Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay and Argentina
profil.presentation: One of the first Corydoras known, described as early as 1842 by Jenyns from fish collected during Darwin's voyage on the *Beagle*. The genus name means “helmet skin”, referring to the bony plates that cover its flanks. Like its cousins, it sometimes gulps air at the surface: it can absorb oxygen through its gut.
profil.habitat: It lives in rivers, tributaries and still water: pools, ponds and small lakes.
profil.comportement: Peaceful, it suits small community tanks, in a group, with tetras and dwarf cichlids. An opportunistic omnivore, it accepts almost anything: good-quality sinking food and live or frozen prey. Coming from subtropical regions, it tolerates cooler water than most Corydoras.

profil.repartition: Upper Peruvian Amazon (Ucayali basin)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1971 by Han Nijssen and Isaäc Isbrücker, the panda corydoras owes its name to the black patches over its eye, on its dorsal fin and at the base of its tail, on a pinkish-white body, which recall the giant panda.

The IUCN lists it as near threatened. FishBase now places it in the genus *Hoplisoma*. Almost all fish in the trade come from farms in Eastern Europe and Asia, and are hardier than wild ones.
profil.habitat:
It is native to the upper Amazon basin in Peru. It lives in clear-water or blackwater streams and tributaries, often over sand.

Some of these streams receive Andean snowmelt at certain times: the current strengthens and the temperature can drop to around 19 °C. It therefore likes rather cool water for a tropical fish (20 to 25 °C).
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful, it suits many community aquariums, with small tetras, cyprinids, anabantoids and dwarf cichlids, avoiding large or aggressive fish. It is much more confident and active in a group of at least 6.

An omnivore, it feeds on sinking pellets and live or frozen prey. It breeds like other corydoras, in a sand-bottomed tank with Java moss. Seen from above, females have a rounder belly.

profil.repartition: Rio Madeira basin (Brazil)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1966 by Joachim Knaack, the pygmy corydoras is one of the smallest armoured catfish: about 2.5 cm. A thin black stripe runs along its silvery flank, which sets it apart from *C. hastatus*, which has a diamond-shaped spot on the caudal peduncle instead.

Since the 2024 revision of the corydoras, FishBase places it in the genus *Gastrodermus*, with other dwarf species.
profil.habitat:
It seems to be endemic to the Rio Madeira basin, in Brazil. It lives in small tributaries, creeks, pools and flooded forest, often in large numbers in the shelter of bank vegetation or roots.

The water there is soft and slightly acidic to neutral, between 22 and 26 °C.
profil.comportement:
Unlike most corydoras, it readily swims in open water, in tight shoals, sometimes mixed with other small fish: it makes an excellent “dither fish” for dwarf cichlids. Very peaceful but tiny, it is intimidated by larger tankmates, and angelfish or gouramis may eat it.

A group of at least 6, ideally 10, is recommended. Its small mouth calls for fine or crushed food. Seen from above, females are broader and slightly larger.

profil.repartition: Upper Rio Negro (Brazil)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1983 by the American ichthyologist Warren E. Burgess, *Corydoras robineae* (or “bannertail corydoras”) is instantly recognised by its tail fin barred with oblique black and white bands, and by the dark line running along its flank to the tail.

Since the 2024 revision of the corydoras, FishBase places it in the genus *Brochis*, which previously held only a few large, long-finned species.
profil.habitat:
It is native to the upper Rio Negro, in Brazil, where it lives in the main river and its tributaries.

The ranges given by the sources are soft to moderately hard water, slightly acidic to neutral, between 21 and 26 °C.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful, it suits many community aquariums, avoiding large or aggressive fish. It lives in a group: at least 6 for it to show itself with confidence.

It accepts most sinking foods, supplemented with live or frozen prey. It is harder to spawn than other corydoras, but breeds the same way; seen from above, females are rounder and broader.

profil.repartition: Brazil: Rio Purus basin
profil.presentation: Named after the collector Adolfo Schwartz, this spotted Corydoras is often mixed up in the trade with related species. It is now placed in the genus *Hoplisoma*.
profil.habitat: It lives in small tributaries, creeks, flooded forests and on sandbanks in the Rio Purus basin.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, it suits many community tanks, in a group of at least six. Sensitive to poor water, it loses its barbels on a dirty substrate: regular maintenance is essential. An omnivore, it accepts sinking food and live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Rio Guaporé basin (central Brazil and Bolivia)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1962 by the German aquarist Joachim Knaack, Sterba's corydoras is named after Günther Sterba, a zoologist and author of reference books on aquarium fish. It is recognised by its dark, white-dotted head, its spotted body and the bright orange rays of its pectoral and pelvic fins.

Since the 2024 revision of the corydoras group, FishBase places it in the genus *Hoplisoma*. It can live for more than 15 years.
profil.habitat:
The species was described from a specimen from the Rio Guaporé, which marks the border between Brazil and Bolivia. It lives in small rivers, creeks, tributaries and pools in flooded forest, in soft, acidic water that is often flowing and poor in plants.

Almost all fish sold today come from farms in Eastern Europe and Asia; they are more tolerant than wild fish but prefer water that is not too warm (22 to 28 °C).
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful, it suits many community aquariums with small tetras, cyprinids, anabantoids and dwarf cichlids. It is much more active and confident in a group of at least 6.

An omnivore, it sifts the substrate for food: sinking pellets and live or frozen prey. It is one of the easiest corydoras to breed: the female sticks her eggs to the glass or to plants. Seen from above, females are broader and rounder than males.

profil.repartition: Central and Peruvian Amazon, and coastal rivers of Suriname (Brazil, Colombia, Peru, Suriname)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1872 by the American palaeontologist and zoologist Edward Drinker Cope, the three-stripe corydoras owes its name to the dark line that runs along the middle of its reticulated flanks, flanked by two fainter lines. FishBase now places it in the genus *Hoplisoma*.

It is very often sold as *C. julii*, a related species from north-eastern Brazil. The wormlike markings on its head usually tell them apart, although some individuals are dotted.
profil.habitat:
It is a fairly widespread species: the Amazon basin in Colombia, Peru and Brazil, and several coastal rivers of Suriname.

It lives in small tributaries, creeks, pools and flooded forest, over sandy or leaf-covered bottoms, in soft to moderately hard water between 22 and 26 °C.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful, it suits many community aquariums, with small tetras, cyprinids, anabantoids, dwarf cichlids and other calm catfish. It is much more confident and active in a group of at least 6.

An omnivore that is easy to feed, it accepts sinking pellets and live or frozen prey. It is one of the easiest corydoras to breed, ideal for beginners; seen from above, females are rounder and broader.

profil.repartition: Western Amazon basin, in Peru
profil.presentation:
Described in 1971 by the Dutch ichthyologist Han Nijssen, this corydoras is named after Stanley Weitzman, an American specialist in small characiforms. It has a dark band running through the eye and a large black blotch on the back.

A genetic revision published in 2024 split the old genus *Corydoras* into several genera: FishBase now places it in *Hoplisoma*, as *Hoplisoma weitzmani*.
profil.habitat:
FishBase places it in the western Amazon basin, in Peru. Like most corydoras, it lives on the bottom of small streams, among sand, leaf litter and wood.

The parameter ranges given by FishBase are wide: pH 6 to 8, low to medium hardness, 22 to 26 °C.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful and gregarious like all corydoras, it sifts the substrate in a group for small invertebrates and debris. A group of at least 6 to 8 makes it more active and less fearful; fine sand protects its barbels.

It can breathe air: it is sometimes seen darting up to the surface to gulp a bubble, a normal behaviour in corydoras.

profil.repartition: Borneo, Sumatra, Malay Peninsula, southern and western Thailand, perhaps southern Myanmar
profil.presentation: It belongs to a small group of almost identical species sold as the “Siamese algae eater” or “*Crossocheilus siamensis*”, a name that actually refers to another species. The genus is named after the fringed barbels on its upper lip.
profil.habitat: It lives in flowing streams and tributaries with a bottom of rocks, pebbles and sand, often near submerged wood. The clear, shallow water lets a rich biofilm grow, which it grazes. It is thought to move with the seasons into deeper, murkier water.
profil.comportement: Peaceful, it lives with most common species, ideally river fish from Southeast Asia. It is famous for eating black beard algae (red algae), which are hard to get rid of otherwise, and this has made it a much sought-after fish for planted tanks. It must also be given a varied diet.

profil.repartition: Middle Congo basin (Congo, DR Congo, Central African Republic)
profil.presentation: The leopard bushfish mimics a drifting dead leaf to approach its prey, like the South American leaffish, to which it is not related. Very hardy, it can live for more than fifteen years: a good first “unusual” fish. It breathes air at the surface.
profil.habitat: It lives in the middle Congo basin, from Pool Malebo to the Boyoma Falls, and in large tributaries such as the Kasai and Ubangi; there it shares the water with butterflyfish, elephantfish and Congo tetras.
profil.comportement: An obligate predator, it swallows fish that fit in its mouth: keep it with larger, calm species. It generally accepts dead prey (bloodworms, worms, shrimp); dry food should not be the basis of its diet.

profil.repartition: Endemic to the northern half of Lake Tanganyika
profil.presentation: The frontosa owes its name to the frontal hump of adults and its genus to the Greek word for “hump”. Populations are sold under their locality names to keep the lines pure; most have six vertical bands, except the Kigoma form, which has seven.
profil.habitat: Lake Tanganyika, the oldest of the great Rift lakes, is home to about 250 endemic cichlids. The frontosa lives there over rocky, sediment-rich bottoms, between 6 and 120 m deep, mostly between 15 and 70 m.
profil.comportement: It can eat much smaller fish, but fits into a selected Tanganyikan community in a very large aquarium. Gregarious, it is kept in a group of at least five, ideally ten; males form a hierarchy rather than territories. A generalist predator, it eats fish, invertebrates and molluscs; females brood the eggs in their mouths.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Tanganyika
profil.presentation: One of hobbyists' favourite Tanganyikan cichlids. It comes in several geographic forms, each with a blue or yellow tail; the “Jumbo” form is larger. In the wild it forms shoals of several thousand fish.
profil.habitat: An open-water fish, it lives off rocky slopes, in intermediate zones with scattered rocks and a sandy bottom, where it feeds on zooplankton. It often hovers motionless, head down.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, it does not tolerate mbuna. It lives with Tanganyikans that use other zones of the tank: *Julidochromis*, *Altolamprologus*, shell-dwelling species. Keep it in a shoal of at least eight. It has a small mouth: small live and frozen prey. Females brood the eggs in their mouths.

profil.repartition: Mainland Southeast Asia and Sumatra: Irrawaddy, Salween, Mekong, Chao Phraya and Mae Klong basins
profil.presentation:
Described in 1860 by the English zoologist Edward Blyth from fish from the “Tenasserim provinces” (southern Myanmar today), the pearl danio owes its Latin name, “white-lined”, to its pearly sheen. Some authors place it in the genus *Brachydanio*.

Its populations vary markedly in colour depending on their origin: orange on the back in western Thailand, blue in the centre of the country, a pinker form in Yunnan. It may in fact be a complex of several closely related species. Old records from Sri Lanka and India are mistaken.
profil.habitat:
Very widespread, it is known from Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Peninsular Malaysia and Sumatra, in the Irrawaddy, Salween, Mekong, Chao Phraya and Mae Klong basins.

It occupies varied habitats: clear, well-oxygenated hill streams over rocky bottoms in forest, but also pools, ditches and rice paddies. It stays near the surface, where it catches insects that fall into the water.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful, lively and undemanding, it suits most community aquariums. A shoaling fish, it is kept in a group of at least 8 to 10, in a tank long enough to swim in.

It feeds mainly on aquatic and terrestrial insects and their larvae, with a little algae and zooplankton. An egg scatterer with no parental care, it often spawns when in good condition; females are rounder and slightly larger than males.

profil.repartition: Northern Myanmar: Mogaung Chaung basin (Kachin State), a tributary of the Irrawaddy
profil.presentation: Named after Dr B. N. Chopra, who collected the first specimens, this small orange-and-black danio, sometimes placed in the genus *Celestichthys*, reached the hobby around 2003 and soon became one of the most popular dwarf danios. It is now bred commercially.
profil.habitat: It prefers small hill streams with gravel and rocky bottoms; it has also been found in a clear-water pool with a muddy, plantless bottom at the foot of a hill.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful and undemanding about water quality, it suits a community tank with other small cyprinids, tetras, livebearers, rainbowfish, anabantoids and loaches. It mainly hunts insects: dry food, supplemented with small live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Jaintia Hills, Meghalaya State (northeast India)
profil.presentation:
Described in 2007 by the Indian ichthyologist Nibedita Sen, this danio is named after the Jaintia Hills district of Meghalaya, where the type series came from. Some authors place it in the genus *Brachydanio*, with the zebra danio.

Like its cousins, it is recognised by the dark horizontal stripes on its body and fins; it is listed as vulnerable by the IUCN and remains rare in the hobby.
profil.habitat:
Meghalaya is a region of wooded hills among the wettest in the world, where many upland streams are very fast. This species seems confined to the calmer small hill streams, over gravel and stones, lined with dense vegetation overhanging the water.

Its mid-altitude climate explains why it prefers cool water, between 18 and 23 °C.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful, it lives in a shoal and should be kept in a group of at least 8 to 10. Its need for cool water makes it poorly suited to a classic tropical community aquarium: a species tank, or one shared with cool-water species (small cyprinids, loaches, *Rhinogobius* gobies, shrimp), suits it better.

It feeds mainly on insects and their larvae. Its breeding in the aquarium is not documented, but it should resemble that of other danios: scattered eggs, with no parental care.

profil.repartition: Northern Myanmar: tributaries of the upper Irrawaddy near Myitkyina (Kachin), Sagaing and Chin
profil.presentation: Its name comes from the Burmese word for “leopard”, referring to its spots. Its pattern varies: unbroken stripes in some individuals, wavy or broken into dots in others. It is sometimes placed in the genus *Brachydanio*.
profil.habitat: Where it was discovered, a small stream shaded by bamboo flowed fast, with clear, slightly brownish water, over a bottom of mud and stones.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful and undemanding, it does well in a community tank with other small cyprinids, tetras, livebearers, rainbowfish and loaches. In a shoal, it mainly hunts insects: dry food supplemented with small live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Shan State (eastern Myanmar), Salween basin, down to northern Thailand
profil.presentation:
The “galaxy” or celestial pearl danio is one of the most publicised discoveries in the hobby: spotted in August 2006, it was shown online by a Thai exporter the following month, to the point that some thought the picture had been doctored. Thousands of fish were exported within a few months.

It was described in 2007 by Tyson Roberts as *Celestichthys margaritatus* (“celestial fish adorned with pearls”); it is now placed in the genus *Danio*. It barely reaches 2 cm. The IUCN lists it as data deficient.
profil.habitat:
It was first found in shallow pools at the foot of a mountain near Hopong, in Shan State, at about 1,040 m above sea level; other populations have since been discovered in the Salween basin and as far as northern Thailand.

These spring-fed pools, about thirty centimetres deep, have clear water and thick beds of *Elodea* and similar plants, in the middle of open grassland. In January the water was at 22–24 °C. It lives there with a predatory snakehead (*Channa harcourtbutleri*).
profil.comportement:
Gregarious but not a tight shoal: males spar all day long and nipped fins are common within the group, though other species are not targeted. A group of around twenty spreads out these tensions.

Shy, it is easily intimidated or beaten to the food by larger fish; it rarely comes up to the surface. It feeds on small invertebrates, algae and zooplankton. An egg scatterer, it was bred in the aquarium only a few weeks after it arrived in Europe. It is better not to keep it with *Danio erythromicron*, with which it could hybridise.

profil.repartition: Plains of the Indian subcontinent: India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Pakistan, Myanmar
profil.presentation:
Described in 1822 by the Scottish surgeon Francis Hamilton from fish from the Kosi River, a tributary of the Ganges, the zebra danio is also called the “zebrafish” for its blue and gold stripes. Some authors place it in the genus *Brachydanio*.

It is one of the main model organisms in biology: its transparent embryos, which develop in a few days, are used to study development, genetics, regeneration and toxicology. Domestic strains live 3.5 years on average, up to 5.5 years for the oldest.
profil.habitat:
A 2007 study in northeast India found it mainly in slow or still water over silt, with submerged or overhanging vegetation: seasonal pools, flooded margins and mature rice paddies, rather than in river channels. In rocky streams, shoals stay at the edges, under the vegetation.

Its historical range runs from Pakistan to Myanmar, but many old records probably concern related species discovered since. In the wild it behaves almost like an annual species, breeding just before the monsoon.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful, hardy and lively, it is a shoaling fish to keep in a group of at least 8 to 10; the slimmer males then compete in colour to attract the females. It swims mainly at the surface and in midwater.

A micropredator, it feeds on small crustaceans and insect larvae (mosquitoes in particular), but accepts anything in the aquarium. It is an excellent choice for a first breeding: it scatters its eggs among plants, with no parental care, and breeds all year round.

profil.repartition: Captive-bred form of *Danio rerio* (a species native to the Indian subcontinent)
profil.presentation:
The leopard danio is not a wild species but a form of *Danio rerio*: its stripes are replaced by a scattering of dark spots. It was first described in 1963 by Hermann Meinken as *Brachydanio frankei*, from aquarium fish whose wild origin was unknown.

Crosses later showed that it is a recessive mutation of the zebra danio, called *leopard* by geneticists; it affects how the pigment cells are arranged. The name *frankei* therefore has no taxonomic standing.
profil.habitat:
Existing only in captivity, it has no natural habitat of its own. The species it comes from lives in the plains of the north and east of the Indian subcontinent: rice paddies, pools and flooded margins, slow streams with silty bottoms.

Its needs are those of the zebra danio: water at 18 to 24 °C, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, well oxygenated.
profil.comportement:
The same as the zebra danio: peaceful and very active, it lives in a shoal and should be kept in a group of at least 8 to 10. It can be mixed with striped danios, with which it breeds freely.

An undemanding micropredator, it accepts all foods. An egg scatterer with no parental care, it breeds easily in a planted tank; females are rounder and slightly larger than males.

profil.repartition: Tributaries of the Brahmaputra in West Bengal and Assam (India), perhaps Bhutan
profil.presentation:
Described in 1822 by Francis Hamilton, the scarlet badis is one of the smallest perciform fish: the male measures about 2 cm. Its name comes from *darhi*, its Bengali name. The adult male, bright red barred with iridescent blue, has pelvic and dorsal fins edged in blue; the female is drab.

It was long placed in the genus *Badis*: a 2002 revision by Sven Kullander and Ralf Britz created the genus *Dario* for it and designated a neotype, as no original specimen existed. The IUCN lists it as data deficient.
profil.habitat:
It lives in tributaries of the Brahmaputra, in West Bengal and Assam; the neotype comes from the Janali River, in Kokrajhar district.

It inhabits shallow streams (30 to 70 cm) with crystal-clear water, over sand and gravel, with dense aquatic vegetation (*Limnophila*, *Hygrophila*, *Vallisneria*, *Rotala*). In the dry season the water there is around 26 °C.
profil.comportement:
Slow and discreet, it is intimidated and outcompeted by larger tankmates: a species tank or one shared with small midwater fish suits it. Rival males are very aggressive towards each other; keep a pair or one male with several females, except in a spacious tank with well-separated territories.

A micropredator, it often refuses dry food and needs brine shrimp nauplii, daphnia or microworms. It spawns on a surface, in a temporary pair. Shops often offer only males.

profil.repartition: Myanmar: Irrawaddy basin (Kachin State, Lake Indawgyi, Mandalay region)
profil.presentation: Its name comes from the Greek *hysginon*, a scarlet dye, referring to the bright red of the males. It is sold as the “melon red dario” or “flame red dario”. It is one of the smallest aquarium fish (2 cm).
profil.habitat: It prefers small, often murky pools overgrown with aquatic plants or submerged grasses, and also lives in clear streams with a moderate current, alongside *Badis corycaeus* and *B. kyar*.
profil.comportement: Not a shoaling fish, it can be kept alone; rival males can be very aggressive. In a small tank, keep a pair or one male with several females; in a larger tank a group can live together if each male has its own territory. A shy micropredator, it needs small live or frozen prey and often refuses dry food.

profil.repartition: Southern India: Kaveri (Cauvery) basin
profil.presentation: The genus *Dawkinsia*, created in 2012, honours the biologist Richard Dawkins for his contribution to popular science. This barb, whose males have filamentous dorsal fins, is listed as endangered; it seems to have disappeared from its type locality, probably because of a dam built upstream.
profil.habitat: It prefers clean, well-oxygenated, flowing rivers and streams with bottoms of gravel, pebbles and rocks. The monsoon makes the flow vary greatly there, to the point of partial drying.
profil.comportement: It suits a peaceful river tank, with other shoaling cyprinids and loaches, or with any calm fish too large to be swallowed. Keep it in a shoal. An omnivore, it accepts dry food and live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Southeast Asia; in the strict sense, Java (Indonesia)
profil.presentation: Halfbeaks owe their name to their elongated lower jaw. Males of this species fight by gripping each other by the jaws, hence the name “wrestling halfbeak”; male fights are even staged in some countries. It is a livebearing fish.
profil.habitat: It lives in slow or still water rich in surface vegetation: rivers, canals, ditches, rice paddies, lakes and ponds; it is sometimes found in brackish water near mangroves in the rainy season.
profil.comportement: Peaceful but shy, it lives with species of similar size (livebearers, small rainbowfish, freshwater gobies), not with larger or lively fish. It feeds only at the surface: fruit flies, brine shrimp, larvae. Sensitive to sudden changes in water and temperature, it needs small, frequent water changes.

profil.repartition: Indonesia: southern and western Kalimantan (Borneo), Kapuas, Barito and Kahayan basins
profil.presentation: Its species name describes the diamond-shaped eyespots on its flanks, and its genus (from the Greek for “prisoner”) its dark bars. Long placed in the vast genus *Puntius*, it joined the genus *Desmopuntius*, created in 2013.
profil.habitat: It lives mainly in peat swamp forests and their blackwater streams, as well as other calm waters: brown, mineral-free water, sometimes at pH 3 to 4, with a bottom of leaves and roots, and grasses or submerged plants.
profil.comportement: Peaceful, it suits a tank of Southeast Asian species of similar size (small cyprinids, loaches, calm anabantoids), without boisterous companions. A micropredator, it accepts fine dry food, to be supplemented every day with small live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Northeast India, Bangladesh and Nepal (Brahmaputra, Barak, Tista, Meghna)
profil.presentation: Its name has been given to almost every striped Devario, notably the farmed “giant danio”, which according to genetic data is actually *Devario malabaricus*. The true *D. aequipinnatus* comes from northeast India and Bangladesh.
profil.habitat: It lives in hill streams and the upper reaches of small rivers, in clear, well-oxygenated water, over gravel and rocks, under overhanging vegetation; flow and turbidity vary greatly with the season.
profil.comportement: Not aggressive, but its constant activity disturbs slow or shy fish: it suits large tanks, with robust species of the same size. Keep it in a shoal. In the wild it mostly eats insects: dry food, supplemented with live or frozen prey. A good current suits it.

profil.repartition: Brazil: Amazon basin
profil.presentation: This armoured catfish, a cousin of the Corydoras, is recognised by the black and white bands on its tail fin. Every fish sold is wild-caught: fragile on arrival, they become very hardy once acclimatised.
profil.habitat: It lives away from the main channels, in creeks, slow tributaries, floodplain lakes and pools. It breathes air at the surface.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, it leaves even the smallest companions alone (only tiny fry risk being swallowed). It lives with tetras, peaceful cichlids, Corydoras and small Loricariidae, in a group, as it is gregarious. An omnivore, it accepts sinking pellets and frozen prey, and often comes up to feed at the surface.

profil.repartition: Rio Negro basin (Brazil) and Orinoco, from the Inírida (Colombia) to Maripa (Venezuela)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1958 by Werner Ladiges, the chessboard cichlid owes its common name to the checkerboard pattern of dark blotches on its flanks. The male has a lyre-shaped tail fin, with lobes extended into filaments (*filamentosus*), and fins edged in red and blue.

It is a slender, elegant dwarf cichlid, more delicate than the *Apistogramma*, and remains relatively rare in the trade.
profil.habitat:
It lives in Colombia and Venezuela, from the Inírida to Maripa in the Orinoco basin, and in the Rio Negro basin in Brazil.

It is a fish of black water, extremely soft, acidic and warm, over sand and leaf litter.
profil.comportement:
Fairly peaceful, it is dominated by more aggressive companions but fits in well with calm fish (tetras, pencilfish, corydoras). One male can be kept with one or two females.

It feeds on small prey and accepts sinking pellets, supplemented with frozen food. Breeding requires impeccable water, very soft and acidic (pH close to 4.5): the female spawns on a leaf or stone and guards the eggs alone. Females are smaller and have a rounded tail fin.

profil.repartition: Southeastern United States: from North Carolina to Alabama and the northern Everglades (Florida)
profil.presentation: This tiny pygmy sunfish (3 cm), of the family Elassomatidae, is a warm-temperate fish whose males turn black with blue highlights in the breeding season.
profil.habitat: It lives in marshes, heavily vegetated oxbows and small slow streams, usually over mud. It spawns among vegetation, preferably on hornwort (*Ceratophyllum*).
profil.comportement: Peaceful and discreet, it is kept in a small group in a heavily planted species tank or with other calm micro fish. It feeds on worms and small crustaceans: live or frozen prey. It tolerates a wide range of temperatures, including cool water.

profil.repartition: Foto River, near Fria, coastal Guinea (West Africa)
profil.presentation:
Described in 2009 by the German ichthyologist Anton Lamboj, this small West African cichlid required a new genus, *Enigmatochromis*, so much did its features set it apart from its close relatives: hence the name “enigmatic cichlid”. It measures only about 4.5 cm without the tail.

It belongs to the African riverine cichlids (Pseudocrenilabrinae), close to *Pelvicachromis*. Its species name honours Oliver Lucanus, an explorer and photographer specialising in freshwater fish. It has not yet been assessed by the IUCN.
profil.habitat:
It is known only from its type locality, the Foto River, a small savannah river near the bauxite-mining town of Fria, in coastal Guinea, north of Conakry.

It lives there alongside *Pelvicachromis humilis*, in soft, acidic water. Its tiny range, in a mining region, makes it potentially vulnerable.
profil.comportement:
Like the small West African cichlids it is related to, it lives in pairs or small groups, defends a modest territory and sifts the substrate for food (detritus, small invertebrates).

In the aquarium it needs soft, acidic water, fine sand, dead leaves and hiding places, with peaceful companions. Reference sources still give few details on its biology.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Thailand: Chao Phraya, Mae Klong and Bangpakong basins
profil.presentation:
Described in 1931 by the American zoologist Hugh M. Smith, the red-tailed black shark combines a velvety black body with a bright red tail. Long placed in the genus *Labeo*, it now belongs to the genus *Epalzeorhynchos*.

It is one of the most threatened aquarium fish: declared extinct in 1996, it was found again in 2011 in the Chao Phraya basin, then in 2014 in the Mae Klong. The IUCN lists it as critically endangered. The tens of thousands of fish exported every year all come from farms, where spawning is induced with hormones.
profil.habitat:
It was abundant in the early 20th century in the lower Mae Klong, the lower Chao Phraya and the Bangpakong, which flow into the head of the Gulf of Thailand. It lives in the main rivers and, in the rainy season, moves into flooded plains and forests; dams, pollution and river engineering have cut off these migrations.

The specimen found in the Mae Klong was caught in a stretch of clear, flowing water more than a metre deep, over sand and large boulders.
profil.comportement:
Often sold as a community fish, it is not one: discreet when young, it becomes more and more territorial as it grows and may harass species that look like it (other sharks, *Crossocheilus*, *Garra*). The rule is one fish per tank, in a spacious, well-structured aquarium.

It grazes the biofilm on surfaces (algae, small crustaceans, insect larvae) but is not a good algae eater. It can live for more than 15 years. It has not been bred in hobby aquariums.

profil.repartition: Thailand (Mae Klong, Chao Phraya, Mekong), Laos and Cambodia
profil.presentation: This green shark with red fins, a cousin of the red-tailed black shark, is often sold young as an “algae eater”, with no mention of its temperament, its size or its lifespan, which can exceed 15 years. It grazes algae, but far less effectively than *Crossocheilus*.
profil.habitat: It grazes the sandy or rocky bottoms of streams and rivers and moves into flooded plains and forests in the rainy season; these migrations have been disrupted by human works.
profil.comportement: Young fish hide a lot, but the adult becomes territorial and sometimes very aggressive towards species that look like it: one fish per tank, with carefully chosen companions. An aufwuchs grazer, it needs live or frozen prey, dry food and fresh vegetables.

profil.repartition: West Africa: from Monrovia (Liberia) to southern Côte d'Ivoire and south-western Ghana
profil.presentation: Named after the French ichthyologist Jacques Daget, this killifish is a classic of the hobby: the red-throated form was exported from Monrovia as early as 1908. It is not an annual killifish; hardy and easy to breed, it is ideal for starting out with killies.
profil.habitat: It lives in swampy areas of the coastal savannah and the calm parts of lowland streams and rivers, mostly in fresh water, sometimes brackish.
profil.comportement: Peaceful, it does well in a community tank with characins, cyprinids, anabantoids and catfish of similar size. It stays near the surface. Fairly gregarious, it is kept in a group of six or more. An insect predator, it accepts dry food but also needs small live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Coastal West Africa: from the Ouémé River (Benin) to the Sanaga (Cameroon)
profil.presentation: The only species in its genus, the reedfish (or ropefish) is a close relative of the bichirs, the last representatives of a very ancient lineage. With its snake-like body, it swims by undulating along the bottom as well as in open water, breathes air and has poor eyesight: it hunts by smell, mostly at night.
profil.habitat: It lives in shallow, heavily vegetated water, slow rivers and still waters, apparently associated with reed beds, down into estuaries.
profil.comportement: It eats any fish that fits in its mouth, but remains peaceful with others and can live in a small group. Keep it with Synodontis, large characins and cichlids such as the severum or angelfish, not with overly lively species. A carnivore, it generally refuses dry food: shrimp, worms, mussels, larvae. It escapes easily: the aquarium must be tightly closed.

profil.repartition: Lake Valencia and Río Torito basins (northern Venezuela)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1853 by Rudolf Kner, the twig catfish (*acus*, “needle”) has an extremely elongated body and a long snout that make it look like a twig: perfect camouflage among submerged branches.

The IUCN lists it as vulnerable: its range is limited to a few basins in northern Venezuela, including the heavily polluted Lake Valencia. Most “Farlowella acus” on sale are actually other species of the genus.
profil.habitat:
The species is known from the Lake Valencia and Río Torito basins, in northern Venezuela.

*Farlowella* live in calm to gently flowing water, among submerged branches, roots and vegetation, where they graze algae and biofilm. The recommended water is soft, slightly acidic, between 24 and 26 °C.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful and slow, it copes poorly with competition for food from lively fish. It often stays motionless, clinging to a branch or the glass.

It feeds on algae and biofilm, and rasps soft wood; a mature, planted aquarium rich in wood is essential, with blanched vegetables as a supplement. The female spawns on a vertical surface (glass, wood) and the male guards and cleans the eggs until they hatch; adult males have odontodes along the sides of the snout.

profil.repartition: Cross River basin (south-eastern Nigeria, western Cameroon) and Benue basin (central Nigeria)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1911 by George Albert Boulenger, the gardneri is named after R. D. Gardner, who collected the type specimens in the upper Cross River basin, near Okwoga. Hardy and colourful, it is one of the most widespread killifish in the hobby.

Its many wild forms are kept separately and named after their locality (Akure, Enugu, Lafia, Nsukka…); three have been described as subspecies, including *F. g. lacustris*, limited to Lake Ejagham. It belongs to the family Nothobranchiidae.
profil.habitat:
It lives in creeks, marshes, streams and pools in humid forest, highland savannah and rainforest, in the Cross River and Benue basins.

Some of these habitats dry out from time to time, but not every year; others hold water all year round. The water is soft, slightly acidic to neutral, between 22 and 26 °C.
profil.comportement:
Hardy, it can live with other fish, but is not a classic community fish: males are aggressive towards each other. With enough hiding places and two or three females per male, a small group does well.

A micropredator, it feeds on small crustaceans, worms and larvae. It has a “semi-annual” breeding strategy: its eggs, laid near the bottom, can hatch underwater in about a month or survive a dry spell.

profil.repartition: Niger Delta (southern Nigeria) and south-western Cameroon
profil.presentation: One of the most spectacular killifish, for the colours of its males and its large size (12 cm). Long called *Aphyosemion sjoestedti*, it comes in several forms, including a dwarf “Dwarf Red” form. It is listed as endangered in the wild.
profil.habitat: It lives in temporary swamps, raffia palm swamps and slow streams in the coastal rainforest. It is not an annual killifish: its eggs, laid in the substrate, incubate for about two months.
profil.comportement: It lives with peaceful species too large to be eaten (calm cichlids, large characins, Corydoras, Loricariidae). Males fight: space is needed to keep several, and two to three females per male. It feeds on small live or frozen prey and rarely accepts dry food.

profil.repartition: Eastern United States, from New Jersey to Alabama; introduced worldwide, including southern Europe
profil.presentation:
Described in 1859 by Charles Girard, the eastern mosquitofish is named after the American zoologist John Edwards Holbrook. It was released in tropical and subtropical countries all over the world to control the larvae of mosquitoes that carry malaria.

The outcome of these introductions is now judged to be poor: its effect on mosquitoes was minimal, even counterproductive since it also devours the invertebrates that eat them, and it has seriously threatened many local species, notably small endemic killifish in Europe. It is now widely established in southern France.
profil.habitat:
Its natural range covers the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico basins of the eastern United States, from New Jersey to Alabama. It is established throughout southern Europe and on every continent.

It lives in still or slow water: vegetated ponds and lakes, oxbows, calm pools in streams, and even brackish water. Very tough, it tolerates 15 to 35 °C. Shoals stay along the edges, where they hunt small insects that fall into the water.
profil.comportement:
Despite what its small size suggests, it is lively and aggressive: it nips other fish's fins and attacks fry. It is not recommended for a community aquarium.

A livebearer, it breeds very quickly; its life is short, often one to two years in the wild. Releasing mosquitofish (or any aquarium fish) into the wild must never be done.

profil.repartition: Middle East: Jordan, Orontes and Tigris–Euphrates basins, coastal rivers of southern Turkey and northern Syria
profil.presentation: The “doctor fish” is used in treatment pools where it nibbles dead skin, with debated effectiveness against psoriasis. It is often unclear whether the fish sold are really *G. rufa*: the species, as currently understood, probably includes several species.
profil.habitat: It prefers headwaters and fast tributaries, in clear, oxygen-saturated water where a rich biofilm grows, but also lives in lowland rivers, reservoirs and temporary habitats that partly dry out.
profil.comportement: Fairly peaceful, it tolerates its own kind poorly in a small tank; kept alone, it becomes aggressive towards fish of the same shape. A group of three or four settles into a hierarchy without harm. It grazes algae but is not strictly herbivorous: live or frozen prey, sinking food and vegetables. It likes current and fairly cool water.

profil.repartition: Peruvian and middle Amazon, the Guianas and Venezuela; reported from the Paraguay basin
profil.presentation: Its genus name means “hatchet belly”, and *sternicla* refers to its very rounded chest. Like other hatchetfish, it can leap out of the water and glide for several metres, to catch flying insects or escape a predator.
profil.habitat: It lives in slow forest streams, tributaries and marshes, especially where floating vegetation is abundant.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful but nervous and shy, it is outcompeted at feeding time by boisterous species. Keep it with small fish living at other levels (tetras, dwarf cichlids, Corydoras). It only settles in a group of at least six. It mainly eats insects at the surface: live or frozen prey. A covered aquarium is essential.

profil.repartition: Borneo (Sarawak, Sabah, Brunei and Kalimantan)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1961 by Robert Inger and Chin Phui Kong, *Gastromyzon punctulatus* is a “hillstream loach” from Borneo, with a flattened, sucker-shaped body covered in fine dots, hence its name. It measures about 6 cm.

It belongs to the family Gastromyzontidae, split from the Balitoridae: its broadened pectoral and pelvic fins form, with its flat belly, a sucker that lets it cling to stones in the current.
profil.habitat:
It is endemic to Borneo, home to many *Gastromyzon* species, often each confined to a single basin.

These loaches live in fast-flowing forest streams and torrents, over pebbles and rocks, in clear water that is cool for the tropics (23 to 25 °C) and highly oxygenated. They scrape off the biofilm of algae and micro-organisms covering the stones.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful towards other species, it is territorial with its own kind, which squabble over the best stones without injuring each other. A small group in a spacious tank spreads out these contests.

It needs a strong current, highly oxygenated water and smooth stones covered in biofilm; supplement with plant-based tablets and small prey. Its ideal companions are other fast-water fish (danios, hillstream gobies).

profil.repartition: Brazil: middle and lower Amazon basin (Xingu, Tapajós, Trombetas, Madeira, Negro, Purus)
profil.presentation: The type species of the genus *Geophagus* (“earth eater”), it is nevertheless one of the most often misidentified, since the populations of the Orinoco, the Guianas and the Tocantins are now separate species. Females brood the eggs in their mouths.
profil.habitat: It lives in the lower reaches of rivers, up to the first rapids, and in flooded-forest lakes (várzea), mostly in clear or black water, along gently sloping banks with a bottom of sand, fine gravel and mud.
profil.comportement: Outside breeding it is surprisingly peaceful and eats only tiny fish: it lives with most peaceful freshwater species, but not with aggressive bottom-dwellers. It constantly sifts the sand: a fine sand substrate is essential, as is a varied, fine diet.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Cuba
profil.presentation:
Described in 1854 by the Cuban naturalist Felipe Poey, *Girardinus metallicus* owes its genus name to the French zoologist Charles Girard and its species name to the metallic sheen of its body. The smaller males have a black band running from the mouth to the gonopodium, along the underside.

Females reach almost 9 cm, males about 5 cm.
profil.habitat:
It is endemic to Cuba, where it lives in pools, ponds, lakes and streams.

It prefers clear, still or very slow water, sometimes slightly brackish, hard and close to neutral, between 22 and 26 °C.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful, it suits a hard-water aquarium with hardy corydoras, tetras and small rainbowfish, or a brackish tank with small gobies. It copes poorly with soft, acidic water.

An omnivore, it feeds on diatoms, algae, detritus, insect larvae and plant matter. A livebearer, it breeds easily after a gestation of about 24 days; several females per male and densely planted areas reduce harassment.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Sentani, near Jayapura (Papua, Indonesia)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1907 by the Dutch zoologist Max Weber, the red rainbowfish (FishBase spells it *Glossolepis incisa*) is one of the largest rainbowfish, up to 15 cm. Only adult males take on this intense red colour, with a very high back; females stay golden olive.

The IUCN lists it as endangered: Lake Sentani suffers from the pollution of a growing city and the introduction of foreign species.
profil.habitat:
It is endemic to Lake Sentani, a hill lake at about 75 m above sea level in northern New Guinea, connected to the sea by a small river.

Shoals stay near areas of dense vegetation. The water is hard and alkaline, warm at the surface (around 29 °C according to measurements), but the species adapts to 24–28 °C in the aquarium.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful but fast, it can disturb slow fish. Timid, it feels better in a shoal of at least 6 to 8; the males then show their finest colours.

An undemanding omnivore, it accepts dry, frozen and live food. It breeds fairly easily: the eggs are laid among fine-leaved plants or a spawning mop, in slightly hard, alkaline water.

profil.repartition: Africa: from the Niger basins to the Congo basin
profil.presentation: The elephantnose fish, the most common of the Mormyridae in the hobby, probes the substrate with its “trunk”, an extension of the lower jaw. It emits weak electric discharges that help it find prey and communicate with others of its kind.
profil.habitat: It lives near the bottom in calm, heavily vegetated stretches of rivers, over dark, muddy bottoms. It hunts mainly at night, for worms and insects.
profil.comportement: Calm but territorial and aggressive towards its own kind and other Mormyridae, it is peaceful with other species. Keep it with calm African fish (butterflyfish, Congo tetras, Synodontis, Ctenopoma). It needs a fine, soft substrate, dim light and plenty of hiding places, otherwise it wastes away. It loves worms.

profil.repartition: Paraguay and Guaporé basins (Brazil, Bolivia, Argentina)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1895 by George Albert Boulenger of the British Museum, the black skirt tetra (or black widow tetra) owes its name to the rear half of its body, black like a mourning veil, which fades with age. It reaches 7.5 cm without the tail.

Many captive-bred forms exist: long-finned, albino, and genetically modified fluorescent strains sold under the GloFish brand in some countries. The classification revised in 2024 places the genus in the family Acestrorhamphidae.
profil.habitat:
It lives in the Rio Paraguay and Rio Guaporé basins, in Brazil, Bolivia and Argentina, in a subtropical region where the water can cool down in winter (20 to 26 °C).

It frequents small streams, tributaries and creeks with a slow current, usually lined with dense vegetation overhanging the water.
profil.comportement:
It is one of the best tetras for a community aquarium: lively and generally peaceful, it occupies the middle and upper layers of the water. Its reputation as a fin nipper usually disappears when it lives in a shoal of a dozen, the squabbles then staying within the group.

An undemanding omnivore, it feeds on worms, small crustaceans and insects. It breeds easily in a separate tank, scattering adhesive eggs among fine-leaved plants. Males are slimmer, with more pointed dorsal and anal fins.

profil.repartition: Paraná basin (Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina) and lower Uruguay (Uruguay, Brazil)
profil.presentation: This eartheater from southern South America is recognised by the strongly domed forehead of adult males. Several colour forms exist depending on the locality. A fascinating species, it is nevertheless for hobbyists able to provide the particular conditions it needs, including cooler water.
profil.habitat: It lives away from the main channels, in slow tributaries and creeks.
profil.comportement: Poorly suited to a community tank: males in particular tolerate other cichlids badly. Characins and medium-sized shoaling fish that occupy the top of the tank are generally left alone, provided they tolerate cooler water (Buenos Aires tetras, some Danio). It feeds only on the bottom: sinking food, small live or frozen prey and a little plant matter.

profil.repartition: Mae Klong, Chao Phraya, middle and lower Mekong and Dong Nai basins: Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam
profil.presentation: Sold as the “Chinese” or “Indian algae eater”, it lives in neither China nor India. Young fish are sold with no information on their temperament, adult size (28 cm) or lifespan, which can exceed 15 years. All fish in the trade are farmed; there are albino, golden and piebald forms, and the golden form is sometimes artificially coloured by injection.
profil.habitat: It lives in flowing streams, over boulders, pebbles, gravel and sand, often near submerged wood or roots, and moves into flooded fields. Attached to surfaces by its sucker mouth, it breathes through a small opening above the gills without letting go in the current.
profil.comportement: Despite common practice, it is poorly suited to a community tank: discreet when young, it becomes more and more territorial as it grows, very aggressive towards fish that look like it (Crossocheilus, Epalzeorhynchos, Garra), and may latch onto the flanks of slow or flat-bodied fish. An aufwuchs grazer: fresh vegetables (courgette, cucumber, peas), dry food and small live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Rio São Francisco basin, Minas Gerais (Brazil)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1875 by the Danish zoologist Christian Frederik Lütken, the silvertip (or copper) tetra has a coppery sheen and white tips on its fins; it has no adipose fin, which sets it apart from most tetras.

The genus *Hasemania* honours John D. Haseman, a collector for the Carnegie Museum in Brazil. The species measures about 4 cm without the tail.
profil.habitat:
It is endemic to the Rio São Francisco basin, in the state of Minas Gerais in Brazil.

It frequents creeks and tributaries rather than main channels, and is found in both clear and black water; it tolerates neutral to slightly alkaline water (pH 6 to 8).
profil.comportement:
Lively, colourful and peaceful, it is one of the best tetras for a community aquarium, with livebearers, danios, rasboras, other tetras and calm bottom-dwellers. Kept alone, it may nip fins; in a group of at least 6, ideally 10, this behaviour almost disappears.

It eats everything: dry food, live and frozen prey. It breeds easily in a separate tank, scattering adhesive eggs. Males are slimmer and more colourful than females.

profil.repartition: Southern Indochina (Vietnam, Cambodia, Thailand), Peninsular Malaysia, Borneo, Sumatra and Java
profil.presentation: The kissing gourami owes its name to the “kisses” exchanged by two individuals, which are actually a form of confrontation. The pink form, one of the best-selling in the world, does not exist in the wild: it is a selected leucistic variety. The deliberately deformed “balloon” form should be avoided.
profil.habitat: It prefers slow or still water (floodplain lakes, oxbows, marshes), black or clear, near submerged weed beds. The black water of ancient peat swamps can drop to pH 3 or 4. It breathes air at the surface.
profil.comportement: It only suits large community tanks of robust fish: unable to catch prey larger than a few millimetres, it can live with shoaling cyprinids, catfish, characins, cichlids and other anabantoids of suitable size. It becomes aggressive if short of space. A specialised filter feeder, it also scrapes algae with its lips lined with horny teeth: fine food and plant matter.

profil.repartition: West Africa: from Guinea to central Liberia (including Sierra Leone)
profil.presentation: Considered the true “jewel cichlid” of hobbyists, and now placed in the genus *Rubricatochromis*, it is also used as a study animal by physiologists and ethologists. It has three black spots on its flanks, one of them on the caudal peduncle, against two in *H. lifalili*, which has become more popular.
profil.habitat: It lives in small streams and canals over mud or sand, under overhanging and floating vegetation, inland, in intact or recently disturbed forest.
profil.comportement: Despite common practice, it suits neither beginners nor community tanks: territorial, it becomes extremely aggressive when breeding. It lives with large Alestidae (Congo tetras), Synodontis, Loricariidae and, in a large tank, other African cichlids such as Steatocranus. Keep it in a pair, ideally formed within a group of juveniles. It eats almost anything, with live prey and plant matter.

profil.repartition: Congo basin (except Katanga and Kasai): Democratic Republic of the Congo, Republic of the Congo and Central African Republic
profil.presentation: This red jewel cichlid, now placed in the genus *Rubricatochromis*, is often confused with *Hemichromis bimaculatus*: *H. lifalili* has only two black spots on its flanks, against three in *H. bimaculatus*, which has an extra one on the caudal peduncle.
profil.habitat: It lives in calm or slow creeks and tributaries that are nevertheless rich in oxygen, mostly in forest but also in savannah with gallery forests. It is absent from rapids and marshes. It spawns on an open surface and forms well-established pairs.
profil.comportement: Territorial, it becomes extremely aggressive when breeding but remains fairly calm the rest of the time. It lives with large Alestidae (Congo tetras), Synodontis and Loricariidae. Keep it in a pair: it is better to let a pair form within a group of juveniles, as two fish bought together often end with the death of the weaker one. Mostly carnivorous: live prey, dry food and a little plant matter.

profil.repartition: Rio Negro and Río Meta basins (Brazil, Colombia)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1986 by Jacques Géry and Volker Mahnert, this rummy-nose tetra is named after Heiko Bleher, the aquarist and explorer who discovered it. Its bright red head and black-and-white striped tail make it easy to spot; FishBase now places it in the genus *Petitella*, named after the French zoologist Georges Petit.

Three very similar species are sold as “rummy-nose tetras”: *H. rhodostomus*, *Petitella georgiae* and this one. They are told apart by the spots on the caudal peduncle and by the band extending the tail's central stripe into the body, almost absent here.
profil.habitat:
It lives in blackwater rivers and tributaries of the Rio Negro and Río Meta basins, in Brazil and Colombia.

The water there is stained brown by tannins released by decaying organic matter and is therefore very acidic and low in minerals.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful, it is one of the small tetras that form the tightest shoals: it should be kept in a group of at least 10, more if possible. It copes poorly with boisterous companions and often accompanies discus in blackwater aquariums.

An omnivore with a small mouth, it accepts flakes, granules and small live or frozen prey. Mature females are rounder; its adhesive eggs are laid among fine-leaved vegetation.

profil.repartition: Guyana: Essequibo basin
profil.presentation: The glowlight tetra, with its thin neon-orange line, is one of the best choices for beginners: hardy, cheap and available in almost every pet shop. All fish in the trade come from farms in Eastern Europe and Asia; there is also an albino form.
profil.habitat: It lives mainly in forest, in tributaries away from the main course of the Essequibo, in water stained brown by tannins and often very acidic.
profil.comportement: Lively, colourful and peaceful, it is one of the best tetras for a community tank: livebearers, Danio, Rasbora, other tetras, Corydoras, small Loricariidae, most gouramis and dwarf cichlids. It is not safe with large species such as the angelfish. Keep it in a shoal. It accepts almost anything; small live or frozen prey brighten its colours.

profil.repartition: Amazon basin, in Peru and Brazil; described from Lake Hyanuary, near Manaus
profil.presentation: Also called the “green neon” or “costello tetra”, this small tetra with a green sheen and a black tail spot is seen much less often in the trade than it used to be. It is sometimes confused with the head-and-tail-light tetra, of which it looks like a more elongated version.
profil.habitat: It lives in slow rivers, tributaries and floodplain lakes.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, it copes poorly with boisterous or much larger companions. Ideally, keep it with other small South American fish (tetras, pencilfish, Apistogramma, Corydoras, small Loricariidae). Always buy a group. It mainly eats small invertebrates: dry food and small live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana, and the Amazon basin in Brazil and Peru
profil.presentation: The head-and-tail-light tetra owes its name to the two bright spots on its eye and tail, like a ship's lights. Popular for decades, it is mass-bred for the trade; there is also an albino form.
profil.habitat: It lives in slow rivers, tributaries and floodplain lakes, in groups, in water with little current. It feeds on worms, small insects, crustaceans and plant matter.
profil.comportement: Hardy, lively and peaceful, it is one of the best choices for beginners and for community tanks: livebearers, Danio, Rasbora, other tetras, Corydoras, gouramis and dwarf cichlids. Not with large species that would eat it, such as the angelfish. Keep it in a shoal. It accepts almost anything, with small live or frozen prey for good colours.

profil.repartition: Upper Peruvian Amazon
profil.presentation:
Described in 1938 by the German ichthyologist Werner Ladiges, *pulcher* means “beautiful” in Latin. This tetra is recognised by the crescent-shaped black blotch on the rear of its body, topped by a coppery area, and by the red on the upper part of its eye. FishBase now places it in the genus *Holopristis*, as *Holopristis pulchra*.

Most fish sold in Europe come from fish farms in Eastern Europe. Beware: the name “diamond tetra” usually refers to another species, *Moenkhausia pittieri*.
profil.habitat:
Endemic to the upper Amazon basin in Peru, it lives in slow tributaries of large rivers, usually under forest cover.

The water there is tropical (23 to 27 °C), soft and acidic.
profil.comportement:
Lively and peaceful, it fits well into most community aquariums: other tetras, rasboras, danios, livebearers, corydoras and small loricariids. Rather shy, it should not live with much larger or boisterous fish.

A shoaling fish, it is kept in a group of at least 6, ideally 10. It breeds fairly easily in a separate tank: spawning takes place among plants and the eggs hatch in 20 to 24 hours. The sexes are told apart by the swim bladder, visible through the body: pointed in the male, rounded in the female.

profil.repartition: Orinoco basin and lower Amazon basin, in Venezuela and Brazil
profil.presentation: This is the “true” rummy-nose tetra, now placed in the genus *Petitella*. The fish most often sold under this name is actually the very similar *Hemigrammus bleheri*, as is the “false” rummy-nose *Petitella georgiae*; they are told apart notably by how far the red of the head extends into the body.
profil.habitat: It lives in blackwater rivers and tributaries, stained brown by tannins and very acidic.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, it copes poorly with boisterous or much larger companions. Keep it with other small South American fish (tetras, pencilfish, Apistogramma, Corydoras); it often accompanies discus. Keep it in a shoal. An omnivore with a small mouth: fine dry and live or frozen foods, varied for good colours.

profil.repartition: Amazon, Rio Negro and Orinoco basins, coastal rivers of Guyana (Brazil, Venezuela, Guyana)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1909 by Marion Durbin, the red-base tetra is recognised by the bright red at the base of its tail, dorsal and anal fins, on a silvery body. The classification revised in 2024 places the genus *Hemigrammus* in the family Acestrorhamphidae.

Its maximum size is debated: FishBase gives 4.3 cm total length, some authors cite up to 6 cm.
profil.habitat:
It is widespread in the Amazon basin, the Rio Negro, the Orinoco and the coastal rivers of Guyana. It lives in slow rivers, tributaries and floodplain lakes.

The water there is tropical (23 to 27 °C), rather soft and slightly acidic.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful, it cannot compete with boisterous or much larger companions. It lives well with other tetras, pencilfish, dwarf cichlids, corydoras and small loricariids.

A shoaling fish, it is kept in a group of at least 6, ideally 10. It feeds on small invertebrates and is not fussy in the aquarium. Adult males are slightly smaller and slimmer than females.

profil.repartition: Lower Rio Grande basin (Texas, United States) and north-eastern Mexico; introduced elsewhere in Texas, Florida and Mexico
profil.presentation: The only cichlid native to the United States, speckled with turquoise-blue dots. The type species of the genus *Herichthys*, it has been moved several times between this genus and *Cichlasoma*. Introduced outside its range, it forms wild populations there, notably in Florida.
profil.habitat: It prefers slow water: pools, deep holes and calm stretches of rivers, often near submerged rocks, branches or dense weed beds. It likes warm water and vegetation.
profil.comportement: Like most large cichlids, it is very belligerent and territorial, especially males and in a tank that is too small: it needs a very large aquarium and robust companions. It mainly eats aquatic invertebrates, but also plant matter: varied food, with a plant component.

profil.repartition: Amazon basin: Solimões and main course of the Amazon, tributaries of the Ucayali (Peru), reported from the Xingu
profil.presentation: The severum, one of the most popular and widely available cichlids, comes in a wild green form and a golden form. Many people do not realise that it grows quite large (30 cm) and is therefore not suited to every aquarium. Fish in the trade, long sold as *Heros severus*, mostly belong to this species.
profil.habitat: It lives in slow rivers, tributaries and floodplain lakes, mainly in deep, calm water among submerged roots and branches, but also in flooded areas and tidal estuaries.
profil.comportement: Outside breeding it is fairly calm for a cichlid of its size: a good choice for a tank of large, peaceful South American fish, with no fish small enough to be eaten. A lone fish may become cantankerous with age: the company of its own kind often prevents this. An omnivore, mainly a fruit eater in the wild: dry food, meaty prey and plant matter (peas, spinach, spirulina).

profil.repartition: Southeastern United States, from North Carolina (Cape Fear basin) to southern Louisiana
profil.presentation:
Described in 1859 by the French zoologist Charles Girard, who worked at the Smithsonian, *Heterandria formosa* is the smallest known livebearer and one of the smallest fish in the world: adult males measure about 1.5 cm, females just over 3 cm.

It interests biologists because of the way it reproduces: the female nourishes her embryos during gestation and carries several broods at different stages at the same time (superfetation), so that she gives birth to a few young almost every day. It is sometimes confused with mosquitofish, which are far more aggressive.
profil.habitat:
It is endemic to the southeastern United States, from North Carolina to Louisiana; the type localities are Charleston (South Carolina) and Palatka (Florida).

It lives in still or slow, shallow and heavily vegetated water: marsh margins, ponds, ditches, sometimes brackish water. The subtropical climate means it tolerates cooler water in winter.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful but tiny, it is not a community fish: many common species would eat it. It does best in a small colony, alone or with very small, calm species (pencilfish, dwarf corydoras, *Otocinclus*, shrimp).

An omnivore, it enjoys small live or frozen prey and grazes algae. It breeds without difficulty in a densely planted tank; the much smaller males have an outsized gonopodium.

profil.repartition: Endemic to the Volta Grande of the Rio Xingu (Pará, Brazil)
profil.presentation:
Arriving in Europe in the late 1980s under the code L046, the zebra pleco was described in 1991 by Isaäc Isbrücker and Han Nijssen, who created the genus *Hypancistrus* for it. Its black and white stripes make it one of the most sought-after loricariids; it does not exceed 8 cm.

The IUCN lists it as critically endangered. Brazil has banned its export since 2004, and the Belo Monte dam has greatly reduced the flow of the Xingu's Volta Grande, its only habitat. The fish sold in Europe today are captive-bred.
profil.habitat:
It is known only from one stretch of the Rio Xingu, the Volta Grande, a great loop of rapids in the state of Pará.

It lives in flowing, warm (26 to 30 °C) and highly oxygenated water, at depth, in crevices and rock piles resting on a sandy bottom.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful but shy, it is easily beaten to the food: it does best in a species tank, or with small midwater fish that tolerate the same heat (tetras, rasboras, discus, dwarf cichlids). Males are territorial towards each other around caves.

Contrary to the image of an “algae eater”, it is mainly carnivorous: bloodworms, mussels, shrimp and protein-rich tablets. It breeds in caves, the male guarding the eggs; adult males have a broader head and odontodes on the first pectoral fin ray.

profil.repartition: Rio Araguaia basin, central Brazil
profil.presentation:
Described in 1987 by Jacques Géry and André Uj, the ember tetra honours Amanda Bleher, mother of the explorer and aquarist Heiko Bleher, who took part in its discovery. It is one of the smallest *Hyphessobrycon*: about 2 cm without the tail.

It is also sold as the “dwarf red tetra” or “fire tetra”, referring to its bright orange colour.
profil.habitat:
It is native to the Rio Araguaia basin, a large tributary of the Tocantins in central Brazil. Field information is scarce, but it probably lives in small tributaries, oxbows and meander lakes rather than in the main channels.

In the Araguaia, these habitats have soft, slightly acidic water, with a bottom covered in leaf litter and branches.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful, it copes poorly with boisterous or much larger companions. It swims in the middle and upper layers of the water and does not hunt fry, which makes it an excellent “dither fish” for dwarf cichlids such as *Apistogramma*.

A micropredator, it feeds on tiny invertebrates and zooplankton: in the aquarium it accepts small dry food but benefits from brine shrimp or moina nauplii. A shoal of at least 8 to 10 makes it less fearful.

profil.repartition: Amazon basin (Brazil, Colombia, Peru); type locality at Óbidos, Pará
profil.presentation:
Described in 1908 by the American ichthyologist Marion Durbin, the rosy tetra is named after Colonel Bentos, a volunteer on Louis Agassiz's Thayer Expedition to Brazil (1865–1866), during which the type specimens were collected. The classification revised in 2024 places it in the genus *Megalamphodus*.

It belongs to the “rosy tetra clade” defined by Weitzman and Palmer in 1997: a pink to reddish body, a dark spot on the dorsal fin and elongated fins in males.
profil.habitat:
Its type locality lies on the main channel of the Amazon at Óbidos, between the mouths of the Trombetas and Tapajós rivers, and the species is reported from the Amazon basin in Brazil, Colombia and Peru.

Like related tetras, it mainly frequents slow tributaries, side channels and forest lakes, near roots, fallen branches, bank vegetation and aquatic plants. The water there is very low in minerals, weakly buffered and stained brown by tannins.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful, it forms temporary hierarchies in which males compete for the females' attention by spreading their dorsal and anal fins. A mixed group of at least 8 to 10 shows this behaviour and better colours.

An omnivore, it accepts a varied diet (small invertebrates, crustaceans, algae). An egg scatterer with no parental care, it often spawns when in good condition. Males are slimmer, slightly smaller and more colourful than females.

profil.repartition: Río Acandí, Chocó department, north-western Colombia near the Panamanian border
profil.presentation:
Described in 2002 by Axel Zarske and Jacques Géry, this tetra is named after its country of origin, Colombia. It is close to *Hyphessobrycon savagei*, endemic to Costa Rica, but differs by its clearly deeper body, an iridescent blue sheen on the upper body in both sexes and blood-red tail and anal fins.

The IUCN lists it as data deficient: its known range is tiny and its biology in the wild remains little studied.
profil.habitat:
The species is known only from the Río Acandí basin, in the Colombian Darién, on the Caribbean coast near the border with Panama. The type locality is a small stream about 6 km downstream from Acandí.

FishBase reports it from small coastal streams; in the absence of detailed measurements, aquarium parameters rely on breeders' experience: soft to slightly acidic water, between 24 and 29 °C.
profil.comportement:
Generally peaceful, it lives in a shoal and is more at ease in a mixed group of at least 8 to 10, with characins of similar size, small catfish and non-predatory cichlids. Its size (up to 7 cm) and liveliness make it a robust shoaling fish.

An omnivore, it probably feeds on worms, insects and zooplankton, with a little plant matter. The slimmer, more colourful males develop a longer dorsal fin; it is an egg scatterer with no parental care.

profil.repartition: Upper Solimões (Brazil) and Mana and Approuague rivers (French Guiana, Suriname)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1908 by the American ichthyologist Marion Durbin from material collected by the Thayer Expedition, this tetra is named after the ichthyologist Herbert Edson Copeland. The classification revised in 2024 places it in the genus *Megalamphodus*, with the red tetras of the *eques* group.

Its range is curiously fragmented, between the upper Amazon and the coastal rivers of the Guiana Shield. In French Guiana, “yaya” is the Creole name given to small characins of this kind.
profil.habitat:
It is often found in slow-flowing water or in the backwater zones of small creeks, with clear water and a sandy bottom. In French Guiana it occupies notably the upper reaches of rivers, above the falls.

Measurements indicate tropical water at 24 to 28 °C; its range includes the upper Solimões in Brazil, the Mana and Approuague basins in French Guiana, and Suriname.
profil.comportement:
Its capture in large numbers in the wild reflects gregarious behaviour: it is kept in a shoal of at least ten. Peaceful, it lives with other small South American fish.

An omnivore, it accepts small live prey and dry food. Its breeding in captivity has not been documented.

profil.repartition: Amazon, Guaporé and Paraguay basins (Brazil, Peru, Bolivia, Paraguay, Argentina, Uruguay)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1882 by Franz Steindachner, the serpae tetra (or jewel tetra) takes its Latin name *eques*, “horseman”, from its slender shape. The classification revised in 2024 places it in the genus *Megalamphodus*, reinstated for this group of red tetras.

Its wild populations vary greatly in colour depending on their origin, and several were once described as separate species. It belongs to a complex of “blood tetras” whose hybrids are common in the aquarium trade.
profil.habitat:
Its range is huge: much of the Amazon basin in Brazil, Peru and Bolivia, and the Paraguay basin down to Argentina, connected to Amazonia by the Rio Guaporé. The type locality is Óbidos, on the Amazon.

It mainly frequents calm or still water: slow tributaries, oxbows, ponds and small lakes. Shoals gather around bank vegetation, between the stems of emergent plants, or near submerged roots. It has been introduced to French Guiana through the aquarium trade.
profil.comportement:
Gregarious, it forms loose hierarchies in which males constantly compete for the females and their place in the group.
