It has a reputation for nipping other fish's fins, especially if there are too few of them or they are cramped: a group of at least 12 turns this aggression towards their own kind.

Avoid it with slow, long-finned fish (angelfish, bettas). An omnivore, it feeds on worms, crustaceans, insects and plant matter; it is an egg scatterer with no parental care.

profil.repartition: Upper Amazon, Brazil–Peru–Colombia tri-border region, from the Rio Purus to the Río Nanay
profil.presentation:
Described in 1943 by Henry W. Fowler, the bleeding heart tetra owes its name to the bright red spot on its flank, behind the gill cover; *erythrostigma* comes from the Greek for “red mark”. This red humeral spot exists in no other characin apart from two closely related species (*H. socolofi* and *H. pyrrhonotus*).

The classification revised in 2024 places it in the genus *Megalamphodus*. At over 6 cm, it is one of the largest tetras in its group.
profil.habitat:
It lives in the upper Amazon basin, in the region where the borders of Brazil, Peru and Colombia meet, from the Rio Purus to the Río Nanay basin near Iquitos.

It frequents slow tributaries, side channels and forest lakes, near roots, fallen branches, overhanging vegetation or aquatic plants. The water, very low in minerals and stained brown, can drop below pH 4: in some igarapés, measurements found a pH of 3.8 to 6.4 and oxygen-poor water.
profil.comportement:
Generally peaceful, it suits a well-planned community aquarium, but adult males defend a small territory. Their displays, with dorsal, pelvic and anal fins spread, are spectacular; a mixed group of at least 8 to 10 makes it possible to watch them.

An opportunistic omnivore, in the wild it feeds mainly on fruit fallen into the water, supplemented by insects and their larvae. It is an egg scatterer that does not care for its eggs.

profil.repartition: South-eastern Brazil: Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo states (Guanabara Bay, Rio Paraíba do Sul, upper Rio Tietê)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1924 by George S. Myers, the flame tetra (or “tetra from Rio”) owes its Latin name *flammeus* (“flame-coloured”) to its orange-red colouring. It was redescribed in 2014, which clarified the features that separate it from related species: two well-marked vertical humeral spots and a transparent tail fin.

The IUCN lists it as endangered. Its wild populations, in heavily urbanised regions around Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo, have declined sharply; on the other hand, it is bred commercially in several countries, in orange, golden, “diamond” and albino forms.
profil.habitat:
It lives in small, shallow streams (under 50 cm) with a slow current, often overgrown with aquatic vegetation, and more rarely along the edges of the main channel of the upper Rio Tietê. The water there is clear to brownish, over sand, between 22 and 28 °C.

Its range includes the coastal rivers flowing into Guanabara Bay, the middle Rio Paraíba do Sul and the Rio Guandu in Rio de Janeiro state, as well as the upper Rio Tietê in São Paulo state.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful, it forms fairly large shoals within which dominant males establish temporary hierarchies and display to the females: a group of at least 8 to 10 shows these interactions and better colours.

An omnivore, it eats small insects, worms, filamentous algae and organic debris. The female lays 200 to 300 eggs on plants or submerged debris; they hatch in 2 to 3 days. The slimmer, more colourful males have small bony hooks on the anal and pelvic fins.

profil.repartition: Upper Rio Paraguai basin, around the Pantanal (Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1961 by Jacques Géry, the black neon tetra is named after Herbert R. Axelrod, an American publisher and author of aquarium books. Despite its common name, it is not a *Paracheirodon*: it is recognised by the double pale-and-black band along its flank and the bright red upper part of its eye.

It belongs to the “*H. agulha* group”, species whose lower half of the body is dark, especially above the anal fin.
profil.habitat:
The species seems widespread in the upper Rio Paraguai, both north and south of the Pantanal, Brazil's great tropical wetland. Its type locality is in the upper Rio Taquari basin, near Coxim; it has also been observed in the upper Rio Sepotuba, 700 km further north.

It frequents small tributaries, headwater rivers, oxbows and seasonal floodplains. These streams, a few metres wide, have clear, slightly brownish water and thick bank vegetation, sometimes beds of *Echinodorus* or *Eleocharis*.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful, it swims in the middle and upper layers of the water and feeds on worms, small crustaceans and plant matter. A mixed group of at least 8 to 10 gives it natural shoaling behaviour.

It spawns in open water, with no parental care; the eggs hatch in 24 to 30 hours. Adult females are deeper-bodied and slightly larger than males.

profil.repartition: Eastern Brazilian Amazon: Pará and Maranhão, from the Rio Tapajós to the Atlantic coastal rivers
profil.presentation:
Described in 1894 by Albert Ulrey, the flag tetra (or “Belgian flag tetra”) has a black lateral band edged with gold and red that recalls the three colours of the Belgian flag. Its name comes from the Greek *heteros* (“other”) and *rhabdos* (“rod”), probably referring to this stripe.

The name was long applied to similar fish from all over Amazonia, the Orinoco and the Guianas; several of these populations have since been described as separate species (*H. amapaensis*, *H. eschwartzae*, *H. montagi*).
profil.habitat:
In the strict sense, the species lives in the eastern Brazilian Amazon: tributaries and coastal rivers of Pará and Maranhão states, around Belém (Guamá, Acará, Tocantins, Xingu, Gurupi, Pindaré rivers…), as far as the Rio Tapajós.

It has almost always been collected in terra firme igarapés, the small headwater streams that are not flooded every year. Shaded by the forest, they have clear water over sand or mud, with roots, branches and leaf litter, but usually no aquatic plants.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful, it feeds on worms, small crustaceans and plant debris. It lives in a shoal: a mixed group of at least 8 to 10, accompanied by other shoaling fish, makes it more confident.

It is an egg scatterer with no parental care; adults in good condition spawn often, and a few fry may appear spontaneously in a well-established aquarium. Adult females are deeper-bodied and slightly larger than males.

profil.repartition: Upper Rio Madeira basin (Guaporé, Mamoré, Beni) in Bolivia and Brazil, and upper Rio Paraguay (Pantanal)
profil.presentation: The black phantom tetra, with its large dark fins, is popular and bred commercially in several countries; there is a long-finned form. Males compete for the females by displaying with fins spread, without injuring each other.
profil.habitat: It lives in calm tributaries and oxbows, pools and small lakes, in groups near bank vegetation or submerged roots. In the Pantanal it frequents very clear water rich in aquatic plants (*Echinodorus*, *Bacopa*, *Ludwigia*, *Salvinia*).
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, ideal in a community tank with characins, hatchetfish, pencilfish, Corydoras or small Loricariidae and medium-sized non-predatory cichlids. A mixed group of at least 8 to 10 is needed, within which males establish passing hierarchies. An omnivore: dry food, live and frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Brazil: Tapajós basin, perhaps also the Xingu
profil.presentation: The lemon tetra owes its Latin name (“beautiful fins”) to the bright yellow of its fins and the pale yellow sheen of its body. The cheap fish in the trade come from farms; the origin of the commercial strain remains uncertain, and there is an albino form.
profil.habitat: It probably frequents small tributaries, small rivers, oxbows and flooded forests rather than the main channels.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, ideal in a community tank with characins, hatchetfish, pencilfish, Corydoras or small Loricariidae and non-predatory cichlids. A mixed group of at least 8 to 10 is needed, within which males compete for the females. An omnivore: dry food, live and frozen prey, for good colours.

profil.repartition: Guyana, Suriname and Brazil: Essequibo, Corantijn and Suriname basins
profil.presentation: This rosy tetra with a black, white-edged dorsal fin looks almost identical to *Hyphessobrycon bentosi*, of which it was long considered a subspecies; *H. bentosi* has a dark mark just behind the gill cover, absent in *H. rosaceus*. Fish in the trade come from farms.
profil.habitat: It lives mainly in forest, in slow tributaries away from the main channels, in water stained brown by tannins and very acidic.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, it copes poorly with boisterous or much larger companions. Keep it with other small South American fish (tetras, pencilfish, Apistogramma, Corydoras, small Loricariidae), or in a community tank with small Rasbora, barbs, anabantoids and Pelvicachromis. Keep it in a shoal. It eats small invertebrates: dry food and small live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Brazil: Rio Negro basin (Branco, Padauari, Marauiá) and Rio Nhamundá
profil.presentation: Named after the American fish dealer Ross Socolof, this tetra belongs to the “bleeding heart” group, with *H. erythrostigma* and *H. pyrrhonotus*: all have a red spot behind the gill cover, a feature found in no other characin.
profil.habitat: It lives mainly in slow tributaries, side channels and forest lakes, often near roots, fallen branches, bank vegetation or aquatic plants. The water, almost free of minerals, is stained brown by tannins.
profil.comportement: Peaceful, it suits a well-planned community tank, but adult males are slightly territorial, sometimes towards species of the same shape. Keep it with characins of similar size, hatchetfish, pencilfish, Corydoras or small Loricariidae and non-predatory cichlids. In a mixed group of at least 8 to 10. An opportunistic omnivore, mainly a fruit eater in the wild: varied food.

profil.repartition: Upper and middle Orinoco basin, in Colombia and Venezuela (Atabapo, Guaviare, Inírida, Meta, Arauca, Apure, Caura...)
profil.presentation: The red phantom tetra, named after the fish distributor Kyle Swegles, is popular and bred commercially in several countries; wild fish are fairly rare in the trade. A particularly colourful form, called “red”, keeps its bright red in captivity.
profil.habitat: It prefers small tributaries, small rivers, oxbows and flooded forests. In the Venezuelan llanos it frequents morichales, with clear water over sand rich in plants, and elsewhere flowing black water or floodplain lakes.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, ideal in a community tank with characins of similar size, hatchetfish, pencilfish, Corydoras or small Loricariidae and non-predatory cichlids. A mixed group of at least 8 to 10 is needed, within which males compete for the females. An omnivore: dry food, live and frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Brazil (Mato Grosso): Rio Aripuanã and upper Rio Madeira basin
profil.presentation: The only species in its genus, this royal blue tetra is sold under several names (“blue emperor”, “royal tetra”). It is sometimes confused with the emperor tetra *Nematobrycon palmeri*, but it has an adipose fin, which *Nematobrycon* lacks.
profil.habitat: It lives mainly in forest, in slow tributaries away from the main channels, in water stained brown by tannins and very acidic.
profil.comportement: Peaceful, it copes poorly with boisterous or much larger companions. Keep it with small tetras, pencilfish, hatchetfish, Apistogramma, Corydoras and Otocinclus, or with small gouramis, Rasbora and peaceful barbs. Its reputation as a fin nipper is largely undeserved. Keep it in a shoal. Dry food, with regular small live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Endemic to southern Lake Malawi: Boadzulu, Chinyankwazi and Chinyamwezi islands
profil.presentation: One of the smallest and least aggressive mbuna, with a rusty, purplish colouring. Its temperament, its discreet but unusual colours and its small size make it an excellent first mbuna, content with a more modest tank. It is listed as near threatened.
profil.habitat: It lives in shallow coastal zones along rocky shores.
profil.comportement: Easily dominated by larger, boisterous species, it needs carefully chosen companions: Aulonocara, Copadichromis, Protomelas or Labidochromis caeruleus, even some calm Tanganyikan species. Rival males are territorial. An omnivore: plant matter (spirulina, spinach) should make up a large part of its diet, supplemented with small live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Southern New Guinea (from Merauke to the Fly River, Indonesia and Papua New Guinea) and northern Australia
profil.presentation: Males of this tiny rainbowfish have long filaments on their dorsal and anal fins, hence its English names “threadfin” or “featherfin rainbowfish”. Widespread and bred commercially, it is nevertheless delicate and has precise needs: it is not a fish for beginners.
profil.habitat: It prefers slow streams, marshes, lagoons and billabongs with clear, plant-rich water, especially in margins less than 1.5 m deep, often near water lilies. Females and young form shoals, while males defend small territories in open water where they display.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, it does not suit a classic community tank: its food gets stolen and the males' long fins attract nippers. Keep it alone or with fish of similar size and temperament (Pseudomugil, Boraras, dwarf Corydoras, Otocinclus). Its tiny mouth needs very fine food, mostly live (Artemia, Daphnia, microworms).

profil.repartition: United States: Florida peninsula, south of the Ochlockonee and St Johns basins
profil.presentation: This flagfish, named after the ichthyologist David Starr Jordan, is a classic of the hobby and bred commercially. It is not an annual killifish. It was listed in the Guinness Book of Records as the fish that lays the fewest eggs: about twenty, over several days. The male guards the eggs.
profil.habitat: It lives in shallow, weed-choked water: oxbows, marshes, canals and ditches, pools, lakes and slow streams, sometimes in slightly brackish water.
profil.comportement: It is best kept alone, especially for breeding, but can live in a well-planned community tank if it has enough room: each male defends a territory, which usually makes it possible to keep two or more. A micropredator that also eats algae: dry food, small live or frozen prey and plant matter. It likes cooler water.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Tanganyika (Burundi, DR Congo, Zambia), especially at the northern and southern ends
profil.presentation: This checkered “julie” is a cichlid full of character, which swims pressed against the rocks whatever their angle. Several geographic forms are available. As with other Julidochromis, large water changes can drive pairs to kill each other.
profil.habitat: It lives along rocky shores, in fairly deep water. A typical rock-dweller, it never ventures far from their shelter and does not swim in open water; it spawns in crevices and caves.
profil.comportement: Territorial, it lives with other Tanganyikan cichlids of similar size (Altolamprologus, Cyprichromis). Except in a very large tank, keep it as a pair, as adults are very aggressive towards each other. A good share of live and frozen prey, quality dry food and a little plant matter.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Tanganyika (Burundi, DR Congo, Tanzania, Zambia)
profil.presentation: The largest of the “julies”, striped with dark bands along the body, it is also the least aggressive of the genus. Several geographic forms are available. As with other Julidochromis, large water changes can drive pairs to kill each other.
profil.habitat: Widespread throughout the lake, it is less tied to rocks than its cousins: it is found mainly over sandy bottoms scattered with rocks, in shallow water, but it always spawns in rocky caves.
profil.comportement: Territorial, it lives with other Tanganyikan cichlids (Altolamprologus, Cyprichromis). Except in a very large tank, keep it as a pair, as it is aggressive towards its own kind. Mostly live and frozen prey, dry food less often, and a little plant matter.

profil.repartition: Mekong and Chao Phraya basins, Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Borneo and Java
profil.presentation:
Described in 1840 by the French zoologist Achille Valenciennes from fish from Java, *Kryptopterus bicirrhis* is a catfish of the family Siluridae. *Kryptopterus* means “hidden fin”, for its tiny dorsal fin, and *bicirrhis* “two barbels”.

Its name was long wrongly applied to the aquarium glass catfish (*K. vitreolus*), which is smaller and transparent. It reaches 15 cm and remains rare in the hobby. In Cambodia it is used to make prahok, a fermented fish paste.
profil.habitat:
It is widespread across much of Southeast Asia: Mekong, Chao Phraya, Batang Hari, Rajang, Kapuas and many smaller rivers, from Thailand to Vietnam, Malaysia and the Sunda Islands.

It lives in large, turbid rivers, often in the current near the banks, and moves into flooded fields in the rainy season; in the lakes of Danau Sentarum, on Borneo, it is abundant at the end of the wet season. It forms shoals of up to a hundred fish.
profil.comportement:
Gregarious and diurnal, it lives in a shoal: at least 4, ideally about ten, in a tank of at least one metre. It remains peaceful with fish of similar size.

A predator, it feeds mainly on surface insects (water bugs), crustaceans and small fish; in the aquarium it accepts sinking food, bloodworms and tubifex. Its breeding is not documented; adult males are slimmer.

profil.repartition: Western Borneo (West Kalimantan, Indonesia)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1989 by Tyson Roberts, *Kryptopterus minor* is a small translucent catfish of about 7 cm. The name was long wrongly used in the trade for the glass catfish, which is actually *K. vitreolus*, described in 2013.

It belongs to the “*bicirrhis* group” of *Kryptopterus*, catfish with a compressed body, a reduced dorsal fin and two long barbels. The IUCN lists it as near threatened.
profil.habitat:
It is known from western Borneo, in the Indonesian province of West Kalimantan, which drains notably the Kapuas basin.

Reference sources give few details of its habitat; FishBase gives tropical water (24 to 28 °C) of low to medium hardness.
profil.comportement:
Like its relatives, it is a shoaling fish that stays in open water and must live in a group of at least 6 to 10 to avoid wasting away.

Peaceful and rather shy, it feeds on small invertebrates and zooplankton. Its breeding in the aquarium is not documented.

profil.repartition: Coastal rivers of peninsular Thailand and south-eastern Thailand (Cardamom Mountains)
profil.presentation:
The aquarium glass catfish was only described in 2013, by Ng Heok Hee and Maurice Kottelat, as *Kryptopterus vitreolus* (“little glass fish”). Before that it was sold as *K. bicirrhis* or *K. minor*, two different species. A small anecdote: the original paper left out the words “new species”, which forced the authors to publish a short note to make the name valid.

Its almost completely transparent body reveals its skeleton; its two long barbels help it sense its surroundings. It measures about 6.5 cm without the tail.
profil.habitat:
It is known only from the coastal rivers of peninsular Thailand flowing into the Gulf of Thailand south of the Isthmus of Kra, and from a few rivers in the Cardamom Mountains, in the south-east of the country; the type locality is in Trat province.

It prefers slow or still water, brown and turbid or black and acidic. Heavily collected for the hobby and never bred commercially, it is being watched for the state of its wild populations.
profil.comportement:
Very gregarious, it forms tight shoals and wastes away if kept alone: a group of at least 6 is a minimum. It hovers motionless in open water, slightly tilted, facing the current.

Peaceful but shy, it copes poorly with large or boisterous companions; it may eat eggs and fry. A predator of small invertebrates and zooplankton, it appreciates fine live or frozen prey. Its breeding is not documented.

profil.repartition: Endemic to north-western Lake Malawi; the yellow “electric yellow” form is known only between Charo and Lion's Cove
profil.presentation: One of the most popular African lake cichlids, thanks to its brilliant colour and its fairly calm temperament for a mbuna. The bright yellow form so widespread in aquariums is actually one of the rarest in the wild, where the blue-and-white form dominates.
profil.habitat: It frequents two different habitats in the lake: rocky areas and dense beds of *Vallisneria*.
profil.comportement: Relatively peaceful, it suits many hard-water tanks: in a Malawi biotope with peaceful haplochromines, or with rainbowfish and some hard-water cyprinids. It can live in a group but becomes territorial when breeding; males chase females vigorously, hence several females per male. Mostly plant matter, supplemented with live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Brazil: lower reaches of Amazon tributaries
profil.presentation: This small cichlid is nicknamed the “smiling acara”: its genus name comes from the Latin *laetus*, “joyful”, because of the markings around its mouth that make it look as if it is smiling. A classic of the hobby, its populations differ in the extent of red and blue on the body and fins.
profil.habitat: It prefers clear, transparent water with little current and little sediment: small tributaries, oxbows and marginal lakes, over a bed of leaf litter with plants (*Cabomba*, *Myriophyllum*, *Eichhornia*).
profil.comportement: A calm little cichlid, it is kept as a pair in a planted tank with peaceful fish. In the wild it sifts the bottom for algae, detritus, small insects, worms and crustaceans. Easy to feed, it keeps its best colours with small live or frozen prey (bloodworms, Daphnia, Artemia).

profil.repartition: Upper and middle Orinoco, Casiquiare canal and Rio Negro (Venezuela, Brazil)
profil.presentation:
Known to hobbyists as *Laetacara* sp. “orangeflossen” (“orange fins”), this small cichlid was described in 2007 by Wolfgang Staeck and Ingo Schindler. Its name *fulvipinnis* means “with tawny fins”.

*Laetacara* combines the Latin *laetus*, “joyful”, and *acará*, the Amerindian name for cichlids: the markings around the mouth give these fish a smiling look. It reaches about 7.5 cm.
profil.habitat:
It lives in the upper and middle Orinoco, the Casiquiare canal and the upper and middle Rio Negro, between Puerto Ayacucho in Venezuela and Barcelos in Brazil; the type locality is a lagoon near San Carlos de Río Negro.

It is a fish of clear, tea-coloured black water, extremely soft and acidic: a measurement in the Casiquiare gave a pH of 4.4. It stays along the edges of streams, in 10 to 50 cm of water, in the leaf litter or among flooded terrestrial vegetation.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful for a cichlid, it lives in pairs and suits a blackwater aquarium with calm fish. It sifts the leaf litter for algae, detritus, small insects, worms and crustaceans.

The pair spawns on a hard surface, often a leaf, and guards the eggs together; they hatch in about three days, and the fry swim freely a week later. In the breeding season both sexes take on red colouring; males have longer fins.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Tanganyika (Burundi, DR Congo, Tanzania, Zambia)
profil.presentation: This tiny cichlid lives and breeds in empty shells of *Neothauma* snails. It has the endearing habit of burying its shell and defending it against all comers, sometimes by nipping the aquarist's hand; it also buries neighbouring shells to stop other fish moving in.
profil.habitat: It lives in open sandy areas scattered with rocks, where the bottom is covered in empty snail shells. It is found in small groups, sometimes mixed with *L. brevis*, with which it may compete for shell beds.
profil.comportement: It vigorously defends its shell and the small territory around it, but tolerates species from other zones of the tank: rock cichlids such as *Neolamprologus brichardi* or small Julidochromis, and Cyprichromis in open water. In a group it forms a colony: provide more shells than fish. Mostly live and frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Greater Antilles: Jamaica and Haiti
profil.presentation: This small livebearer from the Antilles, whose female has a black belly patch, has switched genus several times between *Limia* and *Poecilia*: it is still found as *Poecilia melanogaster* in much of the literature. It is uncommon in the trade and listed as near threatened.
profil.habitat: It lives in small streams, near the surface, where it feeds on worms, crustaceans, insects and plant matter.
profil.comportement: Peaceful, it lives with other small fish that tolerate hard water. Very undemanding, it accepts most foods, with a plant component.

profil.repartition: China south of the Yangtze (with Taiwan and Hainan), northern and central Vietnam, north-eastern Laos; introduced to many countries
profil.presentation: The paradise fish is one of the very first ornamental fish imported to Europe: a French soldier, Gérault, brought back about a hundred in 1869, of which 22 survived and were bred the same year in Paris by Pierre Carbonnier. The male builds a bubble nest.
profil.habitat: Very adaptable, it lives in all kinds of lowland habitats: streams, oxbows, pools, irrigation canals, rice paddies and reservoirs, sometimes hill streams. It is an obligate air breather and colonises still water very poor in oxygen.
profil.comportement: Avoid fish of the same shape, but it lives with peaceful shoaling species with similar needs. Males aggressively defend a territory, especially when breeding: a single male unless the tank is very large, with two or more females. Small live or frozen prey (Daphnia, Artemia, white worms) and quality dry food. It tolerates cool water.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Malawi: Mozambique coast, from Metangula and Minos Reef to Gome
profil.presentation: This popular mbuna was only described in 1995: before that it was considered a form of the zebra *Maylandia zebra*. Its genus is still debated, between *Maylandia*, *Metriaclima* and *Pseudotropheus*. Pale blue males and bright orange females earn it the name “red zebra”.
profil.habitat: It lives on the lake's rocky shores and reefs, where it grazes algae; males are territorial there.
profil.comportement: Not very aggressive for a mbuna, but robust: do not keep it with peaceful species (Aulonocara, Copadichromis) but with other mbuna of similar size. A well-stocked tank limits aggression, with several females per male and a single male unless the tank is very large. Plant matter (spirulina, spinach, nori) should dominate its diet; never beef heart or meat.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Malawi (Malawi), including Likoma and Chizumulu islands
profil.presentation: The Malawi zebra, blue barred with black in the male, is one of the most aggressive mbuna and is in no way suited to a classic tropical tank. A maternal mouthbrooder, it breeds best in a species tank, as a harem of one male to at least three females.
profil.habitat: It lives in the lake's rocky areas, at varying depths around shores, reefs and islands. It combs algae and biofilm deposits from the rocks and also feeds on plankton in open water.
profil.comportement: It suits most mbuna tanks, but not with gentle species such as Aulonocara. Three females per male, and a single male in a tank of under 200 L, to spread out aggression. Plant matter (spirulina, spinach, nori) should form the basis of its diet, with little protein. Sensitive to water quality: flawless filtration and maintenance.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Malawi: the whole west coast, the southern end and the south of the east coast
profil.presentation: This very common golden mbuna with black stripes is not recommended for beginners because of its intolerance. The dark males can revert to the golden colouring under stress, and old females sometimes darken so much that they look like males.
profil.habitat: It lives in rocky areas along shores, reefs and islands, where it picks algae from the rocks.
profil.comportement: One of the most aggressive and territorial mbuna, especially towards its own kind. Keep it with other mbuna of different patterns, never with peaceful species (Aulonocara, Copadichromis) or other Melanochromis (hybridisation). It needs a very large, well-stocked tank and several females per male. Mostly plant matter (spirulina, spinach), supplemented with live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Lakes Ajamaru, Hain and Aitinjo, Vogelkop Peninsula (West Papua, Indonesia)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1980 by Gerald Allen and Norbert Cross, Boeseman's rainbowfish is named after the Dutch ichthyologist Marinus Boeseman. The adult male is spectacular: the front of the body blue-grey, the rear orange-yellow, with a very high back.

The IUCN lists it as endangered: its range is tiny, and mass collection for the hobby in the 1980s greatly reduced its populations. Fish in the trade now come from farms.
profil.habitat:
It is known only from the Ajamaru Lakes, in the heart of the Vogelkop Peninsula (the “bird's head” of New Guinea), and the neighbouring lakes Hain and Aitinjo. These lakes drain into the Kais River and then the Ceram Sea.

The fish gather in clear shallows covered in dense aquatic vegetation. The lake water is hard, alkaline (pH 8 to 9) and warm, although the species also lives in a few tributaries with quite different water.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful but lively and rather timid, it does best in a shoal of at least 6 to 8, in a long tank. Its fast movements can disturb slow or smaller fish; it lives with other rainbowfish, barbs, danios and even hard-water African cichlids.

An undemanding omnivore, it colours up better with live or frozen prey. It scatters its eggs among fine-leaved plants or a spawning mop; the tiny fry are delicate to raise.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Kutubu and the Soro River, Southern Highlands (Papua New Guinea)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1964 by Ian Munro, the Lake Kutubu rainbowfish (or “turquoise rainbowfish”) is a brilliant turquoise blue in the adult male, with a back that rises with age. It reaches about twelve centimetres.

The IUCN lists it as endangered, as its entire range is limited to a single lake and its outflowing river.
profil.habitat:
Lake Kutubu, one of the largest lakes in Papua New Guinea, formed when volcanic debris dammed a valley. Very isolated, it is home to 14 fish species, 10 of them endemic. The lake drains through the Soro River, in the Kikori basin, about 220 km from the sea.

The water is very clear, calm, hard and alkaline, rather cool for the tropics (20 to 25 °C); the rainbowfish gather near weed beds, roots and submerged logs.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful but lively, it lives in a shoal of at least 6 to 8 and can disturb slower fish. It lives with other rainbowfish, barbs, danios, corydoras and hard-water cichlids.

An undemanding omnivore, it colours up better with live or frozen prey. It scatters its eggs among fine-leaved plants; breeding is easy, raising the fry more delicate.

profil.repartition: Endemic to the Mamberamo basin, northern New Guinea (Papua, Indonesia)
profil.presentation: This small neon-blue rainbowfish with red fins (yellow in the female) comes from one of the largest rivers in New Guinea, more than 2,000 km long. It scatters its eggs and breeds easily, but the fry are delicate to raise at first.
profil.habitat: It frequents the river's fast-flowing tributaries and the surrounding marshes, and gathers near aquatic vegetation, roots and submerged logs.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful and small, it suits many community tanks: other rainbowfish, tetras, Danio, barbs, dwarf cichlids, freshwater gobies, Corydoras. Fairly timid, it feels much better in a shoal of at least 6 to 8, where males show their finest colours. An omnivore, it accepts almost anything, with live prey for brilliance.

profil.repartition: Amazon (Tapajós, Jamari, Madre de Dios, Guaporé, Mamoré) and Paraguay basins: Peru, Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay
profil.presentation: The festivum, or flag cichlid, is recognised by the dark oblique band running from the mouth to the tip of the dorsal fin. Still popular, it is found in most pet shops, but the fish sold under this name is usually *Mesonauta insignis*.
profil.habitat: It lives in slow, heavily vegetated water, along sandy or muddy banks, near aquatic plants.
profil.comportement: A peaceful cichlid, more aggressive when breeding. It lives with other calm cichlids (Geophagus, Apistogramma) and peaceful community fish (tetras, barbs, small catfish), but very small fish may be eaten. A generalist omnivore: prepared foods, live prey (bloodworms, Artemia) and a little plant matter.

profil.repartition: Amazon and Paraguay basins and rivers of the northern Guiana Shield: Guyana, Brazil, Peru, Bolivia
profil.presentation: This silver dollar, a vegetarian cousin of the piranhas, is sold under the same name as *Metynnis argenteus*, almost identical in appearance and care; *M. hypsauchen* has a black spot a little above and behind each eye. Its powerful teeth can inflict serious bites.
profil.habitat: It lives in densely vegetated tributaries.
profil.comportement: Peaceful, it is kept in a group of at least five with other large, calm species, but much smaller fish may be eaten. It occupies the middle and top of the tank: large peaceful catfish (Loricariidae, Doradidae) complete the bottom well. It devours plants: plenty of vegetables (courgette, cucumber, peas, lettuce), spirulina and dry food.

profil.repartition: Amazon basin (Brazil, Peru)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1878 by Edward Drinker Cope, *Metynnis luna* is one of the fish sold as “silver dollars”, for their round, very flattened body, silvery like a coin. Like the pacus, they are Serrasalmidae, herbivorous cousins of the piranhas.

It reaches about 13 cm without the tail. FishBase notes that it filters phytoplankton with long gill rakers, as well as grazing plants.
profil.habitat:
It is native to the Amazon basin, in Brazil and Peru.

*Metynnis* live in shoals in rivers, lakes and flooded areas rich in vegetation, in warm, soft, slightly acidic water.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful and gregarious, it must live in a group of at least 5, in a large tank with swimming space. Nervous when kept alone, it calms down in a group and with hiding places.

A herbivore, it devours most aquarium plants: choose robust or artificial plants and a diet rich in plant matter (vegetables, spirulina flakes). It lives well with medium-sized, peaceful fish.

profil.repartition: Congo basin (Republic of the Congo, DR Congo) and Chiloango River
profil.presentation: The most colourful of the African anabantoids, much sought after: a male in breeding dress, orange barred with dark bands, is a sight to behold. Hard to collect in numbers, it remains fairly rare in the trade. The male builds a bubble nest.
profil.habitat: It lives in small streams, in dense vegetation near the banks. It can breathe air at the surface.
profil.comportement: Slow, it is outcompeted at feeding time by boisterous species: keep it with small, peaceful fish of other levels (hatchetfish, lampeyes, Corydoras, small Loricariidae), or better in a species tank. Males may fight, especially when breeding. Mostly small live or frozen prey; it rarely accepts dry food.

profil.repartition: Western peninsular Thailand (Ranong, Phang Nga) and Salween basin down to southern Myanmar
profil.presentation:
Described in 1999 by Maurice Kottelat and Kai-Erik Witte, this tiny neon-green cyprinid is named after Katsuma Kubota, who helped the authors in the field in Thailand. It is sold as the “neon green rasbora” or “Microrasbora kubotai”.

The genus *Microdevario* was created in 2009 after phylogenetic analyses showed that some *Microrasbora* were actually closer to *Devario*. The species is recognised by its transparent dorsal and anal fins.
profil.habitat:
It is known from Ranong and Phang Nga provinces, on the north-western side of the Thai peninsula, and from the basin of the Ataran River, a tributary of the Salween in southern Myanmar; an introduced population exists in the upper Khwae Noi basin.

Its rivers have clear, well-oxygenated water, a bottom of branches, leaves, gravel and rocks, and heavily vegetated banks; *Cryptocoryne crispatula* and *Pogostemon helferi* grow in the calm stretches.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful, in the wild it lives in shoals of 20 to 50 fish. In the aquarium it is kept alone or with species of similar size (*Boraras*, harlequins, small loaches), in a group of at least 8 to 10.

It feeds on small invertebrates and zooplankton; fine live or frozen prey suit it better than dry food alone. An egg scatterer with no parental care, it has been bred in the aquarium. Males are more compact and more colourful than females.

profil.repartition: North-eastern coast of South America, from Trinidad to the Amazon delta (Trinidad and Tobago, Guyana, French Guiana, Brazil)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1913 by Charles Tate Regan as *Poecilia picta* (“painted”), the swamp guppy is a close relative of the guppy. Some authors place it in the genus *Micropoecilia*, others, like FishBase, keep it in *Poecilia*.

The male, which barely exceeds 3 cm, wears orange or red colouring barred with black, while the silvery female reaches 5 cm. Unlike the guppy, there are almost no captive-bred forms: the fish sold remain close to the wild form.
profil.habitat:
It lives along the north-eastern coast of South America, from Trinidad to the Amazon delta, via Guyana and French Guiana.

It mainly frequents the slightly brackish water of canals and drainage ditches along coastal marshes, but also travels quite far inland. The water there is warm (26 to 28 °C), hard and alkaline; a little salt benefits it in the aquarium.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful, it lives in a group and suits a species tank or one shared with other small species that tolerate hard or even brackish water. It is more delicate than the guppy and copes poorly with soft, acidic water.

A livebearer like the guppy, it gives birth to fully formed fry; several females per male reduce harassment. It feeds on small prey and algae.

profil.repartition: Upper Rio Madeira basin (Mamoré, Guaporé, Orthon), in Bolivia and Brazil
profil.presentation: This dwarf cichlid, sold as the “Bolivian ram”, is probably a better choice for a less experienced hobbyist than its cousin *M. ramirezi*. Its name comes from the elongated first spiny rays of its dorsal fin.
profil.habitat: Little is known of its habitat, probably tributaries, margins, oxbows and lakes over sand or mud. The upper Madeira is home to more than 400 fish species, including many tetras known in the hobby.
profil.comportement: Despite its reputation, it does not suit a classic community tank: it needs impeccable water and feeds poorly against competitors. A group of peaceful tetras swimming in open water reassures it. It sifts the substrate for food: fine sand, sinking food and small live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Llanos of the Orinoco basin (Venezuela, Colombia)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1948 by George Myers and Robert Harry, the ram (or “butterfly cichlid”) is a dwarf cichlid with electric-blue highlights and black first dorsal rays. The name *ramirezi* simply took up the one under which it was already being sold. *Mikrogeophagus* means “little earth eater”.

Intensively bred forms (golden, “electric blue”, “balloon”) are often genetically fragile, prone to disease and short-lived; wild fish are hardier but more demanding about water.
profil.habitat:
It lives in the Llanos, a vast region of savannahs, plains and flooded forests of almost 600,000 km² in Venezuela and Colombia, drained by the tributaries of the Orinoco. The climate is hot all year round, with a marked rainy season and dry season.

The water there is warm (27 to 30 °C), soft and acidic.
profil.comportement:
Often sold as a community fish, it is not really one: it needs impeccable, warm water and is easily outcompeted. Small, peaceful shoaling fish (cardinals, neons) reassure it; avoid territorial species, including most other cichlids.

It feeds by taking mouthfuls of sand and sifting them, ejecting the grains through its gills. The pair spawns on a flat stone or in a pit and guards eggs and fry together. Females often have a pink patch on the belly.

profil.repartition: East Asia: Siberia (Amur), Sakhalin, Korea, Japan, China down to northern Vietnam; introduced to Europe, North America, Australia and Hawaii
profil.presentation: The weather loach owes its name to its restlessness when the air pressure changes before a storm. Very hardy and adaptable, it has become established all over the world, mainly through the aquarium trade, to the point of worrying conservationists.
profil.habitat: It lives mainly in slow, shallow stretches of rivers, marshes, oxbows and rice paddies, often rich in plants and roots, over mud in which it buries itself with only its head sticking out. It breathes air when the water lacks oxygen.
profil.comportement: Peaceful with its own kind and other species, but it may eat eggs, fry and very small fish. More at ease and active in a group, it goes well with active, medium-sized fish that swim higher up. A fine substrate is essential. A predator of larvae and small crustaceans: sinking food and live or frozen prey. Cool water.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Valencia and its tributaries, Venezuela
profil.presentation: This “ugly duckling” is sold young, silvery and dull; with time and good feeding it becomes a magnificent adult with scales that sparkle like diamonds, hence its name diamond tetra. Now placed in the genus *Makunaima*, it is listed as endangered in the wild.
profil.habitat: Lake Valencia, Venezuela's second largest lake, suffers from agricultural and industrial pollution, eutrophication and algal blooms: its fish diversity fell by almost 60% during the 20th century. The species lives in the lake's shallow, vegetated areas and in a few slow tributaries.
profil.comportement: Colourful, peaceful and fairly large for a tetra, it is a good choice for a community tank: livebearers, Danio, Rasbora, other tetras, Corydoras, small Loricariidae, gouramis and dwarf cichlids. A large shoal in a planted tank is superb. It accepts almost anything; small live or frozen prey for sparkle.

profil.repartition: Paranaíba, São Francisco, upper Paraná, Paraguay and Uruguay basins: Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina, Uruguay
profil.presentation: The red-eye tetra, with the bright red upper part of its eye and the black-and-white band on its tail, is found in almost every pet shop. All fish in the trade are captive-bred, which makes them undemanding about water and food: an excellent choice for beginners. It is now placed in the genus *Bario*.
profil.habitat: It lives mainly in the clear-water rivers that feed the Pantanal. Unlike the often murky waters of Amazonia, vegetation grows in abundance there: rafts of floating plants (*Eichhornia*, *Salvinia*) and vast beds of *Echinodorus*.
profil.comportement: A good, if slightly boisterous, choice for a community tank: it can intimidate calm species (anabantoids, dwarf cichlids). Keep it with active fish: tetras of similar size, rainbowfish, large Rasbora, barbs, Danio, with Corydoras, small Loricariidae or loaches on the bottom. Keep it in a shoal. It accepts almost anything, with small live or frozen prey and a little plant matter.

profil.repartition: Southeast Asia, from Thailand to Indonesia (Malaysia, Singapore, Sumatra, Borneo)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1835 by the British zoologist John Edward Gray, this leaffish belongs to the small family Nandidae. Marbled brown, with a deep, compressed body, it looks just like a dead leaf floating in the water, hence its name.

Its highly protrusible mouth, which shoots forward like a tube, lets it suck in prey in a fraction of a second. It measures about ten centimetres.
profil.habitat:
It is widespread from Thailand to Indonesia: the Malay Peninsula, Singapore, Sumatra and Borneo.

It lives in varied habitats, from hill streams to peat swamp forests, in small streams and flooded forest, among leaf litter and submerged wood.
profil.comportement:
Solitary and discreet, it is an ambush predator: it drifts or stays motionless, tilted like a leaf, before sucking in small fish and crustaceans. Any fish that fits in its mouth is prey.

Keep it alone or with species too large to be swallowed, in a calm, dim tank rich in hiding places. It needs live or frozen prey (shrimp, bloodworms, small fish).

profil.repartition: Coastal plain from Guyana (Rio Aruka) to the lower Marowijne (Suriname)
profil.presentation: This dwarf cichlid, beautiful, hardy and cheap, is an excellent first cichlid for learning about breeding. Males are larger and more colourful, with longer unpaired fins. As in some Apistogramma, the mother communicates with her fry through body movements and colour changes. Fish in the trade come from farms.
profil.habitat: It often lives in the flooded savannahs of the coastal lowlands.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, it lives with most calm fish, but the female becomes very aggressive when guarding her fry, which can be a problem in a community tank. One male to several females. A micropredator of worms, insects and crustaceans: cichlid pellets, plant matter and live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Central and upper Amazonia (Brazil, Peru, Colombia: Tapajós, Trombetas, Madeira, Negro, Japurá, Putumayo) and Orinoco basin
profil.presentation: Its Latin name, “horseman”, refers to its oblique swimming, head up, a behaviour it shares within its genus only with *N. unifasciatus*. Long placed in the genera *Poecilobrycon* and *Nannobrycon*, it is popular in the hobby.
profil.habitat: It lives in slow tributaries, small rivers and swampy areas rich in plants, submerged wood and leaf litter, often in flooded forest and blackwater floodplain lakes. In the lower Atabapo it was recorded in tea-coloured water at pH 4.4, among submerged terrestrial vegetation.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful but shy and small: not ideal in a community tank. Keep it with small, calm characins, Corydoras or small Loricariidae. It occupies the middle and top of the tank and does not hunt fry: an excellent companion for Apistogramma. Very gregarious. A micropredator: fine dry food and small live or frozen prey every day.

profil.repartition: Guyana, Suriname and the middle and lower Amazon basin in Peru, Colombia and Brazil
profil.presentation: This tiny, stocky pencilfish, one of the smallest in the genus, remains popular. Together with *N. mortenthaleri* and *N. rubrocaudatus*, it forms a group of short-bodied species; it differs from them in having no colour difference between males and females.
profil.habitat: It lives in slow tributaries, small rivers and marshes rich in plants, submerged wood and leaf litter, often in flooded forest and blackwater lakes: shallow, almost motionless water, very soft, pH 4 to 6, with small characins and Apistogramma.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful but shy and tiny: not ideal in a community tank. Keep it with small, calm characins, Corydoras or small Loricariidae; it is a very good companion for dwarf cichlids, as it swims in the middle and top of the tank without hunting fry. Very gregarious: buy as many as possible. Fine dry food and small live or frozen prey every day.

profil.repartition: Peru (Loreto): Nanay and Río Tigre basins
profil.presentation: The coral red pencilfish, discovered by Martin Mortenthaler, was first described as a subspecies of *N. marginatus* before being raised to species rank in 2003. Males are a brilliant red. Its tiny range earns it the status of critically endangered.
profil.habitat: It lives in slow tributaries, small rivers and marshes rich in plants, submerged wood and leaf litter, in black water: shallow, almost motionless water, very soft, pH 4 to 6.
profil.comportement: Peaceful with other species, but shy and tiny: keep it alone or with small, calm characins, Corydoras or small Loricariidae. It is a very good companion for dwarf cichlids and does not hunt fry. Gregarious, it forms hierarchies among males. Fine dry food and small live or frozen prey every day (Artemia nauplii, Moina).

profil.repartition: Guyana and the western Amazon basin (Brazil, Peru, Colombia, Bolivia: Negro, Madeira, Guaporé, Juruá, Napo, Ucayali...)
profil.presentation: This pencilfish with three dark bands and red spots on its fins is common in the trade and, less demanding than many of its cousins, makes an excellent first pencilfish. Wild fish are still regularly exported.
profil.habitat: It lives in slow tributaries, small rivers and marshes rich in plants, submerged wood and leaf litter, often in flooded forest and blackwater lakes: shallow, almost motionless water, very soft, pH 4 to 6.
profil.comportement: Fairly peaceful, it copes poorly with boisterous or much larger companions. Keep it with small, calm characins, Corydoras or small Loricariidae, but not with hatchetfish, calm surface swimmers, especially in a small tank. An excellent companion for dwarf cichlids. Keep it in a group. Fine dry food and small live or frozen prey every day.

profil.repartition: Colombia: San Juan and Atrato basins
profil.presentation: The emperor tetra, with its violet sheen and trident-shaped tail in the male, is one of the best choices for beginners: beautiful, hardy and cheap. Almost all fish in the trade are captive-bred. It is sometimes confused with *N. lacortei*, the only other species in the genus.
profil.habitat: It is ubiquitous within its range, in slow stretches of rivers, small tributaries and oxbows, with livebearers (*Priapichthys*), cichlids (*Andinoacara*) and various characins and Loricariidae.
profil.comportement: One of the best tetras for a community tank: lively, peaceful and colourful, it lives with most livebearers, Danio, Rasbora, other tetras, Corydoras, small Loricariidae, gouramis and dwarf cichlids, but not with large species that would eat it. Keep it in a shoal. A micropredator: fine dry food, but not exclusively, with small live or frozen prey every day.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Tanganyika (Burundi, DR Congo, Tanzania)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1974 by the Belgian ichthyologist Max Poll, the princess of Burundi is named after Pierre Brichard, a Belgian exporter based in Burundi who introduced the world to the cichlids of Lake Tanganyika. Elegant, pinkish beige with lyre-shaped fins edged in white, it measures about 9 cm.

With its very close relative *N. pulcher*, it is a classic model of cooperative breeding: young from previous broods stay in the family territory and help their parents defend and maintain it.
profil.habitat:
It lives on the rocky shores of Lake Tanganyika, especially in the north of the lake, where colonies occupy rock piles and crevices.

The lake water is warm, very stable, hard and alkaline (pH 8 to 9). It feeds mainly on the plankton drifting over the rocks.
profil.comportement:
The pair, then the family, defends a territory together around the spawning cave, with marked aggression when there are fry. It does best in a species tank or with other Tanganyikan cichlids that occupy other levels (*Cyprichromis*, shell-dwellers).

Easy to breed, it spawns on the ceiling of a cave; several generations of fry live together and the colony grows. A group of juveniles allows pairs to form. It eats frozen and live prey and a little plant matter.

profil.repartition: Endemic to the southern half of Lake Tanganyika (DR Congo, Tanzania, Zambia)
profil.presentation: This lemon cichlid, a brilliant orange-yellow when healthy, is one of the most popular Tanganyikan cichlids. Yet it is less easy to keep than its popularity suggests, because of its intolerance of its own kind and its sensitivity to deteriorating water.
profil.habitat: It lives in rocky coastal areas, usually deep in crevices, where it searches for invertebrates in the algae and nooks. Solitary in the wild, the male visits the females' caves to breed.
profil.comportement: Aggressive and territorial when breeding, it is fairly calm the rest of the time. Keep it with small or medium Tanganyikan cichlids living elsewhere in the tank (Cyprichromis), or even with other rock fish (Julidochromis, Altolamprologus) in a large tank with enough territories. Never with mbuna or boisterous species. Mostly live and frozen prey, a little spirulina.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Tanganyika (Burundi, DR Congo, Tanzania, Zambia)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1906 by George Albert Boulenger, *Neolamprologus multifasciatus* is one of the smallest cichlids in the world: males reach 4 cm, females about 2.5 cm. Its body is barred with many thin vertical bands, hence its name.

It is a “shell-dweller”: each fish lives in an empty shell of a *Neothauma* snail, which serves as shelter and spawning site. Its highly structured colonies are studied by behavioural biologists.
profil.habitat:
It is endemic to Lake Tanganyika. It lives in fairly deep areas near the shore, over soft bottoms where empty snail shells accumulate.

The lake water is warm, very stable, hard and alkaline (pH 8 to 9).
profil.comportement:
It lives in large colonies, but each individual fiercely defends its shell and a tiny territory around it; pairs have their shells side by side. It constantly digs in the sand to bury or uncover shells, reshaping the decor.

It feeds on the plankton passing over the colony. It lives with species from other levels of the tank (small *Julidochromis*, *Cyprichromis*). The female spawns in her shell and guards the fry; provide more shells than fish.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Malawi (Malawi, Mozambique, Tanzania), widespread throughout the lake
profil.presentation: This large haplochromine, with a giraffe-like spotted pattern, is an ambush predator: it lies motionless near rocks, in *Vallisneria* beds or on the bottom. Young adults have been seen half-buried in the sand, waiting for small fish that come to forage nearby.
profil.habitat: It lives in fairly shallow water (15 m or less), on rocky shores as well as over sand or mud. Young fish stay near the rocks in shallow water, while adults hunt further offshore over the sand.
profil.comportement: A predator, it eats small mbuna and young fish, but remains calm with species too large for it (Cyphotilapia frontosa, Dimidiochromis compressiceps, large mbuna). Solitary, and males fight: a single fish, or a harem of several females for breeding. Exclusively piscivorous in the wild, it accepts dead food: shrimp, fish; never meat.

profil.repartition: South-eastern Zimbabwe (Gonarezhou reserve) and southern Mozambique; reported from the Save River
profil.presentation: This annual killifish holds one of the shortest lifespan records among vertebrates: under 12 weeks in captivity, which makes it a much-studied model in ageing research. It is rare in the wild and threatened by habitat destruction and insecticide spraying.
profil.habitat: It lives in temporary savannah pools that dry out every year. The eggs, laid in the bottom, survive the dry season in the mud: their incubation lasts 5 to 7 months.
profil.comportement: The very colourful males quarrel among themselves: keep it in a species tank, one male to several females. A predator of small invertebrates, it needs live or frozen prey. Breeding it requires storing the eggs in damp peat before putting them back in water.

profil.repartition: Floodplains of the lower Pungwe and lower Zambezi (Mozambique)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1926 by Ernst Ahl, Rachow's nothobranch is named after the German aquarist Arthur Rachow. It is one of the most colourful annual killifish: the male is covered in a network of blue, red-edged scales, with a flame-coloured tail.

Its life is governed by the seasons: it hatches with the rains, reaches adulthood in three weeks, breeds and dies when its pool dries out, leaving only eggs buried in the mud. The oldest aquarium strain descends from an import made in 1958.
profil.habitat:
It lives in depressions, pools and temporary marshes on the floodplains of the lower Pungwe and lower Zambezi, in Mozambique.

The depth of these pools decreases during the dry season until they dry out completely for several months. The vegetation includes grasses, water lilies (*Nymphaea*), *Ottelia* and bladderworts; some pools are used to grow rice. It shares them with other *Nothobranchius*, the African catfish and the lungfish.
profil.comportement:
Males are territorial and display to each other; keep one male with two or three females in a small species tank. A micropredator, it needs live or frozen prey.

In the aquarium the pair spawns in a tank of fine peat; the peat is then removed and kept damp for several months, like the pool's soil in the dry season, before being re-wetted to hatch the eggs. Its life is short: about a year in the aquarium.

profil.repartition: Indonesia: west-central Sumatra (North Sumatra); introduced to Colombia
profil.presentation: The checker barb, whose black-edged scales form a checkerboard, is one of the most common fish in the trade, mass-bred; wild fish are almost never available. Long placed in the catch-all genus *Puntius*, it has received its own genus, whose name combines *oligolepis* and *Puntius*.
profil.habitat: It lives in creeks, rivers and lakes; the exact extent of its range remains poorly known, the few recent records coming from the lower reaches of a few rivers in North Sumatra.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, ideal in a well-planned community tank. A shoaling fish, buy at least 6 to 10: less fearful, they form a natural group and the males show their finest colours to their rivals. An omnivore: easy to feed, with small live or frozen prey for condition and colour.

profil.repartition: East Asia: Japan (from the Ryukyus to Honshu), Korea, eastern China (with Hainan and Hong Kong), Taiwan, Vietnam and Laos
profil.presentation: The medaka, or “rice fish” (*Oryzias* comes from the Greek *oryza*, “rice”), has been a model organism in biology for more than a century, and was the first vertebrate to mate in space, in the mid-1990s. There are many ornamental forms, especially in Japan.
profil.habitat: Mostly coastal, it is very adaptable: tidal brackish mangroves, acidic forest streams, rice paddies, farm canals, pools and oxbows, and even tide pools on some coasts of Japan and Korea. It tolerates a wide range of salinity and temperature.
profil.comportement: Peaceful, but its needs (cool, sometimes brackish water) limit its companions: small fish with similar requirements (Dermogenys, Pseudomugil, Brachygobius) or Neritina snails; for breeding it is best kept alone. A micropredator: fine dry food and small live or frozen prey every day. It also lives in outdoor ponds.

profil.repartition: Indonesia: Muna Island, off south-eastern Sulawesi (a single known site)
profil.presentation: Described in 2010 and named after the carcinologist Daisy Wowor, this blue ricefish with red fins caused a sensation as soon as it reached the trade, at very high prices. Sulawesi is a centre of diversity for the genus, with 17 endemic species. It is listed as endangered.
profil.habitat: The type locality is a karst stream under 80% forest cover, over mud, sand and leaf litter. It was caught in a calm pool 3 to 4 m deep, facing a spring, in a shoal with a *Nomorhamphus* halfbeak, at pH 6 to 7.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, but too small for most community tanks: keep it with other micro fish (Boraras, Trigonostigma, Pseudomugil, dwarf Corydoras, Otocinclus) or with Caridina and Neocaridina shrimp. It needs food to match its size: fine dry food and live prey (microworms, Artemia nauplii). Adults also graze surfaces.

profil.repartition: Sumatra, Borneo, Java, Malay Peninsula, Thailand and Mekong basin; introduced elsewhere for aquaculture
profil.presentation:
Described in 1801 by the French naturalist Bernard-Germain de Lacepède, the giant gourami is the largest of the gouramis: it reaches 70 cm and can live for more than 20 years. Miocene fossils have been found in central Sumatra.

It is above all a highly prized food fish in Southeast Asia, farmed in many countries. Able to breathe moist air, it survives a long time out of water, which allows it to be transported alive without refrigeration. In the aquarium it needs a tank of several thousand litres.
profil.habitat:
Its natural range is thought to include Sumatra, Borneo, Java, the Malay Peninsula, Thailand and Indochina; it has been introduced to many countries for aquaculture.

It lives in marshes, lakes, medium to large rivers and slow canals, among vegetation, and enters flooded forest. It tolerates a wide range of water, soft to hard, and even brackish.
profil.comportement:
Generally peaceful with other large fish (knifefish, large catfish, loricariids), it eats small ones. Some adults become aggressive, especially when cramped.

An omnivore, it eats aquatic plants, fish, frogs, earthworms and even carrion. Mature at six months, the male builds a large nest of plant material (grass, roots) near the surface and guards the eggs; males have pointed dorsal and anal fins.

profil.repartition: South-eastern Brazil, Rio de Janeiro region
profil.presentation:
Described in 1877 by Franz Steindachner, *Otocinclus affinis* is one of the oldest names in the genus. *Otocinclus* comes from the Greek for “ear” and “grille”, for the perforated bone behind the head.

In the trade, the name “Otocinclus affinis” is very often applied to other species, notably *O. macrospilus* or *O. vittatus*, which are exported far more: the true species, native to south-eastern Brazil, is rarely offered.
profil.habitat:
Its natural range lies in the small coastal rivers of the Rio de Janeiro region, in Brazil, in a subtropical climate.

Otocinclus live in shoals on bank vegetation, leaves and wood in calm streams, where they scrape off algae and biofilm. It tolerates cooler water than its Amazonian cousins (20 to 26 °C).
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful, it is kept in a group of at least 5 to 6, with calm fish that do not steal its food. It often clings to the glass and leaves.

It is an algae grazer: a planted, mature aquarium rich in biofilm is essential, supplemented with blanched vegetables and spirulina tablets. Like all otocinclus, it often suffers from starvation during transport and must be acclimatised in a well-established tank.

profil.repartition: Lower Paraná, lower and middle Uruguay and Río de la Plata (Argentina, Brazil, Uruguay)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1909 by Charles Tate Regan, *Otocinclus arnoldi* is named after the German aquarist Johann Paul Arnold. This small 5 cm grazer has a dark, irregular lateral band and differs from its relatives in details of the colouring of the head and tail.

It is one of the southernmost otocinclus: it lives in a subtropical climate, which means it tolerates cooler water than the Amazonian species.
profil.habitat:
It occurs in the lower Río Paraná basin, the lower and middle Río Uruguay and the Río de la Plata, in Argentina, Uruguay and southern Brazil.

Like its cousins, it lives among bank vegetation and on submerged wood in calm water, where it scrapes off algae and biofilm. The water is cool to temperate depending on the season (20 to 25 °C in the aquarium).
profil.comportement:
Peaceful and gregarious, it is kept in a group of at least 6, with calm fish that tolerate the same temperature.

A grazer, it needs a planted, mature aquarium rich in algae, supplemented with blanched vegetables and spirulina tablets. Like all wild otocinclus, it must be carefully acclimatised after transport.

profil.repartition: Upper Amazon in Peru (Morona, Nanay and Marañón basins); reported from Colombia and Ecuador
profil.presentation:
Described in 1942 by Carl Eigenmann and William Ray Allen, *Otocinclus macrospilus* (“large spot”) has a large, round black spot at the base of the tail. It is probably the best-selling otocinclus in the hobby, often under the generic name “oto”.

Almost all fish in the trade are wild-caught. Delicate on arrival, they often starve during transport: this small grazer needs to eat almost continuously.
profil.habitat:
It is native to the upper Peruvian Amazon; its type locality is the Río Morona, in the department of Loreto. It is also recorded from the Nanay and Marañón basins, Colombia and Ecuador.

It lives in the dense vegetation along the banks of streams, creeks and rivers, and in large numbers in “floating meadows”, rafts of plants that shelter many fish.
profil.comportement:
Very shy, it is outcompeted by livelier species: keep it with small peaceful characins, *Apistogramma* and small corydoras. It seeks the company of its own kind, in a group of at least 6.

It feeds mainly on algae and micro-organisms: a planted, mature aquarium, fresh vegetables and plant-based tablets. It has been bred: the pair adopts the corydoras “T position”, then the eggs are scattered around the tank. Seen from above, females are broader.

profil.repartition: Orinoco basin and southern tributaries of the middle and lower Amazon (Venezuela, Colombia, Brazil)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1877 by Wilhelm Peters, the royal pleco (L190 and related forms) is recognised by its black lines on a grey-green background, its red eyes and its strong spoon-shaped teeth. It exceeds 40 cm.

It is famous for “eating wood”: it constantly rasps submerged roots and logs. Studies have shown, however, that it hardly digests the cellulose in wood, which passes through its gut very quickly; it actually feeds mainly on the biofilm, algae and detritus covering it. Wood nevertheless remains essential to its well-being in the aquarium.
profil.habitat:
It lives in the Orinoco basin, in Venezuela and Colombia, and in the southern tributaries of the middle and lower Amazon, in Brazil.

It frequents rivers where submerged trunks and branches accumulate, in tropical water of low to medium hardness, close to neutral (22 to 26 °C according to FishBase).
profil.comportement:
Solitary and territorial towards other large plecos, it defends its wooden shelter with its spines; it tolerates robust midwater fish. The rule is one fish per tank.

Its adult size, its longevity and the abundant sawdust it produces call for a large aquarium (over 400 litres) with very good filtration. Feed it vegetables, plant-based tablets and soft wood to rasp at all times.

profil.repartition: Lower Mekong (Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam), Chao Phraya and Mae Klong; introduced elsewhere for aquaculture
profil.presentation: The iridescent shark, formerly called *Pangasius sutchi*, is sold very small (5 to 8 cm), silvery and bluish, with no information on its adult size: it exceeds one metre. It therefore ends up in many completely unsuitable beginners' tanks. Mass-bred, it is also widely farmed for food. In the wild it is listed as endangered.
profil.habitat: An open-water fish, it lives in the main channels and large tributaries. A migratory species, it travels up the Mekong to spawn. It can breathe air.
profil.comportement: Not aggressive, but it eats much smaller fish, disturbs calm species with its constant activity and is intimidated by aggressive ones. It is only suited to public aquariums or very large ponds, with large Doradidae, pacu or large cyprinids. An omnivore: protein for young fish (worms, pellets), more plant matter with age.

profil.repartition: Sunda Islands (Java, Sumatra, Borneo) and Malay Peninsula
profil.presentation:
Described in 1846 by Achille Valenciennes, the kuhli (or “coolie loach”) is a small, eel-like, orange-yellow loach barred with dark bands. Its name honours the German naturalist Heinrich Kuhl, who died on Java in 1821.

Its identity is muddled: the true *P. kuhlii* is thought to come from Java, while most “kuhlis” sold are *P. semicincta*, from Malaysia, Sumatra and Borneo. This group is probably a complex of closely related species, with at least three genetic lineages identified.
profil.habitat:
These loaches live in calm, shallow parts of forest streams, marshes, oxbows and canals, often linked to peat forests, in black or clear water.

The water there is shaded, almost free of minerals and sometimes very acidic (pH as low as 3 or 4). The bottom of peat, mud or sand is covered in dead leaves, where kuhlis gather in large numbers.
profil.comportement:
Totally peaceful, it never bothers its companions, but may eat eggs and fry. Gregarious, it gathers in the same hiding place to rest: a group of at least 5 to 6 is recommended.

Nocturnal and discreet, it sifts the fine sand through its mouth and gills to extract larvae and small crustaceans. It escapes through the smallest gap and must be kept in a covered tank. Its breeding in the aquarium remains poorly documented.

profil.repartition: West and Central Africa: Nigeria, Lake Chad, Cameroon, Ogooué and Congo basins, upper Zambezi; reported from Benin and Sierra Leone
profil.presentation: Seen from above, this surface fish looks like a butterfly with its large pectoral fins. They camouflage it as a floating dead leaf and, together with the tail fin, power impressive leaps to catch insects or escape a predator. It is the only member of its family.
profil.habitat: It lives in calm or slow water in creeks, lakes, marshes and oxbows, usually under dense aquatic or overhanging vegetation, and stays at the surface. It breathes air.
profil.comportement: Fairly peaceful, but its long fins attract nippers; it eats any fish that fits in its mouth and is often aggressive towards other surface fish. Keep it with African species: Congo tetras, elephantfish, Synodontis, Ctenopoma, small West African cichlids. An insectivore: live and frozen prey, insects. A tightly covered aquarium.

profil.repartition: Middle and upper Rio Negro, Casiquiare canal and upper Orinoco (Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela)
profil.presentation:
The cardinal tetra was described in 1956 by the American ichthyologist Leonard P. Schultz in the aquarium magazine *Tropical Fish Hobbyist*, as *Cheirodon axelrodi*. George Myers and Stanley Weitzman were about to publish the same species as *Hyphessobrycon cardinalis*: the rule of priority kept Schultz's name, dedicated to Herbert R. Axelrod, the magazine's founder.

It differs from the neon tetra by its red band covering the whole underside, from head to tail. A revision of tetra classification published in 2024 now places it in the family Acestrorhamphidae, separate from the Characidae.
profil.habitat:
It frequents small forest streams and slow side channels. In the Rio Negro basin these are igapós and igarapés with black water: very acidic, almost without hardness, stained brown by humic substances from decaying leaves, under dense bank vegetation. In the Orinoco it lives rather in morichales, with clear water over sand.

The rhythm of the floods shapes its life: in the dry season the fish gather in large shoals in the channels, then disperse into the flooded forest as the water rises. Genetic studies have shown that the upper Rio Negro populations are ancient, distinct lineages, considered priorities for conservation.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful and gregarious, it swims in tight shoals in the middle water layer and feeds on worms, small crustaceans and plant debris. In the wild it is almost an annual fish: individuals over one year old are rare, whereas it lives several years in the aquarium.

A group of at least 8 to 10 gives it confidence and reveals natural shoaling behaviour. Its breeding in captivity remains tricky: many cardinals in the trade are still caught in the middle Rio Negro, notably through Project Piaba, a managed fishery that supports riverside communities.

profil.repartition: Upper Amazon (Rio Solimões): Leticia–Tabatinga, Codajás and Rio Purus regions (Peru, Colombia, Brazil)
profil.presentation:
The neon tetra was described in 1936 by the American ichthyologist George S. Myers, from fish that arrived through the aquarium trade. Its name honours William T. Innes, an American aquarist, photographer and publisher who did much to popularise the freshwater aquarium.

It is one of the best-selling aquarium fish in the world; the vast majority now come from fish farms. It is particularly susceptible to “neon tetra disease”, caused by a microsporidian (*Pleistophora hyphessobryconis*) that can affect other species and is practically incurable once advanced.
profil.habitat:
The type locality originally given, “near Iquitos” in Peru, was based on imported fish, and the true extent of its range remains poorly known. Confirmed records are concentrated around Leticia and Tabatinga (the “triple border”, with the lower Río Putumayo), then further east around Codajás and the Rio Purus.

It lives in forest streams and small tributaries rather than in the large whitewater channels. The water there is acidic, very soft, black or clear, over branches, roots and leaf litter, sometimes with aquatic plants.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful and gregarious, it lives in shoals in the middle water layer and feeds on worms, small insects, crustaceans and plant matter. It is kept in a group of at least 8 to 10, with fish of similar size.

It likes slightly cooler water than the cardinal (20 to 26 °C). In the aquarium the female lays a fairly small number of eggs among fine vegetation, ideally in very dim light; the eggs hatch in about a day.

profil.repartition: Middle and upper Rio Negro above the Rio Branco, and Orinoco on the Venezuela–Colombia border
profil.presentation:
Described in 1963 by the French ichthyologist Jacques Géry, the green neon owes its Latin name *simulans* (“imitating”) to its resemblance to the neon and cardinal tetras. It is the smallest of the three *Paracheirodon*: it rarely exceeds 2.5 cm. Its blue-green band extends to the tail, but the red is limited to the rear of the belly.

The type locality first published (“Rio Purus, Manaus”) was wrong and has been corrected to the Rio Jufaris, a tributary of the Rio Negro. Some wild individuals have golden scales and are sold as “platinum”: this sheen is thought to be caused by a parasite that stimulates guanine deposits in the scales.
profil.habitat:
Unlike the neon and cardinal, it lives only in black water, in the upper parts of tributaries draining terra firme forest. These streams have a slow to moderate current, banks covered in vegetation and a sandy bottom strewn with branches, roots and dead leaves. The water is very acidic, almost free of minerals and stained by humic acids.

Although it partly shares the range of the cardinal, the two species do not occur in the same streams; the green neon generally occupies warmer water.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful but tiny and demanding about water quality, it is best suited to a species tank or one shared with very small, calm fish (small characins, dwarf corydoras). Gregarious, it forms shoals: a group of at least 8 to 10 makes it less fearful.

It is not bred commercially; the fish sold are wild-caught, which makes it rarer and more expensive than its cousins. Adult females are recognised by their rounder belly.

profil.repartition: South and Southeast Asia: Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, Malaysia
profil.presentation: The glassfish owes its name to its translucent skin, through which its skeleton and organs can be seen. In Asian farms it was long injected with fluorescent dyes to be sold as “disco fish”: a cruel practice, as most of the fish did not survive for long. These coloured fish should be refused.
profil.habitat: It lives in slow or still water, in large numbers in the rainy season, and thrives in reservoirs. It breeds during the rains, builds a nest and guards its young.
profil.comportement: Peaceful and shy, it should not live with lively or aggressive species. In fresh water it lives with barbs, livebearers, small rainbowfish and loaches; in brackish water, with mollies, Brachygobius and Etroplus. A shoaling fish. Undemanding, it accepts most live, frozen and dry foods.

profil.repartition: Indonesia: endemic to Bangka Island, mainly in the north and east
profil.presentation: The only recognised member of its genus for almost a century after its description in 1859, this licorice gourami has lent its name to many fish from other regions, since described as separate species. The true *P. deissneri* has probably always been very rare in the hobby. It is listed as endangered.
profil.habitat: It lives among the vegetation of jungle swamps and streams, in slow, tea-coloured water. Under a dense canopy, light barely penetrates; the water, stained by humic acids, is almost free of minerals, with a pH that can drop to 3 or 4. Some populations now survive only in heavily degraded forest remnants.
profil.comportement: It does not suit a community tank: its needs, its temperament and above all its conservation status call for a species tank, at most with a group of small peaceful cyprinids (Boraras, Sundadanio). Never mix Parosphromenus species, which can hybridise. A micropredator: varied small live prey (Artemia nauplii, Daphnia, Moina, mosquito larvae).

profil.repartition: Rio Tapajós basin (Pará, Brazil)
profil.presentation:
Long known to hobbyists by the code L134 or the name “leopard frog pleco”, this small loricariid was only described in 2010 by a team of Brazilian researchers (de Oliveira, Zuanon, Rapp Py-Daniel and Rocha). *Compta* means “adorned” in Latin, for its broad dark brown bands on a yellow background.

It differs from other *Peckoltia* by a pale line inside the dark bands running from the snout to the eyes. It barely exceeds 8 cm. The IUCN lists it as endangered.
profil.habitat:
It is native to the Rio Tapajós basin, a large clear-water tributary on the right bank of the Amazon, in Brazil.

It lives among rocks and wood piles in flowing stretches, in clear, warm, well-oxygenated water. Its populations are exposed to dam projects and gold mining in the basin.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful with midwater fish, it is territorial towards other small plecos and defends its hiding place. Mainly nocturnal, it shelters by day in caves and crevices.

An omnivore, it eats sinking food, small frozen prey and a little plant matter. It is a cave spawner: the male guards the eggs in a narrow shelter until the fry are independent.

profil.repartition: Brazilian Amazon (lower Tapajós, Madeira, Xingu, Uatumã, Trombetas, Capim) and Río Ventuari in Venezuela
profil.presentation: This small pleco striped with dark and light bands stays a reasonable size (13 cm) and therefore suits more modest tanks than most Loricariidae. It can breathe air, like other members of its genus.
profil.habitat: In Venezuela it has been caught on rocks in areas of current.
profil.comportement: Peaceful and nocturnal, it grazes algae and nibbles plants and roots. It can be kept in a group, with calm fish. Plant-based sinking food, soft wood to rasp and frozen prey.

profil.repartition: West Africa: eastern Benin, southern Nigeria and western Cameroon
profil.presentation: The kribensis, or “krib”, is one of the most common and popular cichlids. The vast majority of fish in the trade are captive-bred: far more adaptable than wild fish, they are also less aggressive when breeding. There is an albino form.
