The pair spawns in a cave and guards the fry.
profil.habitat: It lives in calm or slow, shallow and heavily vegetated water; some populations live in brackish water. In the Sombreiro River (Nigeria) it feeds mainly on diatoms, algae, plants and detritus.
profil.comportement: Recommended for community tanks, but very territorial when breeding. Rather shy, it should not live with very lively or large species. Good companions: small characins, barbs, Danio, Rasbora, Corydoras, gouramis, Loricariidae, and other West African dwarf cichlids if space allows territories. Keep it as a pair. It accepts almost anything, with live and frozen prey.

profil.repartition: West Africa: from eastern Benin to Nigeria (including the Niger Delta), in fresh water near the coast
profil.presentation: This striped kribensis, with a well-marked upper lip that is often bright yellow, comes in more than a dozen geographic forms (“Nigeria Red”, “Calabar”...), which should not be crossed with each other. According to FishBase, the Cameroonian forms, including “Moliwe”, “Dehane” and “Kienke”, now belong to *P. kribensis*.
profil.habitat: It lives in calm or slow forest streams and rivers, often heavily vegetated. It spawns in a cave and guards its fry.
profil.comportement: Recommended for community tanks, but territorial when breeding. Shy, it should not live with lively or large species: small characins, barbs, Danio, Rasbora, Corydoras, gouramis, Loricariidae, or other West African dwarf cichlids with enough space. Keep it as a pair. It accepts most foods, especially live and frozen prey.

profil.repartition: From Pakistan (and Afghanistan) to India, Nepal and Bangladesh; reported from Myanmar
profil.presentation: The rosy barb is one of the hardiest small cyprinids and an excellent choice for beginners. The silvery male turns a deep burgundy when breeding. Selective breeding has produced long-finned, “veil”, “super red”, “neon” and golden forms. Populations vary by locality.
profil.habitat: It lives in very varied habitats: flowing hill streams and tributaries, but also lakes, ponds and marshes.
profil.comportement: Peaceful, ideal in a well-planned community tank; undemanding about water, it lives with most popular fish: small cyprinids, tetras, livebearers, rainbowfish, anabantoids, catfish and loaches. A shoaling fish, at least 8 to 10. A generalist omnivore: dry food, small live or frozen prey and plant matter. It tolerates cooler water.

profil.repartition: Ganges and Brahmaputra basins (northern India, Nepal, Bangladesh); more recently reported from Tamil Nadu and the Irrawaddy delta
profil.presentation: This tiny golden barb spotted with black was only clearly defined in 2013, when *P. canius* was revalidated and *P. aurea* described: these three species were previously considered forms of *P. gelius*. It is widespread in the hobby.
profil.habitat: It lives mainly in slow, often murky water over mud or silt, and along river margins. In West Bengal it frequents the small streams that run through rice paddies; depth, current and turbidity vary with the season.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful but small and shy: not ideal in a community tank. Keep it alone or with other micro fish (Trigonostigma, small Danio, Lepidocephalichthys) and shrimp. A shoaling fish, at least 8 to 10. A micropredator: fine dry food, but not exclusively, with small live or frozen prey every day.

profil.repartition: Endemic to south-western Sri Lanka: Kelani and Nilwala basins
profil.presentation: The black ruby barb owes its French name (“purple-headed barb”) to the purplish-red head of the male in breeding colours. Export of wild fish from Sri Lanka is banned: fish in the trade should all come from farms. Pressure from the aquarium trade is said to have reduced a very colourful introduced population. It is listed as vulnerable.
profil.habitat: It lives in Sri Lanka's “wet zone”, which receives 2,000 to 3,000 mm of rain a year: clear, cool, shaded forest streams over gravel or sand, and calm pools along the edges, up to 300 m above sea level. It spawns among the bank vegetation.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, ideal in a well-planned community tank; undemanding about water, it lives with most popular fish. A shoaling fish, at least 6 to 10: less fearful, they form a natural group and males show their finest colours to their rivals. An omnivore: algae, detritus and small invertebrates, with live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Central Myanmar: around Pyin Oo Lwin (Mandalay region) and the lower Chindwin
profil.presentation: The Odessa barb has been in the trade since the early 1970s, but its origin remained a mystery until 2003. First appearing in Ukraine, hence its name taken from the port of Odessa, it was thought to be a hybrid of related species. Described in 2008, it bears the Burmese word for “ruby”, referring to the bright red of the males.
profil.habitat: The type specimens come from an artificial pond fed by a small stream, in the village of Toe Gyi, just above the Anisakan Falls. The water there is clear, poor in plants and flows over limestone, over gravel or mud.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, ideal in a well-planned community tank, ideally with midwater cyprinids of similar size, loaches and bottom-dwelling cyprinids (Crossocheilus, Garra). A shoaling fish. A foraging omnivore: easy to feed, with small live or frozen prey for condition and colour.

profil.repartition: Indian subcontinent: Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka; records from Myanmar and China remain to be confirmed
profil.presentation: The ticto barb, silvery with two black spots, is often confused in aquarium literature with *P. padamya* (Odessa barb), which is nevertheless easy to tell apart: *P. ticto* is far less colourful and its males have no orange-red on the body. It tolerates fairly cool water.
profil.habitat: It is especially abundant in shallow streams and small tributaries, sometimes at altitude, over mud or silt, and in the calm margins of reservoirs and rivers, where it forages near the bottom. The female lays about 150 eggs in batches of around twenty.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, ideal in a well-planned community tank, ideally with midwater cyprinids of similar size, loaches or bottom-dwelling cyprinids (Crossocheilus, Garra). A mixed group of at least 8 to 10 is needed, in which males compete harmlessly. A foraging omnivore: dry food with a plant component and small live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Upper Amazon in Peru, Purus, Negro and Madeira basins in Brazil
profil.presentation:
Described in 1964 by Jacques Géry and Henri Boutière, the false rummy-nose is the type species of the genus *Petitella*, named after the French zoologist Georges Petit (1892–1973); the species name honours Georgie, Géry's wife.

It looks very much like the two other “rummy-noses” (*Hemigrammus rhodostomus* and *Petitella bleheri*). It is recognised by the absence of a dark spot under the caudal peduncle and by the broad black band that extends the tail's central stripe into the body.
profil.habitat:
It is native to the upper Amazon basin in Peru and the Purus, Negro and Madeira basins in Brazil.

It lives mainly in clear-water tributaries and small rivers, at 22 to 26 °C, in soft, slightly acidic water.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful, it forms one of the tightest shoals among small tetras: at least ten are needed, more if possible, for it to feel safe. It does not tolerate boisterous or much larger companions.

Its tiny mouth calls for fine food: worms, small crustaceans and plant matter in the wild, small live prey and crushed dry food in the aquarium. Its breeding in captivity is said to be tricky; mature females have a rounder body.

profil.repartition: Lower and middle Congo basin: Democratic Republic of the Congo and Republic of the Congo
profil.presentation: The Congo tetra is often sold young, grey and dull, at 4 cm, and goes unnoticed. Once adult it takes on iridescent highlights and males develop spectacular long, fringed fins. Most fish in the trade are bred in the Far East and Eastern Europe.
profil.habitat: Wild populations live in part of the Congo basin, where they feed on small worms, insects, crustaceans and algae.
profil.comportement: Peaceful, but its active swimming and size can frighten shy species. Keep it with other tetras, rainbowfish, Corydoras, Loricariidae, Synodontis and calm cichlids (Pelvicachromis, Cleithracara), never with fin nippers or boisterous species. Timid, it must be kept in a group. Sensitive to water quality, which determines the state of its fins and colours. A good share of live and frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Amazon and Orinoco basins: Colombia, Venezuela, Peru, Brazil
profil.presentation: This silvery angel catfish with black spots and very long barbels is often sold as a bottom fish for community tanks of small species, which has cost the lives of countless neons and guppies. It lives 4 to 8 years on average in captivity; one fish reached 18 years.
profil.habitat: It lives in shallow, flowing water over sand or mud, in large rivers as well as their tributaries.
profil.comportement: Fairly peaceful, but a predator: it only suits large tanks with fish that cannot be swallowed. Very active, especially at night, it can also disturb slow species such as many cichlids with its barbels. It does better in a group. It eats everything greedily: live or frozen prey, worms and sinking food. Its spines can sting when handled.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Malawi: Likoma Island and the north-eastern shores of the lake (Malawi, Mozambique)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1979 by Warren E. Burgess, the “deepwater hap” or electra is a haplochromine from Lake Malawi. The adult male takes on electric-blue colouring barred with dark bands, hence its name; the female stays silvery.

Like many Lake Malawi cichlids, it belongs to a spectacular radiation: several hundred species that arose in less than two million years.
profil.habitat:
It is endemic to Lake Malawi, around Likoma Island, Mara Point and along the north-eastern shores of the lake.

It lives over sandy bottoms, generally below 7 m. It picks up invertebrates and algae stirred up from the sand by other fish digging in the bottom. The lake water is warm, hard and alkaline (pH 7.6 to 8.8).
profil.comportement:
Very gentle, it cannot bear the bustle of a mbuna community; it lives well with *Aulonocara*, *Copadichromis* and other peaceful lake species. Also peaceful with its own kind, it becomes slightly territorial when breeding; keep several females per male.

It is a maternal mouthbrooder: the female keeps the eggs, then the fry, in her mouth for several weeks. It accepts most foods, with a plant component (spirulina).

profil.repartition: Paraná–Paraguay basin (Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay); Seriously Fish gives it a much wider range (Orinoco, Amazonia, the Guianas)
profil.presentation: This black-and-white striped catfish, also called the “talking catfish”, makes audible creaking sounds by rubbing its pectoral spines. Hardy and tolerant, it is seen as a beginner's fish, but its secretive habits, its adult size (24 cm) and its taste for small fish make it best suited to tanks of large species.
profil.habitat: It lives in slow or still water (tributaries, creeks, marshes), usually sheltering among roots or submerged vegetation.
profil.comportement: Completely peaceful, but it eats small fish: keep it with peaceful species too large for it (medium characins, cyprinids, anabantoids, cichlids, non-territorial catfish). It tolerates its own kind, which often share the same shelter by day. An omnivore: sinking tablets and live or frozen prey, given after the lights go out.

profil.repartition: Coasts of the south-eastern United States and the Gulf of Mexico, from North Carolina to Veracruz (Mexico)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1821 by the French naturalist Charles Alexandre Lesueur, the sailfin molly owes its Latin name *latipinna* (“broad fin”) to the huge, sail-shaped dorsal fin of adult males, which they spread during displays.

It is told apart from the very similar *Poecilia velifera* by the rectangular (not rounded) dark spots on its dorsal fin. Introduced to many countries, from Kenya to New Zealand, it often competes there with local species.
profil.habitat:
It is native to the coastal plains of the south-eastern United States, from North Carolina to Florida, and around the Gulf of Mexico as far as Veracruz.

It lives in calm, warm water in small streams, ponds, marshes, canals and tidal ditches, often brackish, rich in algae and vegetation. It tolerates hard fresh water as well as seawater.
profil.comportement:
It suits a hard-water community aquarium, but may harass small fish as it grows, and males are aggressive towards each other in the breeding season.

In the wild it is almost exclusively herbivorous, grazing algae and plants, with a few small crustaceans and insects: vegetables or plant-based flakes are essential in the aquarium. Gestation lasts about two months and produces up to about fifty large fry; one male to two females is recommended.

profil.repartition: North-eastern South America and the southern Caribbean (Venezuela, the Guianas, Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1859 by the German zoologist Wilhelm Peters from fish from the Río Guaire, in Caracas, the guppy owes its common name to Robert Lechmere Guppy, who sent specimens from Trinidad to the British Museum in 1866.

It is one of the most popular aquarium fish, with countless captive-bred varieties with outsized fins. It is also a famous model in evolutionary biology: in the rivers of Trinidad, populations exposed to different predators have evolved, within a few generations, distinct colours, sizes and breeding strategies.
profil.habitat:
Its native range covers Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana, Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, Antigua and the Netherlands Antilles. It has been introduced to some fifty countries, often to control mosquitoes: with little effect on them, but with negative impacts on local fish.

Incredibly adaptable, it lives everywhere from mountain torrents to murky pools and ditches, and even in brackish water, but prefers calm water rich in algae and vegetation.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful, it suits a calm community aquarium; avoid fin nippers (tiger barbs, serpae tetras). Males constantly chase females: several females per male are recommended.

A livebearer, the female gives birth to fully formed fry about every four weeks, which adults readily eat: dense vegetation and floating plants protect them. It feeds on zooplankton, small insects and detritus.

profil.repartition: From Mexico to Colombia and Venezuela, with a few populations in the Caribbean
profil.presentation:
Described in 1846 by Achille Valenciennes, the molly (or “short-finned molly”) is the ancestor of many aquarium forms, including the famous black molly, a melanistic variety. It is often confused with *Poecilia mexicana*, a closely related species.

Decades of intensive production have weakened many farmed strains, which are prone to disease when kept in soft, mineral-poor water. The species is so salt-tolerant that it can live in seawater.
profil.habitat:
Its natural range extends from Mexico to Colombia and Venezuela, with isolated populations on some Caribbean islands. Introduced populations exist in the United States, Japan, Singapore and Eastern Europe.

It lives in fresh and brackish water alike, in hard, alkaline water, between 18 and 28 °C.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful, it only suits fish that tolerate the same hard, even slightly salty water: other *Poecilia*, rainbowfish, hard-water barbs and tetras.

An omnivore, it eats small invertebrates and detritus, but its diet must include plenty of plant matter; it grazes green algae. A livebearer, it breeds easily after a gestation of about two months; several females per male limit harassment.

profil.repartition: South-eastern Mexico: Yucatán Peninsula and lower Usumacinta; introduced to Colombia, Israel, Singapore and Taiwan
profil.presentation: The Yucatan sailfin molly, whose males have a huge sail-like dorsal fin, has given rise to many varieties (albino, black, red), sometimes crossed with *P. latipinna*. The deformed “balloon” form should be avoided. It is listed as vulnerable in the wild.
profil.habitat: It lives in the coastal waters of the Yucatán, fresh to brackish, where it feeds on invertebrates, detritus and plant matter.
profil.comportement: Peaceful, it only lives with species that tolerate hard water: swordtails, platies (not other mollies, which hybridise), some gouramis, hardy Corydoras or Loricariidae, barbs and tetras, or in brackish water with Etroplus and gobies. An omnivore: it accepts anything, but needs some plant matter (spinach, cucumber, plant-based flakes).

profil.repartition: Campoma and Buena Vista lagoons, near Carúpano (north-eastern Venezuela)
profil.presentation:
Endler's guppy was discovered in 1937 by Franklyn Bond, then rediscovered in 1975 by the biologist John Endler in the Laguna de Patos, Venezuela. It was only described in 2005 by Fred Poeser, Michael Kempkes and Isaäc Isbrücker, who named it after the Danish geneticist Øjvind Winge, a pioneer in the study of colour and sex determination in guppies.

Its species status has been debated, since it hybridises with the guppy and produces fertile offspring; a 2009 genetic study confirmed it as a valid species. The IUCN lists it as endangered.
profil.habitat:
It lives in coastal lagoons in north-eastern Venezuela, near Carúpano. The Laguna de Patos, its type locality, was originally a brackish lake cut off from the sea by a sandbar, which became fresh over time.

When it was rediscovered, the water there was very warm, hard and green with algae. The population there is now thought to be extinct, after a rubbish dump was set up beside the lake.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful, it is too small for a classic community aquarium: keep it with tiny, calm species (dwarf corydoras, *Pseudomugil*, small tetras). Males tolerate each other, but females can be territorial towards one another.

Very prolific, it breeds continuously. It should not be kept with guppies, to avoid hybrids that threaten the purity of the lines. An omnivore, it eats small invertebrates, detritus and plant matter.

profil.repartition: Coastal plains of Venezuela, the Guianas and northern Brazil, Amazon and Orinoco basins
profil.presentation: The only species in its genus, the X-ray tetra is recognised by the black spot edged with yellow and white on its dorsal fin. Peaceful, hardy and cheap, it is one of the best choices for beginners; there is a semi-albino “golden” form. Fish in the trade are mass-bred.
profil.habitat: In the dry season it lives in clear-water streams and tributaries; with the rains it moves into flooded savannahs, where it spawns among submerged vegetation. It even tolerates slightly brackish water.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful and gregarious, it copes poorly with boisterous or much larger companions. Keep it with small tetras, pencilfish, hatchetfish, Apistogramma, Corydoras and small Loricariidae, or in a community tank with small Rasbora, barbs, livebearers, loaches, anabantoids and Pelvicachromis. Keep it in a shoal. A micropredator: dry food and small live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Paraná (Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina) and Uruguay basins
profil.presentation: The Buenos Aires tetra, named after Professor Anisits of Asunción who collected the first specimens, is one of the hardiest tetras. There is an albino form, sold as “golden”. It devours soft plants.
profil.habitat: It frequents small streams and tributaries more than large rivers, as well as floodplain lakes, oxbows and pools, in a subtropical region with fairly mild winters. In the Iberá marshes (Argentina), it lives alongside many Hyphessobrycon.
profil.comportement: It has a reputation as a fin nipper, especially when too few or cramped. Gregarious, it forms loose hierarchies in which males constantly quarrel: a group of at least 8 to 10 is a minimum. An omnivore: easy to feed, with plant matter and live or frozen prey. It tolerates fairly cool water; use hardy or artificial plants.

profil.repartition: Rio Xingu basin (Pará, Brazil)
profil.presentation:
Long known to hobbyists by the code L025 or the name “scarlet pleco”, this large loricariid was only described in 2016 by Carine Chamon and Leandro Sousa. Its name *pirarara*, “macaw fish” in Tupi, refers to the bright red of its fins, like a macaw's feathers.

It is one of the largest plecos in its genus: it exceeds 40 cm and nearly a kilogram. Its body bristles with small spines (odontodes), like its *Pseudacanthicus* cousins.
profil.habitat:
It is known from the Rio Xingu basin, in the state of Pará, Brazil.

It lives in the rocky stretches of the river, with clear, warm, highly oxygenated water, and shelters in deep crevices and under boulders.
profil.comportement:
Territorial, it vigorously defends its hiding place against other bottom-dwellers, especially plecos, and can injure tankmates with its spines. It tolerates robust midwater fish, but the rule is one fish per tank, except in a very large volume.

Mainly carnivorous and a scavenger, it needs shrimp, mussels, fish and protein-rich food. Its adult size calls for an aquarium of over 1,000 litres, with powerful filtration and water movement.

profil.repartition: Coastal plains of southern Guinea, Sierra Leone and north-western Liberia
profil.presentation:
Described in 1915 by George Albert Boulenger, the clown killifish (or “rocket killifish”) is a small surface killifish of about 4 cm, barred with four broad dark bands alternating with yellow, hence its name *annulatus* (“ringed”). Males have a fan-shaped tail with red and blue rays.

It was placed in its own genus, *Pseudepiplatys*, now abandoned: FishBase puts it in *Epiplatys*, as *Epiplatys annulatus*. It is not an annual killifish.
profil.habitat:
It is widely distributed in the coastal lowlands of southern Guinea, Sierra Leone and north-western Liberia, around Monrovia. Breeders give the locality of origin (Kasewe, Monrovia, Fallaba…) to avoid mixing populations.

It lives in marshes, slow streams and small rivers in savannah and rainforest, among bank vegetation. The water is warm, soft and acidic, sometimes slightly brackish.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful, it is too small and too demanding for a classic community aquarium: keep it with small African tetras or other tiny, calm species. Fairly gregarious, it is less shy in a group of 8 to 10.

It hunts small insects and zooplankton at the surface. It breeds fairly easily: the eggs are laid among fine-leaved plants or floating roots, and fry sometimes appear spontaneously in a well-established tank.

profil.repartition: Río San Miguel basin, western Amazon basin (Ecuador)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1978 by Isaäc Isbrücker and Han Nijssen, *Pseudohemiodon apithanos* is a very flattened loricariid of the subfamily Loricariinae, related to the “twig” whiptail catfish. Its species name comes from the Greek *apithanos*, “improbable”.

It measures up to 14.5 cm without the tail. Its ray-shaped body, beige spotted with brown, blends perfectly with the sand.
profil.habitat:
It is known from the Río San Miguel basin, in the western Amazon basin, in Ecuador.

*Pseudohemiodon* live on river sandbanks, where they partly bury themselves with only their eyes showing, and sift the substrate for small invertebrates.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful and discreet, it spends most of its time buried in the sand: a fine, soft sand substrate is essential, as are calm companions that do not steal its food.

It feeds on small prey (larvae, worms, crustaceans) that it seeks in the sand. Like other Loricariinae, the male carries the eggs stuck under his enlarged lower lip until they hatch.

profil.repartition: Endemic to the lowlands of eastern Papua New Guinea, between Dyke Ackland Bay and Collingwood Bay
profil.presentation: This small yellow blue-eye, with a forked tail edged in bright yellow, is very popular but comes from a small area; wild fish are not available. It was placed in a separate genus, *Popondetta*, before returning to *Pseudomugil*.
profil.habitat: It lives in lowland forest streams, heavily vegetated, with a slow to moderate current and clear water. The December-to-March monsoon swells and clouds the streams; in the dry season they may partly dry out: the type specimens came from pools in intermittent streams, with *Tateurndina ocellicauda*.
profil.comportement: Peaceful, it suits selected community tanks, with fish of similar size and temperament: cyprinids, gobies, small rainbowfish, and especially the peacock gudgeon *Tateurndina ocellicauda*, which lives with it in the wild. In a shoal of at least 8 to 10. Food to match its size, mostly live (Daphnia, Moina, Artemia nauplii, microworms).

profil.repartition: Aru Islands (Indonesia), southern New Guinea and northern Australia
profil.presentation: This tiny spotted blue-eye, with filaments on the male's fins, is named after the wife of the naturalist Hugo Merton. The isolated wild populations vary greatly in colour and shape; all fish in the trade come from a single captive-bred strain.
profil.habitat: It prefers the shallow, heavily vegetated margins of slow or still water: creeks, streams, lakes, billabongs and marshes, among plants, branches and dead leaves. The water is sometimes stained brown and very acidic, sometimes clear, but always with surface vegetation.
profil.comportement: Peaceful but shy, easily dominated at feeding time: keep it alone or with fish of similar size and temperament, and Caridina or Neocaridina shrimp. In a shoal of at least 8 to 10, more if possible. Food to match its size, mostly live (Daphnia, Moina, Artemia nauplii, microworms).

profil.repartition: Endemic to eastern Australia: from Cape York Peninsula (Queensland) to Lake Merimbula (New South Wales), and a few Torres Strait islands
profil.presentation: This is the most widespread blue-eye in Australia, described from around Sydney. Highly variable between populations, with at least 15 recognised geographic forms, it may be split into several species in the future.
profil.habitat: It is found in the sea as well as in fresh water: tidal mangrove creeks, salt marshes, but also clear, cool forest streams, sometimes fast-flowing, and a few acidic blackwaters. The temperature varies from 15 to 28 °C depending on the season and latitude.
profil.comportement: Most forms are peaceful and suit selected community tanks, with cyprinids, gobies, Eleotridae and small rainbowfish of similar size and temperament. In a shoal of at least 8 to 10, more if possible, it is less nervous. Food to match its size, mostly live (Daphnia, Moina, Artemia nauplii), and fine floating dry food.

profil.repartition: Upper Rio Negro and tributaries of the upper Orinoco, including the Inírida and Atabapo (Colombia, Venezuela)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1903 by the French zoologist Jacques Pellegrin, the altum angelfish is the largest of the angelfish: it reaches 18 cm long and nearly 20 cm tall, fins included. Its Latin name *altum* means “tall”.

It is told apart from the common angelfish by a more concave head profile above the mouth, a taller body and more pronounced vertical bands. Almost all specimens sold are wild-caught, as its breeding in captivity remains difficult.
profil.habitat:
It is native to Colombia and Venezuela: the upper Rio Negro and tributaries of the upper Orinoco such as the Inírida and Atabapo, down to Puerto Ayacucho.

It lives in blackwater rivers, extremely soft and acidic (pH 4.8 to 6.2) and very warm (27 to 31 °C), among submerged branches and roots.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful with fish of similar size, it eats anything that fits in its mouth: neons, guppies and small rasboras are prey. It is kept in a group, in a large, tall tank, with large, calm companions.

Wild fish are often hard to feed at first and need live prey. Breeding requires very acidic, soft water; a group of juveniles allows pairs to form. Males develop a small nuchal hump in the breeding season.

profil.repartition: Amazon basin (Peru, Colombia, Brazil), rivers of Amapá, Oyapock (French Guiana) and Essequibo (Guyana)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1823 by the German naturalist Schultze, the angelfish is one of the most famous tropical fish. Its very tall, flattened body, extended by long dorsal and anal fins, lets it slip between the vertical stems and roots of its natural habitat; its dark vertical bands complete the camouflage.

Fish in the trade almost all come from farms in Asia and Eastern Europe, which have produced many varieties (marbled, golden, veil, black). It reaches 15 cm in length and more in height.
profil.habitat:
It is widespread in the Amazon basin in Peru, Colombia and Brazil, along the Ucayali, Solimões and Amazon, as well as in the rivers of Amapá, the Oyapock in French Guiana and the Essequibo in Guyana.

It lives in marshes and flooded areas with dense aquatic and bank vegetation, in clear or silty water; its colour is more intense in clear water. The water is warm (24 to 30 °C), soft and slightly acidic.
profil.comportement:
Generally peaceful, it may quarrel with its own kind and readily eats small fish such as neons. Young fish live in groups; at maturity pairs form and become territorial when breeding.

It feeds on small crustaceans and aquatic invertebrates. The pair spawns on a vertical surface (broad leaf, stone, glass), then carefully guards the eggs and fry. The sexes are hard to tell apart outside spawning.

profil.repartition: Middle and upper Amazon and Orinoco basin (Brazil, Peru, Ecuador, Venezuela)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1854 by Rudolf Kner, the leopard (or “sailfin”) pleco is recognised by its tall, sail-shaped dorsal fin and its brown and cream reticulated pattern. Its name *gibbiceps* means “humped head”, for the crest on top of its head.

It reaches 50 cm and can live for more than 15 years. Like other *Pterygoplichthys*, it can breathe air by gulping it at the surface, which helps it survive in oxygen-poor water.
profil.habitat:
It is widespread in the middle and upper Amazon basin and the Orinoco, in Brazil, Peru, Ecuador and Venezuela.

It lives in slow rivers, floodplain lakes and flooded areas, where it grazes the biofilm on wood and stones. Several *Pterygoplichthys* dig burrows in muddy banks to shelter and spawn in.
profil.comportement:
Nocturnal and peaceful with other species, it becomes territorial towards other large plecos as an adult. Its size calls for a very spacious aquarium and powerful filtration, as it produces a lot of waste.

It feeds mainly on algae and plant matter, supplemented in the aquarium with tablets, vegetables and soft wood to rasp. Breeding in hobby aquariums is exceptional; young fish in the trade come from pond farms.

profil.repartition: Rio Tocantins basin (Brazil)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1991 by the Swiss ichthyologist Claude Weber, *Pterygoplichthys joselimaianus* is the “L001” pleco, the very first fish in the L-number series created in 1988 by the German magazine DATZ to designate unidentified loricariids. It is also called the “gold spot pleco”.

Its dark body is covered with golden dots, and its tall, sail-like dorsal fin recalls that of the leopard pleco. It reaches about 40 cm without the tail.
profil.habitat:
It is endemic to the Rio Tocantins basin, in Brazil.

Like other *Pterygoplichthys*, it frequents calm, warm water (24 to 29 °C), river arms and flooded areas, where it scrapes algae and biofilm from wood and stones; it can supplement its breathing by gulping air.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful towards midwater fish, it is territorial with other large bottom-dwellers. Mainly nocturnal, it hides by day under wood or in caves.

A herbivore and algae grazer, in the aquarium it receives vegetables, plant-based tablets and a little animal food. Its adult size, longevity and heavy waste production call for a large, well-filtered tank.

profil.repartition: Amazon basin (lower, middle and upper reaches): Brazil, Peru; introduced to many countries
profil.presentation: One of the “common plecos” sold very small as algae eaters, although it exceeds 40 cm. Released or escaped from farms, it has become established in many tropical and subtropical regions outside its native range, where it is considered invasive.
profil.habitat: It lives in slow lowland water. It can breathe air, which allows it to tolerate oxygen-poor water.
profil.comportement: Peaceful with other species but territorial towards bottom-dwellers of the same shape, it only suits very large tanks. A heavy waste producer, it needs powerful filtration. A grazer: plant-based sinking food, vegetables (courgette, cucumber), wood to rasp and a little frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Central and southern Sumatra (Indonesia); introduced populations in many countries
profil.presentation:
Described in 1855 by the Dutch physician and ichthyologist Pieter Bleeker, the tiger barb owes its name *tetrazona* (“four bands”) to the four broad black vertical bands across its golden body. The genus *Puntigrus*, created in 2016, combines *Puntius* and *tigris* (“tiger”).

Records from Borneo actually refer to related species. Very widespread in the hobby, it suffers from heavy inbreeding in some farms, and it is among the species subjected to the cruel practice of artificial colouring by injection.
profil.habitat:
The species is thought to be endemic to central and southern Sumatra, with records from the Indragiri, Batang Hari and Musi river basins; the type locality is Lahat, in South Sumatra province. Populations from aquariums have become established in Singapore, Australia, the United States, Colombia and Suriname.

Its exact habitat is not confirmed; its Bornean cousins live in clear-water forest streams over sand and pebbles, between 20 and 26 °C.
profil.comportement:
Lively and boisterous, it is known for nipping other fish's fins, especially if there are too few of them or they are cramped. It forms loose hierarchies in which males constantly provoke each other: a group of at least 8 to 10 keeps these contests within the species.

Avoid it with slow, shy or long-finned fish (guppies, angelfish, gouramis, bettas). An omnivore, it feeds mainly on aquatic invertebrates, supplemented with plant matter. An egg scatterer, it gives no parental care.

profil.repartition: Southern Thailand, Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra, Java and a few islands in the South China Sea (Tioman, Anambas)
profil.presentation: The T-barb, now placed in the genus *Striuntius*, owes its name to the dark pattern on its flanks. It is sometimes sold under the name of the related *B. kuchingensis*, which instead has a row of spots along the lateral line. Several local forms are recognised.
profil.habitat: It lives mainly in clear-water forest streams, often in pools at the foot of waterfalls, over smooth rocks, sand or gravel, with submerged wood, leaf litter and plants (*Cryptocoryne*, *Barclaya*). It has also been found in peat swamps and blackwater streams.
profil.comportement: Fairly boisterous, it can intimidate less robust species with its size and activity, especially at mealtimes. In a large tank, keep it with other robust fish: large Danio and Devario, Barilius, Garra and some loaches. Young fish live in large groups, adult males become more solitary. A foraging omnivore: varied food, live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Sri Lanka: Kelani to Nilwala basins, in the south-western “wet zone”
profil.presentation:
Described in 1929 by the Sri Lankan zoologist Paulus Deraniyagala, the cherry barb takes its species name from a local vernacular name; *Puntius* comes from the Bengali *pungti*, used for small cyprinids. Males in breeding condition turn an intense cherry red.

The IUCN lists the species as vulnerable: its forest habitat has been massively cleared and the most colourful forms may have been overfished. Fish in the trade now almost all come from farms, with albino or “super red” strains.
profil.habitat:
It lives in the “wet zone” of south-western Sri Lanka, which receives 2,000 to 3,000 mm of rain a year and was once covered in lowland rainforest. It has been collected in the Kelani and Nilwala basins and the small streams between them.

It mainly frequents heavily shaded, shallow, slow streams and rivulets over silt covered in dead leaves. Less than 5% of the region's primary forest remains today.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful and undemanding about water quality, it is an excellent beginner's fish, compatible with most small community fish. Gregarious, it is kept in a group of at least 6 to 10; the smaller, slimmer males then compete in colour.

An omnivore, it feeds on detritus, green algae, diatoms, insect larvae and small animals. The female scatters about 200 eggs among the bank vegetation; they hatch in 1 to 2 days, with no parental care.

profil.repartition: Orinoco basin (Venezuela, Colombia): Inírida, Guaviare, Meta, Apure…
profil.presentation:
Described in 1821 by the German naturalist Alexander von Humboldt during his exploration of the Orinoco, the black spot (or “black-shouldered”) piranha has a large black spot behind the gill cover. Its name *cariba* takes up the Venezuelan name for these fish.

Specialists recognise three species of *Pygocentrus*: *P. cariba*, *P. nattereri* and *P. piraya*. Despite their reputation, serious piranha attacks on humans are extremely rare.
profil.habitat:
It is limited to the Orinoco basin, in Colombia and Venezuela, including its large tributaries: Inírida, Guaviare, Meta, Vichada, Casanare, Apure, Guárico.

It is widespread in the lowlands and the Llanos, in channels, oxbows and lagoons, in warm, soft, acidic to neutral water.
profil.comportement:
Young fish live in shoals, adults in loose groups with a hierarchy: keep a single fish or a group of at least 5 to 6, with no other fish, in a very large aquarium. Even when well fed, it regards the fins of fish of its own size as food.

An opportunist, it eats fish, invertebrates, insects, seeds and fruit. Its sharp teeth inflict serious bites: take care during maintenance. Females grow larger and rounder than males.

profil.repartition: Amazon basin, Essequibo, coastal rivers of north-eastern Brazil, Paraná and Uruguay basins
profil.presentation:
Described in 1858 by Rudolf Kner, the red-bellied piranha is named after the Austrian naturalist Johann Natterer, who explored Brazil for eighteen years. *Pygocentrus* means “spiny rump”, for the serrated keel on its belly. Its sharp triangular teeth are replaced in sets, alternately on each side of the jaw.

Its reputation as a man-eater is largely a myth, born notably during Theodore Roosevelt's journey to Brazil in 1913–1914: piranhas that had been starved for weeks in a closed-off river arm devoured a cow before his eyes. It also produces sounds, a kind of barking, with its swim bladder.
profil.habitat:
It occupies much of the Amazon basin, the Essequibo, coastal rivers of north-eastern Brazil and the Guianas, and further south the Paraná and Uruguay basins; the type locality is Cuiabá, in Mato Grosso.

It lives in almost every habitat: large channels, tributaries, oxbows, floodplain lakes and even reservoirs. It breeds twice a year, among the vegetation of flooded banks.
profil.comportement:
Young fish form shoals, mainly to protect themselves from their own predators; adults live in loose groups with a hierarchy. Keep a single fish or a group of 5 or more, in a very large tank, with no other fish.

An opportunist rather than a strict carnivore, it eats fish, invertebrates, insects, seeds and fruit. Large individuals hunt mainly at dawn, late afternoon and night, lying in wait then rushing at their prey. Its bite can be serious: take care during maintenance.

profil.repartition: Mekong, Chao Phraya and Mae Klong basins, and the northern Malay Peninsula
profil.presentation: The red-tailed rasbora, with its thin black line and red caudal peduncle, is one of the most common rasboras and an excellent choice for beginners. A little dull in the shop, it becomes superb once settled and often swims in a tight shoal.
profil.habitat: Very hardy and adaptable, sometimes even in polluted water, it prefers the shallow margins of calm or slow water, often a little murky: pools, ditches, canals, rice paddies, marshes and reservoir banks less than 2 m deep.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, ideal in a well-furnished community tank; undemanding about water, it lives with most popular fish (small cyprinids, tetras, livebearers, rainbowfish, anabantoids, catfish, loaches), provided they are not large enough to eat it. Keep it in a shoal. A micropredator: fine dry food, but not exclusively, with small live or frozen prey every day.

profil.repartition: Southern Thailand, Peninsular Malaysia, Singapore, Sumatra and Borneo
profil.presentation: One of the most common rasboras, ideal for a medium-sized community tank. It looks like *R. jacobsoni*, but lacks dark reticulated scales above its lateral band, whose edges are clearly more irregular than in related species.
profil.habitat: It lives mainly in blackwater streams and rivers of ancient peat swamp forests: brown, very soft and acidic water (pH as low as 3), a bottom of leaves and branches, light filtered by the canopy. These habitats are threatened by rubber and oil palm plantations.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, ideal in a well-furnished community tank; undemanding about water, it lives with most popular fish (small cyprinids, tetras, livebearers, dwarf cichlids, catfish, loaches), or in a biotope with blackwater species from Malaysia and Borneo. Keep it in a shoal. A micropredator: fine dry food and small live or frozen prey every day.

profil.repartition: Katingan and Kahayan river basins, Central Kalimantan (Borneo, Indonesia)
profil.presentation:
Described in 2009 by the Singaporean ichthyologist Tan Heok Hui, this rasbora is named after Patrick Yap. It measures up to 5.7 cm without the tail.

It belongs to the family Danionidae (subfamily Rasborinae). The IUCN lists it as near threatened, because of the rapid decline of Borneo's peat forests.
profil.habitat:
It is known only from the Katingan and Kahayan river basins, in Central Kalimantan. It lives in the shallow, slow swampy areas bordering blackwater streams.

Its habitats are lowland peat forests and degraded heath forests (kerangas), over a mixed bottom of peat and silica sand. The water there is very soft and acidic.
profil.comportement:
Like most rasboras, it is a peaceful midwater fish that lives in a shoal: it is kept in a group of at least ten, with calm species of similar size.

Its needs reflect its habitat: soft, acidic water, dim light, decor of wood and dead leaves. Reference sources do not yet describe its behaviour in detail.

profil.repartition: Chao Phraya and lower Mekong (Laos, Thailand, Cambodia), Peninsular Malaysia, eastern Sumatra and western Borneo
profil.presentation: The scissortail rasbora owes its name to the jerky movement of its black-and-white tail fin at rest, which opens and closes like scissors. An excellent choice for beginners, provided the tank is large enough for this fairly large rasbora. The trade has spread it all over the world.
profil.habitat: Very adaptable, it lives in fast hill streams over boulders, pebbles, sand or gravel, in clear water at pH 6.5 to 7.5, as well as in the slow black waters of peat forests, and in lowland lakes, marshes, canals and ditches.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, ideal in a large community tank; undemanding about water, it lives with most popular fish (cyprinids, tetras, livebearers, rainbowfish, anabantoids, catfish, loaches), bearing in mind its adult size. Keep it in a shoal. It mainly eats insects: dry food, but not exclusively, with live or frozen prey every day.

profil.repartition: Endemic to south-western Sri Lanka: Kalu, Bentota, Gin and Nilwala basins
profil.presentation: This small orange rasbora with a pearly sheen, nicknamed the “pearl of fire”, is uncommon in the trade: little bred commercially, it travels poorly, and Sri Lanka restricts the export of wild fish. It is listed as endangered: almost no forest remains in its range, and the water there is badly degraded.
profil.habitat: It lives in Sri Lanka's “wet zone”, which receives 2,000 to 3,000 mm of rain a year: shallow, cool, clear, calm and heavily shaded forest streams over silt, often rich in dead leaves. There it eats insects that fall into the water and detritus.
profil.comportement: Discreet, it is intimidated or outcompeted at feeding time by larger or boisterous companions. Ideal companions: small cyprinids (Trigonostigma, Boraras, small Rasbora, some Pethia and Puntius) and peaceful loaches such as Pangio. A shoaling fish, at least 6 to 10. Easy to feed, with small live or frozen prey for condition and colour.

profil.repartition: Unknown origin: a form known only in captivity
profil.presentation:
The red whiptail (“red lizard catfish”, sometimes called L010a) is an elongated, twig-shaped catfish of a uniform orange-red. Its origin remains a mystery: it may descend from a wild population, perhaps from Paraguay, or be a selected form or even a hybrid created in captivity.

Lacking a scientific description, it has no species name. All fish sold are captive-bred.
profil.habitat:
No wild population is known for certain, hence the absence of a map. Wild *Rineloricaria* live on sandy and leafy bottoms of South American rivers, often camouflaged on the substrate.

In the aquarium it appreciates a decor of fine sand, dead leaves, branches and caves, with moderate light and soft to moderately hard water, slightly acidic to neutral, not too warm (24 to 29 °C).
profil.comportement:
It is one of the most peaceful catfish: it lives with most calm fish, but is beaten to the food by lively companions. It is only territorial when breeding and does well in a small group.

An omnivore, it eats sinking food, blanched vegetables and frozen prey. It breeds fairly easily in a tube: the male cleans the cave, the female spawns in it, then the male alone guards and fans the eggs, which hatch in 4 to 5 days.

profil.repartition: Atlantic slope of Central America: from the Río Actopan (Veracruz, Mexico) to Belize, Guatemala and western Honduras; introduced populations in the United States, Russia, Australia and Thailand
profil.presentation: This cichlid spotted with blue and green owes its name to the American boxer Jack Dempsey, world heavyweight champion in the 1920s, for its strong features and pugnacious temperament. The electric-blue “EBJD” form is a captive strain arising from a natural mutation, which stays smaller.
profil.habitat: A generalist, it lives mainly in coastal rivers and the slow stretches of lower valleys: marshes with warm, murky water, weed-choked canals and ditches over mud or sand, lakes and ponds.
profil.comportement: It lives with fish too large to be eaten, but a very large tank is needed to keep it with other cichlids. Young fish live together, then become aggressive towards each other at maturity; a pair, once formed, stays together but is hostile towards others of its kind and fish of the same shape. An omnivore with a carnivorous bias: sinking food, larvae, shrimp, with a plant component.

profil.repartition: Southern India: Kerala and Karnataka, in highly fragmented populations (Valapatanam, Chaliyar, Bharatapuzha...)
profil.presentation: The Denison barb, named after a governor of Madras, has become one of the most popular aquarium fish since it arrived in the late 1990s; in India it is nicknamed “Miss Kerala”. Massive collection for the trade has led to it being listed as endangered. FishBase now places it in the genus *Dawkinsia*.
profil.habitat: It lives in the upper reaches of Western Ghats rivers, in pristine, highly oxygenated water, where it gathers in rocky pools lined with dense vegetation. It is said to be most active at dawn and dusk.
profil.comportement: Peaceful, ideal in a well-planned community tank, but it needs space and a good current. A shoaling fish, at least 6 to 10. The related *S. chalakkudiensis*, sometimes sold under its name, is more quarrelsome. An omnivore: worms, insects, crustaceans and plant matter; in the aquarium, live or frozen prey and quality dry food.

profil.repartition: Rio Negro basin (Brazil), Casiquiare and upper Orinoco (Venezuela, Colombia)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1840 by Johann Jakob Heckel, the daemon owes its alarming names (*Satanoperca*, “Satan's perch”, and *daemon*) to its strange appearance, not its temperament. It is a slender “eartheater” that reaches 25 to 30 cm, adorned with two dark spots on the flank and an eyespot at the base of the tail.

The genus *Satanoperca* was long considered a synonym of *Geophagus*, before being reinstated by Sven Kullander in 1986; the eyespot at the top of the tail base sets it apart from other eartheating cichlids.
profil.habitat:
It lives in the Rio Negro basin in Brazil, the Casiquiare canal and the upper Orinoco in Venezuela and Colombia (Uaupés, Atabapo, Guaviare, Inírida, Ventuari, Cinaruco…). Records elsewhere in Amazonia are misidentifications.

It is a fish of black water, very low in minerals and acidic. In the Río Cinaruco it gathers and breeds in floodplain lagoons and lakes, where there is almost no current, over sand, leaves and branches.
profil.comportement:
Outside breeding it is surprisingly peaceful and only hunts very small prey. Gregarious, it lives in loose groups in which a hierarchy forms: keep at least 5 to 8, otherwise the weakest are harassed.

It feeds by taking mouthfuls of sand and sifting out the invertebrates, ejecting the rest through its gills: a fine sand substrate is essential. Breeding in the aquarium remains rare; the pair spawns on a hard surface and guards the young.

profil.repartition: Guiana Shield: eastern Venezuela, Guyana, north-western Suriname and northern Brazil (Roraima)
profil.presentation: This eartheater, whose genus name means “Satan's perch”, is often confused with *S. jurupari*, but is recognised by the clearly visible white spots or vermiculations on the sides of the head. Common in the trade, it is bred in several countries. It broods its eggs in its mouth.
profil.habitat: It lives in main channels, small tributaries and floodplain lakes, usually over sand or mud strewn with dead leaves and submerged branches.
profil.comportement: Outside breeding it is surprisingly peaceful and does not eat fish larger than a few millimetres: it lives with most peaceful species with similar needs, but not with aggressive or territorial bottom-dwellers. An eartheater, it constantly sifts the sand: a fine sand substrate is essential, along with varied sinking food.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Inle and its basin, Shan State (Myanmar)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1918 by Nelson Annandale, the Asian rummy-nose is the only member of the genus *Sawbwa*, from the title borne by the Shan princes. Its Latin name *resplendens* means “resplendent”: the male has a red head and tail tips and flanks with a blue sheen. Its body has no scales.

The IUCN lists it as endangered. The lake lost more than 30% of its area between 1935 and 2000 through silting, eutrophication and agricultural pollution, and non-native predators have been introduced.
profil.habitat:
It lives in Lake Inle, perched at almost 900 m above sea level on the Shan Plateau, and in the surrounding marshes. The lake water is clear and shallow, but muddy and murky at the edges.

The species is found throughout the lake, in clear and peaty water alike, but mainly along vegetated shores, among weed beds and the roots of the Intha people's floating gardens. It forms large groups there; the water is rather hard, alkaline and fairly cool.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful towards other species, it is not ideal in a community aquarium because of its small size and the constant fights between males for dominance. It forms loose groups rather than shoals.

The best answer is to keep more females than males, ideally four to one; the pale olive females are nevertheless rare on sale because exporters prefer the colourful males. It feeds on small invertebrates and zooplankton, and lays its eggs among vegetation or filamentous algae.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Malawi (Malawi, Tanzania), widespread but uncommon
profil.presentation: This electric-blue haplochromine was long imported and described as *Sciaenochromis ahli*, a name still widely used in the literature. There are many forms, all with blue males, differing in fin colour; they should not be mixed, as they hybridise.
profil.habitat: It lives on rocky shores and in the intermediate sandy zones that extend them, where it hunts small fish.
profil.comportement: Not very aggressive but robust, it should not live with mbuna. It suits Nimbochromis venustus, Cyrtocara moorii, Protomelas and Copadichromis, even Aulonocara with care. Avoid fish of the same colour. Several females per male and a single male unless the tank is very large. A predator: varied live, frozen and dry foods, with no need for plant matter; never meat.

profil.repartition: Endemic to the Rio Xingu basin (Pará, Brazil)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1994 by Warren E. Burgess, the sunshine pleco (L014) is a large black loricariid studded with golden-yellow dots, with yellow-edged fins, reaching almost 30 cm. Its Latin name *aureatus* means “golden”.

The IUCN lists it as vulnerable. Like other fish endemic to the Xingu, it is threatened by large-scale river development, in particular the Belo Monte dam, which has profoundly altered the water regime of the Volta Grande since 2016.
profil.habitat:
The species is known only from the Rio Xingu basin, a large clear-water tributary on the right bank of the Amazon, in the state of Pará.

Xingu loricariids live in rocky rapids: clear, warm, highly oxygenated, flowing water, where they shelter in crevices and under rock slabs. In the aquarium, strong water movement and well-oxygenated water are essential.
profil.comportement:
Solitary and fairly territorial towards other plecos, it tolerates most medium-sized midwater fish. Active mainly at dusk and at night, it spends the day hidden in caves.

An omnivore with carnivorous leanings, it needs protein-rich food (shrimp, mussels, tablets for carnivorous plecos) more than plant matter. Its adult size calls for a large tank, and it can live for more than 20 years.

profil.repartition: Central Vietnam (Huong, Thu Bon, Tra Khuc and An Lao basins); reported from the Mekong basin
profil.presentation: This reticulated hillstream loach, stuck to stones like a little disc, was recorded by Diard more than 150 years before it was rediscovered in the early 1990s. Arriving in the trade in the mid-2000s, it soon became popular thanks to its patterns and easy breeding. It is listed as vulnerable.
profil.habitat: It lives in headwaters and fast, shallow, highly oxygenated tributaries, made up of riffles and runs broken by pools or waterfalls, over rock, sand, gravel and boulders, without aquatic plants. The clear water and sunshine let a rich biofilm grow there.
profil.comportement: The most dominant of the hillstream loaches, without being aggressive towards different fish. Keep it with small midwater cyprinids (Tanichthys, Danio, Devario, Rasbora), hillstream gobies (Rhinogobius, Stiphodon) or rheophilic catfish. It needs a strong current, plenty of oxygen and cool water. It grazes algae: algae-based food and small prey.

profil.repartition: Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra and Borneo (Sarawak, West Kalimantan); perhaps extinct in Singapore
profil.presentation: The chocolate gourami, brown barred with golden bands, is by far the best known of its genus of four species. The male broods the eggs in his mouth. Delicate, it suits experienced hobbyists.
profil.habitat: It lives mainly in peat swamps and their blackwater streams, sometimes in clear water: brown water almost free of minerals, with a pH that can drop to 3 or 4, under a canopy so dense that light barely penetrates, over a bottom of branches and leaves. It breathes air at the surface.
profil.comportement: Slow, it is intimidated or outcompeted at feeding time by larger or boisterous companions. Keep it with small, peaceful midwater cyprinids (Trigonostigma, small Rasbora) or Pangio loaches, but not with its cousin *S. selatanensis* (risk of hybridisation). A micropredator, sometimes fussy: small live or frozen prey, dry food being accepted only over time.

profil.repartition: Amazon and Solimões, from the Río Putumayo (Colombia, Peru) to the Tocantins basin (Brazil)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1904 by Jacques Pellegrin, the discus is often called the “king of the aquarium”. Its classification is debated: depending on the authors, the genus *Symphysodon* has two to four species, and *S. aequifasciatus* groups the brown and blue discus, with nine vertical bands of equal intensity (hence *aequifasciatus*).

It is famous for the way it raises its young: during their first days, the fry feed on a mucus secreted by the skin of both parents. Decades of selective breeding have produced a multitude of captive varieties.
profil.habitat:
It lives along the Solimões and the main course of the Amazon, from the Río Putumayo to the Tocantins basin. Introduced populations exist in Guyana and Suriname.

It rarely frequents the main channels and prefers slow tributaries and forest lakes, where it gathers in shoals in deep, sheltered areas, among roots, logs and rocks. The water there is warm (26 to 30 °C), soft and acidic.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful and gregarious, it lives in a group and becomes territorial when breeding. It is sensitive to water quality and stress: a tall, calm tank, very clean water and peaceful companions that tolerate heat (small tetras, Sterba's corydoras, plecos) suit it.

In the wild it feeds on insect larvae, insects and planktonic invertebrates. The pair spawns on a vertical surface and guards the eggs, then the fry, which it feeds with its mucus.

profil.repartition: West and north-east Africa: White Nile, Niger, Volta, Chad and Cross basins
profil.presentation: One of the most popular Synodontis, often sold very young (3 to 8 cm) as the “network Synodontis”, for its reticulated markings, with no mention of its adult size. This network breaks up into simple spots with age. The large dorsal fin with long filaments earns it its name. It sometimes swims upside down.
profil.habitat: It lives over muddy, sometimes rocky bottoms and feeds mainly on insect larvae, but also on algae.
profil.comportement: It should not live with fish small enough to be eaten. Good companions: African tetras (Alestidae), robust West African cichlids, Mormyridae, knifefish, gouramis, large Rasbora and barbs. Slightly territorial with age, especially towards other Synodontis, but much less so than its cousins. An undemanding omnivore, it also rasps plant matter (peas, cucumber).

profil.repartition: Middle Congo basin (Pool Malebo, Kasai, Ubangi): Democratic Republic of the Congo, Republic of the Congo; reported from Cameroon
profil.presentation: The upside-down catfish usually swims on its back. Its belly is darker than its back: reversed countershading that camouflages it in this position, hence its Latin name (“black belly”). It is sometimes confused with *S. contractus*, which has a larger head, mouth and eyes.
profil.habitat: It lives in heavily vegetated areas along the banks, where it feeds mainly at night on insects, crustaceans and plant matter, often grazing upside down under leaves and roots.
profil.comportement: One of the gentlest Synodontis: it lives with most peaceful species, but not with aggressive fish. Ideal companions: African tetras, dwarf cichlids (Pelvicachromis, Anomalochromis) and small Mormyridae. In a group of at least 3 or 4, it gains confidence and shows itself more. An omnivore: live, frozen and dry foods, and plant matter.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Tanganyika (Burundi, DR Congo, Tanzania, Zambia)
profil.presentation: This small black Synodontis with white polka dots and white-edged fins is highly recommended for Tanganyikan cichlid tanks. There is a dwarf form, very adaptable regarding water quality, which can even live in a South American tank.
profil.habitat: It lives among the rocks of the lake.
profil.comportement: It should not live with fish small enough to be eaten, but it complements a tank of hard-water cichlids well, ideally mouthbrooders from the African lakes, or rainbowfish and livebearers of suitable size. Keep it in a group of 4 or more, as a lone fish often stays hidden. An undemanding omnivore: live, frozen and dry foods, and plant matter.

profil.repartition: Río Aguaytía basin, a tributary of the Ucayali, at the foot of the Andes (Peru)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1986 by the Swede Sven Kullander, this cichlid has a genus name taken from *Tawantinsuyu*, the Quechua name for the Inca Empire, hence its English nickname “Inca stonefish”. Its species name, borrowed from a local language, means “stone fish”, referring to the rocky bottoms of its habitat.

It reaches about 12 cm; both sexes have a dark midline band and iridescent markings on the head, and the male takes on orange tones on the face and fins. The IUCN lists it as data deficient.
profil.habitat:
It is known only from the Río Aguaytía basin, a tributary of the Ucayali at the foot of the Peruvian Andes.

It lives in rivers and streams with stony and pebbly bottoms. Measurements indicate very soft water, close to neutral (pH 6.3 to 7.7) and warm (25 to 28 °C).
profil.comportement:
Fairly peaceful for a cichlid, it lives in pairs; it is best to avoid very small tetras or barbs, which may become prey.

Its breeding is unusual: the pair spawns on a movable surface (leaf, thin flat stone) that it moves to keep the eggs safe, then, at hatching, both parents brood the larvae in their mouths. It is a so-called “delayed” mouthbrooder, fairly easy to breed in the aquarium.

profil.repartition: Southern China (Pearl River delta, Hainan Island) and Vietnam; introduced elsewhere
profil.presentation: The White Cloud Mountain minnow, named after the scout leader Tan Kan Fei who first collected it, comes from the “White Cloud Mountain” near Guangzhou, where it has disappeared. It was thought extinct in the wild before a few populations were rediscovered. Very common in aquariums, it comes in long-finned, golden, albino and “super red” forms; inbreeding in farms has weakened many strains.
profil.habitat: One of the rediscovered populations lives in a slow, spring-fed mountain stream, in clear, shallow water with dense aquatic vegetation, alongside the paradise fish. The Hainan population occupies a slow coastal stream over sand, pebbles and dead leaves, less than 60 cm deep. It tolerates water at 5 °C.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, ideal in a community tank provided its need for cool water is respected: rosy and Odessa barbs, golden barb, paradise fish. Despite common practice, it is not a good companion for goldfish. Keep it in a shoal. A micropredator: easy to feed, with small live or frozen prey for condition and colour. It can also live in an outdoor pond in summer.

profil.repartition: Eastern Papua New Guinea
profil.presentation: Despite its name, the peacock gudgeon (or “peacock goby”) is not a true goby but an Eleotridae (“sleeper”): its pelvic fins are not fused into a sucker. It is one of the smallest and most beautiful in its family, with its black eyespot on the tail, and an ideal resident of a planted community tank. It is listed as vulnerable.
profil.habitat: It lives in lowland streams, pools and rivers, mainly in rainforest, where it swims in loose shoals above the bottom.
profil.comportement: Slightly territorial with its own kind, it suits many tanks of small, peaceful fish: ideally other Papuan species such as *Pseudomugil furcatus*, but also tetras, Rasbora, Corydoras. Provide enough space with other territorial species such as dwarf cichlids. It accepts dry food but prefers small live or frozen prey, which brighten its colours.

profil.repartition: Indonesia: southern Sulawesi (formerly Celebes), Bantimurung area
profil.presentation: The Celebes rainbowfish, whose males have yellow fins with black filaments, is now the only species in the genus *Marosatherina*, but is still cited as *Telmatherina* in much of the literature. Overfishing for the hobby has led to it being listed as vulnerable; fortunately it is mass-bred.
profil.habitat: It lives in clear, slow foothill streams and in estuary areas.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful and of modest size, it suits many hard-water community tanks: rainbowfish of similar size, livebearers, freshwater gobies, or even brackish water with mollies and halfbeaks. Fairly timid, it feels much better in a shoal of at least 6 to 8. Easy to feed: varied dry, frozen and live foods for good colours. Plants are needed.

profil.repartition: Upper Amazon in Peru and Rio Araguaia basin in Brazil
profil.presentation:
Described in 1957 by Stanley Weitzman, the penguin tetra is the best known of the *Thayeria*. It owes its nickname to its posture: it holds its body tilted, head up, and a broad black band runs down the flank to the tip of the lower lobe of the tail, like a “tailcoat”.

It measures about 3.5 cm without the tail and can reach 6 cm in total length in the aquarium. The tetra classification revised in 2024 places it in the family Acestrorhamphidae.
profil.habitat:
Its range seems limited to the upper Peruvian Amazon basin and the Rio Araguaia, in Brazil. The Araguaia, which crosses several Brazilian states, receives a multitude of tributaries: the species probably occupies varied habitats there, from wetlands rich in submerged plants to forest streams lined with dense vegetation but poor in aquatic plants.

The waters it frequents are tropical (22 to 28 °C), of low to medium hardness.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful and gregarious, it is a micropredator that hunts insects, worms and small crustaceans. It is kept in a group of at least 6, ideally 10: the fin nipping it is blamed for appears mainly in fish kept in too small numbers, which take out their squabbles on other species.

It breeds fairly easily in a separate, dimly lit tank: the female lays a large number of eggs among fine vegetation, which hatch in 20 to 24 hours. Adult females have a rounder belly and slightly less vivid colours.

profil.repartition: Endemic to French Guiana: Maroni and Approuague basins
profil.presentation:
Described in 1959 by Jacques Géry, *Thayeria ifati* is one of the “penguin” tetras: a black band runs along the flank and then dips into the lower lobe of the tail fin, and the fish swims with its body tilted, head up, like other *Thayeria*.

Records from Brazil and Suriname turned out to be misidentifications. According to the 2024 classification, the genus now belongs to the family Acestrorhamphidae.
profil.habitat:
Endemic to French Guiana, it is known from the Maroni and Approuague basins. It has been collected in varied habitats: rivers, streams, creeks, pools and small lakes.

The bottom is sometimes rich in organic matter, sometimes sandy and rocky, but the species always seeks calm areas: the slow water of creeks and the backwater zones of the main rivers.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful and gregarious, it lives in a group and feeds on small insects, worms and zooplankton. It is kept in a shoal of at least 6, ideally 10: in sufficient numbers, small squabbles stay within the group and it does not nip other fish's fins.

It copes poorly with very boisterous or much larger companions. No breeding in captivity has been documented to date.

profil.repartition: Atlantic slope of Mexico (from the Río Tonalá to Yucatán), northern Belize and Guatemala; naturalised in Hawaii and Puerto Rico
profil.presentation: The firemouth cichlid, named after the ichthyologist Seth Eugene Meek, is recognised by the bright orange-red underside of its head, more pronounced in adults. Facing a rival, it flares its gill covers, marked with a black spot, to look bigger. Almost all fish in the trade are bred for the hobby.
profil.habitat: It lives in very varied lowland habitats, calm or with a moderate current, shallow (under 1.5 m), clear or muddy, fresh or slightly brackish: cenotes, lagoons, pools, ditches, streams, over sand, mud or limestone, with or without plants.
profil.comportement: Not very aggressive, but territorial when breeding, and it may eat much smaller fish. It lives with Central American cichlids of similar size, provided each has its own territory, and with peaceful surface fish such as mollies and swordtails. A foraging omnivore, it sifts the sand: fine substrate and varied sinking food.

profil.repartition: Ganges and Brahmaputra basins (northern India, Bangladesh, Nepal)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1822 by Francis Hamilton, the honey gourami owes its common name to the honey-yellow colouring of displaying males, which then develop a blue-black throat. *Trichogaster* means “hairy belly”, for its pelvic fins transformed into long tactile filaments; *chuna* comes from a local name.

Like all anabantoids, it has a labyrinth, a respiratory organ that lets it use air taken at the surface. Fish in the trade almost all come from farms.
profil.habitat:
It lives in the Ganges, its floodplain and its delta in Bangladesh, as well as in the Brahmaputra system (Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Arunachal Pradesh), with records from Nepal.

It frequents slow, heavily vegetated lowland water: pools, ditches, *beels* (floodplain lakes), flooded fields. These habitats change in volume, chemistry and turbidity with the monsoon, from June to October.
profil.comportement:
Slow and peaceful, it is easily intimidated or outcompeted by livelier companions: small, calm cyprinids and discreet loaches suit it. Without forming a shoal, it enjoys the company of its own kind; in a group of 4 to 6 a hierarchy forms.

In the wild it is said to knock down insects resting on leaves by spitting drops of water at them. The male builds a bubble nest under floating plants and forms a temporary pair with the larger, brownish female.

profil.repartition: Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bangladesh and upper Myanmar
profil.presentation: The banded gourami, the largest in its genus, is eaten in its native range. Beautiful and peaceful, it is nevertheless seldom seen in the trade. Like other anabantoids, it has a labyrinth organ that lets it breathe air at the surface; several colour forms are said to exist depending on locality.
profil.habitat: It lives in slow water, usually covered with floating vegetation: large rivers, estuaries, ditches, pools and lakes. It has been introduced to rice paddies in many regions.
profil.comportement: It suits most peaceful community tanks, but can be a little aggressive when breeding, and males fight in a small tank. Keep it with peaceful species that do not look too much like it: shoals of Rasbora, Danio and barbs, loaches, small Bagridae. Not with the thick-lipped gourami, with which it hybridises. An undemanding omnivore, with live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Southern Myanmar; spread around the world by the aquarium trade
profil.presentation: Despite being easy and peaceful, this thick-lipped gourami is not very popular, although it is imported regularly. There is a golden “sunset” form, selected for the trade, in which the bands are replaced by orange colouring; the female is almost as colourful as the male.
profil.habitat: It lives in slow, shaded rivers and pools, especially in areas rich in floating vegetation. It breathes air at the surface.
profil.comportement: One of the best gouramis for a community tank, far better suited than the dwarf gourami: a group bought young generally lives in peace all its life. It lives with Danio, Rasbora, small barbs, loaches and other peaceful anabantoids, but not with the banded gourami (hybridisation). Undemanding, it loves small live or frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Pakistan, northern India and Bangladesh
profil.presentation:
Described in 1822 by Francis Hamilton, the dwarf gourami has oblique red and turquoise-blue bands in the male; females are silvery. Many captive-bred forms exist (“neon”, “red”, “powder blue”).

All fish in the trade are mass-bred, mainly in Asia. The species is badly affected by an iridovirus (DGIV), a virus widespread in some farms, which explains the fragility of many batches and calls for a serious quarantine.
profil.habitat:
It is widespread in Pakistan, northern India and Bangladesh; records from Nepal and Myanmar are thought to be misidentifications. Feral populations exist in Singapore, the United States and Colombia.

It lives in slow, weed-choked water: pools, marshes, ditches, streams and irrigation canals. Like all gouramis, it supplements its breathing with air taken at the surface.
profil.comportement:
Both shy and territorial, it should be the main fish in a small tank. Males can become very aggressive towards other anabantoids (bettas, gouramis) or brightly coloured fish such as guppies, and hide in the presence of larger species.

Small, peaceful cyprinids (harlequins, rasboras) and discreet loaches are the best companions. An omnivore, it feeds on small invertebrates and algae. The male builds a bubble nest, often mixed with plant debris, and guards the eggs.

profil.repartition: Thailand, Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra and Borneo
profil.presentation:
Described in 1852 by Pieter Bleeker, the pearl gourami is covered in a scattering of pearly dots, hence its name. The adult male develops an orange to bright red throat and dorsal and anal fins extended into filaments.

The IUCN lists it as near threatened: the lowland coastal peat swamps and marshes where it lives are being converted to plantations. Almost all fish in the trade come from farms in Asia and Eastern Europe.
profil.habitat:
It is native to Thailand, Malaysia and the islands of Borneo and Sumatra; introduced populations exist in Singapore and Colombia.

It lives in lowland marshes and streams, often near the coast, among dense vegetation, in acidic water. Like other gouramis, it must breathe air at the surface.
profil.comportement:
It is one of the most peaceful gouramis and an excellent community fish, provided aggressive or overly lively companions, which make it fearful, are avoided. Males are territorial towards each other and can be rough with females before spawning: hiding places are essential.

Undemanding, it accepts most foods. The male builds a large bubble nest, up to 25 cm across, among floating plants, in shallow, calm water.

profil.repartition: Mekong (Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand) and Chao Phraya basins; introduced populations in Singapore and Colombia
profil.presentation: The moonlight gourami, silvery and pearly, is less colourful than other gouramis but very elegant in a community tank. Its thread-like pelvic fins are much longer than in other gouramis. It is eaten in its native range; fish in the trade are bred in the Far East and Eastern Europe.
profil.habitat: It lives in lowland pools, peat swamps and marshes, in shallow, slow or still, heavily vegetated water. It is common on the lower Mekong floodplain and breathes air at the surface.
profil.comportement: Timid, it should live neither with fish small enough to be eaten nor with overly lively species. Ideal companions: other gouramis, Botia, Corydoras, barbs, angelfish and Loricariidae. Males can become territorial towards each other and other gouramis. An omnivore: prepared foods, supplemented with live and frozen prey.

profil.repartition: Mekong basin (southern China, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam), Myanmar, Malaysia and northern Indonesia
profil.presentation:
Described in 1770 by the German naturalist Peter Simon Pallas, the blue gourami is one of the oldest known aquarium fish. Its two black spots on the flank, plus its eye, earn it the English name “three spot gourami”. It reaches 15 cm.

Besides its many captive-bred forms (blue, golden, opaline), it is also a food fish: it is sold fresh in Southeast Asian markets, and salted and dried in Java. It has been introduced to many countries.
profil.habitat:
It lives mainly in the Mekong basin and the plains of Southeast Asia: pools, ditches, marshes, canals and shallow wetlands, still and rich in vegetation.

In the middle and lower Mekong it makes lateral migrations: in the rainy season it leaves the river and permanent water bodies for flooded forests and grasslands, then returns when the water drops. It must breathe air at the surface thanks to its labyrinth.
profil.comportement:
Often presented as a community fish, it is not always one: some individuals become cantankerous with age. Males are territorial and squabble, especially in the breeding season; it is best kept with robust fish (barbs, large tetras, loricariids, loaches, other medium gouramis).

An omnivore, it eats plants, algae, zooplankton, larvae and detritus. The male builds a large bubble nest among floating plants; he may harass an unwilling female, hence the value of offering him two or three.

profil.repartition: Lower Mekong (Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam) and central and southern Thailand
profil.presentation:
Described in 1936 by the German aquarist Johann Paul Arnold, the pygmy croaking gourami (*pumila*, “dwarf”) barely reaches 4 cm. Like its cousins, it produces audible sounds with a mechanism of pectoral fin tendons unique to *Trichopsis*.

It is recognised by its continuous dark lateral band, topped by a row of spots forming a second band, and by its iridescent blue eyes. Most fish sold come from farms.
profil.habitat:
It is widespread in the lower Mekong basin, in Laos, Vietnam, Cambodia and Thailand, as well as in central and southern Thailand; the type locality is Saigon.

It lives in ditches, small pools, peat swamps, rice paddies and canals, usually in still water covered with floating plants, sometimes poor in oxygen, which it compensates for by breathing air at the surface. It lives there alongside the croaking gourami, the three spot gourami and the climbing perch.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful and discreet, it is kept in a pair or small group, alone or with very small, calm species (*Boraras*, harlequins, microrasboras, small loaches). Larger or livelier fish intimidate it and steal its food.

It hunts zooplankton and aquatic insects and may attack young dwarf shrimp. The male builds a bubble nest, often under a leaf; a tight-fitting lid keeps in the warm, humid air the fry need.

profil.repartition: Indochina (lower Mekong, Thailand, Myanmar), Peninsular Malaysia and Singapore; reported from Sumatra, Borneo and Java
profil.presentation:
Described in 1831 by Georges Cuvier from fish from Java, the croaking gourami owes its name to its ability to produce audible sounds, “croaks”, thanks to a mechanism of pectoral fin tendons unique in the family Osphronemidae. *Vittata* means “striped” in Latin.

It is the largest of the *Trichopsis* (up to 8 cm); its filamentous anal fin rays almost reach the tip of the tail. The populations of the Sunda Islands may belong to a separate species.
profil.habitat:
It occurs over much of Indochina (lower Mekong in Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam, Thailand, lower Salween in Myanmar), in Peninsular Malaysia and Singapore. Feral populations exist in the Philippines, India and the United States.
