It occupies all calm lowland habitats: swamp forests, peat swamps, floodplains, irrigation canals, rice paddies and ditches, with a clear preference for still, heavily vegetated water. It must breathe air at the surface.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful except when breeding, it can live in a pair or small group, in which displays and exchanges of “croaks” between males can be observed. It feeds on zooplankton, crustaceans and insect larvae.

The male builds a bubble nest; the eggs, which sink, are picked up by one or both parents and put back in the nest. Soft, slightly warmer water encourages spawning, and a tight-fitting lid protects the fry's air breathing.

profil.repartition: South-western and south-eastern Thailand and south-western Cambodia (Prek Tuk Sap basin)
profil.presentation: Espe's rasbora, or “false harlequin”, looks like *T. heteromorpha* and *T. hengeli*. It differs by its orange body (pinkish in *T. heteromorpha*) and a thinner, hatchet-shaped black patch. Records from Laos are probably misidentifications.
profil.habitat: It lives mainly in the calm stretches of forest streams rich in submerged plants, sometimes in water slightly stained by tannins, soft and neutral to slightly acidic, under dim light. It is also found in heavily vegetated pools and marshes.
profil.comportement: Very peaceful, ideal in a well-kept community tank; undemanding about water, it lives with most popular small fish (small cyprinids, tetras, livebearers, dwarf cichlids, catfish, loaches). Keep it in a shoal. A micropredator: easy to feed, with small live or frozen prey for condition and colour.

profil.repartition: Sumatra (Jambi province) and probably western Borneo (Indonesia)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1956 by Hermann Meinken, Hengel's rasbora is the smallest of the *Trigonostigma*, a genus split from *Rasbora* in 1999. Its black “lambchop” patch is edged with a bright orange glow along the top and front, on an almost colourless greyish body.

This sets it apart from *T. espei*, coppery with a thinner mark, and from the larger *T. heteromorpha*. The type specimens come from the Tambesi River, a tributary of the Batang Hari on Sumatra.
profil.habitat:
Its range is limited to the Greater Sunda Islands: it has been collected in Jambi province on Sumatra, and apparently in West Kalimantan, on Borneo.

It frequents the calm parts of forest streams where beds of *Cryptocoryne* grow, in soft, slightly acidic to neutral water, sometimes stained by tannins, under light filtered by the canopy.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful, it suits a community aquarium of small, quiet fish well. A shoaling fish, it is kept in a group of at least 8 to 10; the slimmer, more colourful males then compete for the females.

A micropredator, it feeds on small insects, worms and zooplankton. Like the harlequin, it sticks its eggs under broad leaves rather than scattering them, with no parental care.

profil.repartition: Malay Peninsula: Malaysia, Singapore, the far south of Thailand, Sunda Islands (Sumatra, Borneo)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1904 by the German ichthyologist Georg Duncker, the harlequin rasbora has a black triangular patch on the rear of its body, which gave its name to the genus *Trigonostigma* (“triangle mark”), split from *Rasbora* by Maurice Kottelat and Kai-Erik Witte in 1999.

A DNA barcoding study (2012) detected two distinct genetic lineages among fish in the trade, suggesting that the current species may include several. Blue, black and golden captive-bred forms exist.
profil.habitat:
Its type locality is Kuala Lumpur. It is found on the Malay Peninsula, notably in the peat swamp forests of Selangor, Kelantan, Terengganu, Pahang and Johor states, in Singapore in the Nee Soon swamp, and in Narathiwat district in Thailand.

It frequents the calm parts of forest streams where dense beds of *Cryptocoryne* grow. The water, soft, slightly acidic and often stained by tannins, is dimly lit under the canopy; in peat swamps it forms shoals of more than a hundred fish.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful, it is an ideal choice for beginners and for a community aquarium of small fish, including shy anabantoids. A shoaling fish, it is kept in a group of at least 8 to 10.

A micropredator, it feeds on small insects, worms and zooplankton. Its spawning is unusual: the pair turns upside down under a broad leaf and sticks its eggs there, with no parental care. In the male, the black triangle is sharper and its front edge reaches down to the belly.

profil.repartition: Endemic to Lake Tanganyika (Burundi, DR Congo, Tanzania, Zambia)
profil.presentation: Despite its popularity, this grazing cichlid, with countless colour forms depending on the locality, is a puzzle in the hobby and not suited to beginners: the best way to keep it is still debated. Females brood the eggs in their mouths. It is listed as near threatened.
profil.habitat: It lives in shallow water along rocky shores, where it grazes algae from the rocks. Adults are solitary.
profil.comportement: Its reputation for aggression is exaggerated: it is fairly peaceful with other species but quarrels with its own kind, hence a large tank and many females per male. Very active, it should not live with shy species; it goes with Julidochromis, Eretmodus or Tanganicodus. Plant matter (spirulina, spinach, nori) should form the basis of its diet; never meat.

profil.repartition: Amazon basin (Brazil, Peru)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1950 by the German ichthyologist Werner Ladiges, this small blue tetra barely exceeds 2 cm without the tail. Like *Tyttocharax tambopatensis*, it belongs to the subfamily Xenurobryconinae, placed since the 2024 revision in the family Stevardiidae.

The species remains little studied: reference sources mainly give its size and general range, without a detailed description of its biology.
profil.habitat:
FishBase places it in the Amazon basin, with known populations in Brazil and Peru. Like other members of its genus, it is associated with small, slow-flowing forest streams.

In the absence of published measurements of its habitats, the parameter ranges in this profile rely on aquarium recommendations for the genus: soft, slightly acidic water, between 23 and 26 °C.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful and gregarious, it lives in a shoal and should be kept in a group of at least ten. Its small size makes it vulnerable to larger or boisterous companions.

It feeds on small prey (zooplankton, larvae): in the aquarium, very fine live or frozen foods suit it better than flakes.

profil.repartition: Manu and Tambopata river basins, Peruvian Amazon (Madre de Dios)
profil.presentation:
Described in 1995 by Stanley Weitzman and Hernán Ortega, this tetra is named after the Tambopata River, in south-eastern Peru. With a maximum length of about 1.6 cm without the tail, it is one of the smallest known characiforms.

The genus *Tyttocharax* belongs to the subfamily Xenurobryconinae; the revision of tetra classification published in 2024 places this group in the family Stevardiidae, separate from the Characidae.
profil.habitat:
It inhabits small blackwater streams running through *Mauritia flexuosa* palm swamps (aguajales) in the Peruvian Amazon. It is found mainly in pools and calm areas of streams 2 to 4 m wide lined with gallery forest, 20 to 60 cm deep.

The current there is weak, the bottom sandy or stony, cluttered with plant debris. It stays near the banks, where vegetation provides shelter from predators.
profil.comportement:
A shoaling fish, it swims near the surface in groups of 20 to 80 in the wild. Its very small size means it should be kept in a species tank or one shared with tiny, peaceful species, with very fine live food.

It remains rare in the trade and poorly documented in the aquarium; keeping it in a large group, in soft, acidic water, best reproduces its natural conditions.

profil.repartition: Amazon basin: middle and lower Rio Negro, and Solimões–Amazon from the Japurá to the Tapajós
profil.presentation: This large South American cichlid is surprisingly peaceful for its size. It needs clean, well-filtered and rather warm water. In the wild it eats a lot of plant matter, invertebrates and even freshwater sponges; trials in captivity show it to be mainly herbivorous.
profil.habitat: It lives in clear-water tributaries, often near submerged branches or roots, at a pH of around 6.8.
profil.comportement: It can live with smaller fish such as tetras. Ideal companions: angelfish (*P. altum* and *P. scalare*), severums, eartheaters, Satanoperca and large characins (Anostomidae, Prochilodus, Metynnis), which must tolerate warm water. Avoid overly aggressive fish. It does well in a pair or group. Plenty of plant matter, with worms, crustaceans and insects.

profil.repartition: Western Mexico
profil.presentation: This livebearer of the family Goodeidae, with an orange-red tail and a bluish back in the male, is incredibly hardy and adaptable, but less popular than it used to be, probably because of its often aggressive temperament. It is listed as endangered in the wild. Males and females differ less in size than in other livebearers.
profil.habitat: It lives in very varied habitats, from clear mountain streams to polluted roadside ditches.
profil.comportement: Unpredictable: some individuals do well in a community tank, others nip fins, or even attack and kill other species. It seems to target catfish in particular, such as Corydoras, tearing their fins and eating their eyes. It is best kept in a species tank. Undemanding, it accepts most foods, with a plant component.

profil.repartition: South-eastern Mexico, Guatemala, southern Belize and north-western Honduras
profil.presentation:
Described in 1848 by the Austrian ichthyologist Johann Jakob Heckel, the swordtail is named after the Austrian botanist Karl Bartholomaeus Heller, who explored Mexico from 1845 to 1848 and brought back the first specimens; the name is spelled with two i's, *hellerii*. The male is recognised by the “sword” extending the lower lobe of its tail fin.

It is one of the best-known aquarium fish in the world, available in a host of varieties, some resulting from hybridisation with the platy. Like the platy, it is a model in genetics and cancer research.
profil.habitat:
Its natural range runs from the Río Nautla, in Veracruz state, to the Usumacinta basin in Guatemala, the Río Sarstún on the Belize border and the Copán and Chamelecón rivers in Honduras; the type locality is Orizaba. It has been introduced to every continent except Antarctica, often to the detriment of local species.

It lives from sea level up to 1,500 m: rocky torrents, springs, ditches, pools and clear or murky rivers, often without plants. Adults stay in the current, young fish in the calm margins.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful with other species, it is livelier and larger than the platy. In a confined space, males establish a hierarchy and spend much time defending their rank: a fairly long tank and several females per male limit tensions.

A generalist omnivore, it eats aquatic and terrestrial invertebrates, detritus, algae and plant matter. A livebearer, it breeds easily; females choose males partly by the length of their sword, a classic example of sexual selection.

profil.repartition: Atlantic slope of Central America, from Veracruz (Mexico) to Guatemala, Belize and Honduras
profil.presentation:
Described in 1866 by Albert Günther of the British Museum, the platy owes its name *maculatus* (“spotted”) to the dark spots of the wild form. *Xiphophorus* means “sword bearer” in Greek, for the pointed gonopodium of males, their anal fin transformed into a copulatory organ.

Together with its cousin the swordtail, it has been a model in cancer research since the 1920s: some hybrids between these two species develop melanomas, which made it possible to identify genes involved in the disease. The countless aquarium varieties (red, “mickey mouse”, wagtail…) often come from these crosses.
profil.habitat:
It is native to the Atlantic coastal plain of Mexico (from Veracruz), Guatemala, Belize and northern Honduras. It has been introduced to many countries, where it has sometimes harmed local species.

It lives in warm springs, canals, ditches, creeks and slow-flowing marshes, over silt and with vegetated banks, in hard, alkaline water.
profil.comportement:
Very peaceful, it suits most community aquariums; even males tolerate each other. They relentlessly chase the females: several females per male are recommended.

An omnivore, it feeds on worms, crustaceans, insects and plant matter, and readily grazes algae. A livebearer, it matures in 3 to 4 months and breeds without any intervention: broods are born continuously in a mixed tank.

profil.repartition: Endemic to the Atlantic slope of Mexico, from southern Tamaulipas to northern Veracruz
profil.presentation:
Described in 1904 by the American ichthyologist Seth Eugene Meek, the variatus platy owes its name to the Latin *varius*, “variegated”, for its highly variable colours. Like other *Xiphophorus*, it is used in genetic research.

Fish in the trade almost all come from farms in Asia and Eastern Europe. Introduced populations have become established in Costa Rica, Colombia, the United States, Hawaii, Singapore and Hong Kong.
profil.habitat:
It is native to Mexico, between southern Tamaulipas and northern Veracruz state, on the Atlantic slope.

It lives in warm springs, shallow streams, pools, marshes, canals and heavily vegetated ditches, often rich in algae and phytoplankton. Its subtropical climate means it prefers slightly cooler water than most livebearers (20 to 26 °C), hard and alkaline.
profil.comportement:
Peaceful and hardy, it is a good community aquarium fish. As with the platy, males relentlessly chase the females: several females per male and densely planted areas are recommended.

An undemanding omnivore, it eats worms, crustaceans, insects, detritus and plant matter. A livebearer, after 4 to 7 weeks of gestation it gives birth to broods that can exceed 100 fry; adults eat few of them.

profil.repartition: Middle and lower Mekong (Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam), Chao Phraya and Mae Klong
profil.presentation: This blue-grey botia with orange or red fins is one of the most common botiids. It is sometimes artificially dyed bright blue or purple: these fish should not be bought, and they are banned in several countries for welfare and health reasons.
profil.habitat: Common within its range, it prefers flowing water, where it hides by day among rocks and roots and comes out at night to look for food, often over mud. A great migrant, it travels up tributaries and streams to spawn and frequents flooded areas depending on the season.
profil.comportement: Gentler than *Y. eos* or *Y. morleti*, it nevertheless goes through aggressive phases and may nip long fins: keep it with active midwater cyprinids (Devario, Rasbora, Barilius) and other Botia, in a group. Mostly carnivorous (snails, insects, worms), it also eats soft plants: sinking food and live or frozen prey.
